entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Dispensational privileges of the Gentiles. The apostle recurs to a subject already treated in ,. few words" in the :first ch~pter-words_ which he reques~~ thorn w read, that they may folly understand his meamng-respectu:~g the new _pos1t10~ of the Gentiles in the kingdom of God. Their position was determmed by a d1spensat1on, that is, by an arrangement organized in all its parts in ~elation to space and time; for God works by order in grace as well as in nature. Consider- !. THE ORIGIN OF THIS DISPENSATION. "The grace of God given to me to you-ward." It was an act of Divine favour to seleot the apostle as the person through whom "the mystery" of the dispensation was to be, not only revealed, but applied in _its redeemiug effects to the Ephebian heathens. It was ~ot the honou~ ?r tbe autho~1ty involved in it that made it precious in his eyes; 1t was the pnv1lege of mak1~g known the unsearchable riches of Christ. Thus, as a good steward of the mystenes of God, it was the delight of his life to dispense them in all their gracious manifoldness to the family of God. lL 'fHE MYSTERY THAT SHROUDED THE DISPENSATION FOB AGES, 1. It U called, "the mystery of Christ," not because "8 i., it11 Author, but because 116_ iB t"8 Centre or Subject of it; for it included far more than the truth that the Gentiles were fellow- OH, DL 1-21.] THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. 113

citizens of the saints. Christ is the Mystery or godliness, as he is God manifest in the flesh, but he is emphatically so as " Christ the Hope of glory" for the Gentiles (Col. i. 27). 2. It was hidden fur ages from the sons of men, both Jew and Gentile. A mystery is either something which bas been concealed, perhaps for ages, anrl which probably would never have been discovered unless the voice of revelation bad proclaimed it; or something which, even when revealed, transcends the power of the human faculties to comprehend it. Now, the Incarnation is a mystery in this double sense; but the call of the Gentiles, as part of "the mystery of Christ," is a mystery ohly in the first-named sense. It was known to the Jews for ages that the Gentiles would share in the blessings of the Messiah's kingdom-and the Apostle Paul quotes Old Testament predictions to prove the fact (Rom. ix. 25-33) ; but it was not known that the Gentiles would be included within the circle of religious privilege by the complete sacrifice of the Hebrew theocracy and the reconstitution of religion on a perfectly new basis, designed equally for all mankind, under which the old di.,tinctions of Jew and Gentile would be done away. There was to be no further room for Jewish particularism. The dispensation which was to carry the world to its last destinies was to be as universal as that embodied in the first promise made to our first parents. 3. The revelation of the mystery. So far as it involved a mission to the Gentiles, it was revealed first to the Apostle Panl at his conversion; for when Christ appeared to him on his journey to Damascus, he said, "I have appeared unto thee for this purpose, to make thee a minister and a witness . . . delivering thee from the people, and from the Gentiles, unto whom now I send thee, to open th_eir eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Sa.tan unto God" (Acts xxvi. 16-18). But tbo fuller exhibition of Gentile privilege is made in this glorious Epistle as well as elsewhere. It was a revelation made by the Lord himself (Gal. i. 12). But it was madE.' especially to "apostles and prophets," both of them belonging to the new dispensation-the only class of inspired men connected with it who received special infonnation from the Holy Spirit, who searches the deep things of God, respecting the new development of the kingdom. The revelation was, indeed, oue of facts as well as of truths. The calling of the Gentiles was made manifest in the Spirit's falling upon Cornelius, and in the widespread success of the gospel among the Gentiles, so that the logic of facts beautifully reinforced the more formal revelations of "apostles and prophets." 4. The substance of the revelation. "That the Gentiles are fellow-heirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ by the gospel." These are the three points of Gentile privilege. 'fhey were not to receive the blessings of the Messiab's kingdom by being merged as proselytes into the old theocracy, which waf to abide in all itB narrow ritualism. (1) The Gentiles are fellow-heirs. Possession by inheritance involves the ideas of right, certainty, and inalienablen~ss. All that is involved in the benefits of the covenant of grace is our inheritance. Now, the Gentiles are" heirs of God and joint-heirs with Christ" as well as the Jews, just because they are" children of God by faith in Christ Jesus." They cannot be heirs unless they are children; they cannot be children unless they have faith. And because they have faith, they are Abraham's seed. "And if ye be Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise" (Gal. iii. 29). The Gentile interest in the inheritance may be recent, but it is entire and beyond cavil. Jews and Gentiles have an equal share in all the blessings of the inheritance. (2) The Gentiles are of the same body. This marks e. more intimate relationship. They were all Jews and Gentiles alike, baptized into one body by one Spirit, and thus coalesced into one Church-state, with Christ e.s the Head of both. But while they were thus, as members of one body, partakers of a common life, the Gentile was not there by the permission of the Jew, or the Jew by the permission of the Gentile. They; were both equally baptized into it by the Spirit. The union in one body obliterntes all previous dis- tinctions of character or culture, and all varieties in dispensatioual privilege ; for there is no schism in the body. The Judaistic section of the Church in the apostle's day fought strenuously against the doctrine of the one body. (3) The Gentiles arefellow- partakers of tlie promise. This refers, not so much to the promise of redemption made first to Adam, repeated to Abraham, and embodied in many Old Testament predictions, as to the promise of the Spirit, who enables us to realize all the blessings involved in EPHESIANS, l 114 THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. OB. m.1-21.

this first prt,mise. This was, indeed, the ble..~ing of Abraham whiah came upon the Gentile,, (Gal. iii. H). It was conspicuously realized when, in the words of the Apustle Peter, '' the Holy Ghost fell upon them as on us.." There is no promise of the new c..weuant that is not equnlly sure to Gentile and to Jew. .All the three points of Gentile privilege, sett.i.ng forth apparently the relation to Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, nnd ropresent~d in a. sort of spiritual climax, are rea.liEed by union with Christ, made kno'IVIl to us m the gospel. Salvation centres, a.sits objective ground, in Christ Jesus, and the gospel is the medium by which it is subjectively applied to sinners ot mankind.-'l'. C.

entries.title: EPH 3:8
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-The apost'le's high privilege. Very often does he refer, with·a sori of grateful humility, to the Divine favour in attaching him to the senice of the gospel . . J. MARK THE OONTRAST BETWEEN HIS CALL AND HIS SENSE OF PERSONAL NOTHINGNESS. "Less than the least of a.11 saints." The expression is exceedingly emphatic, being a comparative formed upon a superlative. But he was likewise conscious of his own weakness and sinfulness, as we know by the very forcible phrase, "of sinners I am chief," v.hich he uses as a 1:iresently believing man. l:iuch language of selfabasement i;; a mark of true saint.ship. The highest saints are usually the most distinguished. by their humility. The term by which he desci:ibes himself illlplies thi,t.t there a.re s.unts in Christ's kingdom-little, less, least; not that there is any dilfei:ence in their title, but a difference at once in their realization of their own unworthiness and in tbe degree of their conformity to him who was ·at once "meek al)d lowly." Now, while the consciousness of his own unworthiness stood out in mal"ked cont{ast to the high function to which he wa.~ ea.lied in God's grace, he does not shrink from asserting his authority as an ambassador of Christ iu the strongest terms, but always with the conviction of one who ascribes all his success, not to his own merits, but to "the gift of the grace of God." His call to the apostleship involved his conven,ion, and his conversion was "by the effectual working of God's power.I' II. CoNSIDER ms MESSAGE TO THE GENTILES. "The -unsearchable riches of Christ." We read of riches of grace and riches of glory, but the plenitude of all Divine blessings is in him. l. The apostle does not specify what is included in the '·' riches of Christ." He who was rich for our sakes became poor that" ye through his poverty might be made rich " (2 Cor. viii. 9). We s,ee the source of all the riche~it is in himself. But Scripture shows that, while in him there was all the fulness of the Godhead bodily, with the real design of his filling us eventually with all the fulness of God, "the riches of Christ" are scattered over the whole path of. a believer, from its starting-point in conversion till it is lost in the glories of the eternal inheritance.· He is rich in love, rich in compassion, rich in mercy, rich in grace, rich in peace,:rich in promise, rich in reward, rich in all the blessings of the new and better covenant, as ho must be because he is "made unto us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, redemption.." 2. Tlt1J richea of Christ are "'llln8eOIT'cluible." The word suggests the idea of the difficulty of tracing footsteps. Who Clln trace the .footsteps of God? Whatever of power is infinite power· whatever of wisdom is infinite wisdom; whatever of love is in.finite love. (1) We ~nnot traco the extent of the "riches of Christ." We may apply a double st;andard of measurement, taking account of t~e infinite _altitude of ~he sources whence his salvation has flowed, and of the depths of sm and misery to which salvation had to descend in order to reach its objects. Yet we have not searched out· the riches of Christ. He put forth upon our salvation all the invention of his omniscient wisdom, applied to it the utmost energies of his omnipotent power, and lavished upon it the exceeding riches of his infinite good?ess-neithe~ mercy_ conflicting wit~ justice, nor love with righteousness, nor compassion for the smner wit? ~a.tred of ?1s sins. (2) The riches of Christ are unsearcha\:>le so far they are undimm1shed with use or time. Who can trace the limits of their application? Millions have drunk of the "water of the wells of salvation," but these wells are still unexhausted and inex.haUBtible. The rivers of the earth may fail; there may bll dry wastes where now there are running streams ; but the riches of Christ can never fail, though thousands of nec-iy souls have drawn from them and twice ten thousand more will yet come to OH, III, 1-21.] THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. 115

draw. The fountain of supply is full as it is free, and free as it is full. 3. 007lsider his larger message to the whole world of man. "And to make all men see the dispensation of the mystery, which from the beginning of the world bath been hid in God." 'l'ho apostle's object was to enlighten the Jew as well a.s the Gentile upon the true nature of the dispensation which displaced so much that was dear to the Jewish heart in order that the true glory of the Lord might shine forth, not as a. mere minister of the circumcision, but as the uniter of Jew and Gentile, bond and free, male and female, in his own body. The mystery was hid for ages, but was now ma.de known by apostles and prophets. We see how revelation was an historical movement, subject to the usual laws of historical development; for the redemptive purpose, "hid for ages," was evolved by a gradual process of growth, till in Christianity it became a full-grown fact. It was pa.rt of the discipline of man to go through all these stages of imperfect knowledge till "the perfect day" dawned upon the world. Bot it was through all the ages " the mystery of redemption," going back to the ages that date from creation- " creation building the platform on. which the strange mystery of redemption was al.isclosed."-'l'. C.

entries.title: EPH 3:10
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
--The Church the means of angelic enlightenment. The Divine purpose in. the dispensation already described was to make known to the angels the manifold wisdom of God. I. THE ANGELS BEOEIVE INSTRUCTION THROUGH THE CHtJRcH. This implies: 1. That the angels are not omniscient, for they have something still to learn. 2. That the angels a.re in. co=unication with the Church on earth as well as in heaven. They rejoice over the conversion of sinners; they minister to those who shall be heirs of salvation (Heb. i. 14); they stand in immediate relation to the individual man (Matt. xviil. 10; Luke xv. 10; xvi. 22). The apostles regard themselves as " specto.cles to angels" as well as men, in the insults heaped ll.pon them by an ungrateful world (1 Cor. iv. 9). The Apostle Peter was liberated from prison by an IIIlgel. Angels a.re present in the assembly of the saint.s (1 Cor. xi. 10). They are associated with the redeemed in. heaven (Heb. xii. 22), so as to derive much information concerning the kingdom of God. 3. The angels desire increased knowledge of the ways of God with man. This might be inferred from the fact that. they come specially into the foreground at great turning-points in. the history of the kingdom of God, such as the founding of the old and new covenants, and the humiliation and exaltation of Christ. But they a.re expressly represented as desiring "to look into" the great realities of redemption (1 Pet. i. 12), and here they are instructed in. the manifold wisdom of God by means of the Church. II. THE INSTRUCTION CONVEYED BY THE CHURCH IS "THE GREATLY DIVERSD'IED WIBDO)[ OF, Goo." It is a curious fact that tbe interest of the angels is not in the power or the goodness of God, but in. bis wisdom, as if to imply that the work of redemption represents the highest order of intelligence. It is also a high honour to man that he should first receive the knowledge which the angels are to receive through man. But the angels, by their great age-for they may be thousands of years oldhave advantages that short-lived man does not possess ,for comparing the wisdom o( God as manifest in widely distant ages. But the wisdom here referred to centres in the Church-the spiritual body constituted in Christ, and its variety is manifest in. the original plan of salvation, in the selection of a Redeemer, in the incarnation, in. the atonement, in the application of salvation to Gentile and Jew, in. the spread of the Greek language, in the triumph of the Homan law, and in. all the dispensa- tions by which the Church has been. led on.ward to her final destiny. Thus our earth, though a mere speck in. space, becomes, in the eyes of angels, the brightest of stars; for it is the platform of that Church which mirrors forth "the manifold wisdom of God." III. IT IS THE CHURCH WHICH IS THE MEDIUM OF ANGELIC INSTRUCTION. Not specifi- cally the preaching of apostles, nor human preaching, but the Church as the exhibition in its long and checkered history of the wisdom of God. IV. THIS EXHIBITION OF THE MANIFOLD WISDOM WAS INVOLVED IN THE ORIGINAL PLAN 0l!' SALVATION. "According to the eternal purpose which he purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord." The scheme was fixed in the counsel of peace; it was executed in all its l'art.s iu and through Jesus Uhrist, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom 116 THE EPISTLE TO THE EPBESIA1TS. [OB. m. 1-21,

ll.lld knowle<lge; ll.lld it found historical realization in the progress and kingdom of God, a.pa.rt from all dispensational limitations.-'!'. C.

entries.title: EPH 3:12
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -The mw spirit of approach to God. As the effect of the work of redemp- t-ion, we stand tn a new relation to God, which entitles us to a continuous access to him, free, unrestricted, and confiding. ~- WE ~AVE BOLDNE~ AND .-'-CCE8:1 ~ Goo. There ~s an open, intrepid speaking which sprmgs from a mmd confident in itself and strong ln the justice of the cause it espouses; but the freedom of speech here referred to is based upon a true appreciation of our relation to Christ and the security enjoyed by the believer in the midst of all bis tremors and dubieties. Our God is indeed a consuming fire, yet the believer can approach him without servile fear, simply because Christ is the way of access, and the bes.rt bas been sprinkled from an evil conscience through his blood. II. IT IS IN CHRIST WE HAVE THIS CHANGED DISPOSITION IN PRAYER. He died that we might have "boldness to enter into the holiest." We see in his atonement, not a means of deliverance out of the hands of God, but the strongest of all reasons for casting onrsel,es into the hands of God as the very best Friend we have in all the universe. Our security from the wrath of God is in the bosom of God. It is Jesus who gi.,es us andience with God, dispelling at the same time from the mind of the worshipper those suggestions which would restrict or narrow the riches of God's love. Ill IT IS BY FAITH IN ClJmIST WE REACH THIS NEW TEMPER OF BOLDNESS. It is by the faith of which Christ is both the Object and the Author, discovering to us the dignity of his person, the efficacy of his work, the security of his love, that we are enabled joyfully to approach God. It is thns we have confidence in our approaches to God. Christ's sacrifice, as it he.s given infinite satisfaction to God, is fitted to inspire the soul of the believer with perfect confidence. He sees that nothing more is needed to ensure his everlasting acceptance, and is thus led to tread with boldness the entrance into the sanctuary of God's presence. He has peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. He has confidence in regard to his interest in God's love, in reg~rd to the power and faithfulness of God to fulfil his promises, and in regard to the continuousness of the supply of grace necessary to his final salvation. IV. TJIE EFFECTS OF THIS BOLDNESS AND ACCESS TO Goo ABE TO MAKE UB SUPERIOR TO ALL THE AFFLICTIONS OF LIFE. The apostle beseeches the Ephesians, on this ground, not to lose heart on account of the afflictions that had come to himself on their account. The cynical philosopher represents most men as easily reconciled to the misfortunes of their friends, but Christianity not only enjoins but sustains a nobler t.emper. So close was the relationship that existed between the apostle and the saints at Ephe.sn.s, that his afflictions had fallen upon them like almost the reality of a personal experience. They were not to be discouraged by his tribulations, which were, after all, the price paid {or his uncompromising assertion of their rights as Gentiles. -T.C.

entries.title: EPH 3:15
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-" The family in MafJt:n and in earth." The prayer of the apostle, which includes a reference to the whole family interest of the universe under the blessed Father, is one of the most fervent, comprehensive, and sublime to be found in al. Scripture. Let us consider the force and beauty of the expression, "the family in heaven and in earth." The primary reference is to the Church of God, but it likewisb includes the angels, who merge with the saints into one family; for " all they are brethren." The Church is the family of God in many respects. I. IT I8 so IN THE TIE THAT BINDS ALL TIIE MEMBERS TOGETHER. A family has its constitution in nature, not in similarity of opinion, or interest, or taste. We cannot choose who shall be our brothers or sisters. There are relationships in human life into which we can enter or not enter at will, such as political associations, literary fellowships, social bonds of various kinds. The family is not of this character. Now, the Church is a family unlike these merely voluntary associations, for it is founded by Goo. himself, in which we have our place by his own adopting grace, and once we arc there, our relations to everything internal and external are determined, not by ourselrns, but by the laws of family life. We become" children of God by faith in Christ Jesu,;" (G-.J. iii. 26). There may be members in this family who may not recognize oa. m. 1-21.] THE EPIS'l'LE TO THE EPHESIANS. 117

us as fellow-members at all, but we are members notwithstanding, by ties which they have done nothing to creato and which they cannot undo by their exclusiveness or their bigotry. Yet all the members are really bound to each other by the tie of a commou life, for they live by faith in Obrist Jesus, and of a common ·love; for faith worketh by love, and never works without it. Jesus says," Love one another, as I have loved you." That is, we are to Jove with a love practical, humble, bountiful, patient, gentle, all-embracing, and lasting as Christ's own love. II. THE CHURCH IS A FAMILY BY ITS UNITY. There is but one Father in the Divine family, who unites in himself the perfection of fatherly and motherly affection. There is but one Church on earth," one body," as there is but one faith, one baptism, one hope. Wherever there is union with Chlist, there is membership in his body the Church. The indwelling of the Holy Spirit is the bond of unity in the Church. It follows, therefore, that believers must be one in faith, love, and obedience. Ill Tim ClWBCH AB A FAMILY ADMITS OF GREAT DIVEBBITIES. TherE: are grea.t diversities of affection, of temperament, of character, in the same family, contributing, indeed, to the fulness and happiness of its life. The completeness of the family depends, indeetl, on the beautiful fusion of its masculine and feminine elements. Now, the Church similarly, though one, exists under great diversities of form and condition. There are, first, the two great divisions of the Church into the heavenly and the earthly membership. It is a mistake to say, as some do, that the Church consists only of living saints, as if the dead ceased to be in its unity. God does not set members in the body that they may die out of it again ; he is the God, not of the dead, but of the living; and if such members are not in the body, they are without a Head, that is, without Jesus Christ, who is the only Head of the body. Can" the whole body" grow to the measure of the stature of a perfect man without including the growth of the entire Church of God? Then, again, there are the diversities of dispensations. Believers of every age, no matter under what dispensation they lived, are members of the Divine family. The way of salvation was always the same (Rom. iv.). The one Lamb of God who took away the sin of man was "slain from the foundation of the world" (Rev. viii. 8). The variety of dispensations marks the onward stages of the family life. Then, again, there are the diversities of opinion which have existed within the Church of God without destroying its unity; and endless diversities of character and temperament, all governed more or less by the subduing grace of God; and the dive1sities of lot, service, and event, illustrated in the career of the members of this family. IV. THE CHURCH 1B A FAMILY WITH A FINAL GATHERING AND A HOME FOR ALL rrs BEPABATED llDlUIEBS. There is a house of" many mansions," which our Saviou.. has gone before to prepare (John :xiv. 2)-" the holy places made without hands;" the grand metropolis of God's moral rule," whither the tribes go up, the tribes of the Lord," from every realm of earth, from every age of time. '!'here angels will minglo with saints, and interchange experiences of the love of God. 'l'he fatherhood of God is thus seen to connect different orders of beings by a new and loving tie. Happy family, whose names are written in heaven I Happy family, whose ranks are unbroken, whose hearts are one I Gathered home at last, to be for ever with th& Lord, and for ever with one anotherl-T. C.

entries.title: EPH 3:16
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-..d prayer fqr apiritt.uJl alrength. Thie beautiful supplication suggests aeveral interesting points. I. IT IS A PRAYER FOR THE SAINTS. It is not for their conversion, but that they might have life still more abundantly. The apostle's desire was to make men emintnt Christians, to quicken them in the heavenly race, to promote in them a growth in grace and knowledge which would contribute to their spiritual robustness. II. THE BLESSING BOUGHT 1B REGARDED AB .A. FREE GIFT. "That he would grant you •.. to be strengthened." All true prayer proceeds upon the supposition that we can expect nothing from God but as a free gift through Jesus Obrist. There must be a aense of want along with a spirit of entire dependence on the Lord, so that the believer may realize the sweetness of the promise, "My God shall supply all your need according to hie riches in glory by Christ Jesus" (Phil. iv. 19). IIL Tu BLEBBDIG IS SPIRITUAL STBENGTH. "Strengthened with might ... in the THE EPISTLE TO 'l'HE EPHESIANS. [OB. m.1-21.

;:rner rn:in." It is not a. prayer for physical strength, which is a matter of slight moment in G'---J.'s sight.. though it is often made the subject of foolish boastincr aruon';,. men· nor for intel!c-..,rnal strength, which is a. much more importa.nt factor in htman life· b~t for "strength in the inuer man." This is not to be confounded with" the new ma~." It is rather •· the hidden man of the heart" (l Pet. iii. 4); the man" created after God" ( eh. iv: 24) _in righteoll:sness and holiness; the interior principle of spiritual life; the p9rsomficat10n of our rntellectual and spiritual life, with its impulses its feelin!r!! its ,rrnggles. This is the sphere, the direction, the destination, of the stre~gth pray~'tl°for. It 1s a prayer that God would make us eminent in grace and goodness, that our souls mny P:~sper and ~e in healt~ like our ?od.ies, that we m~y _be able to grapple with all our spmtual enemies, to resist temptation, to endure affhct1ons, to perform the duties. of our Christian calling. If we have strength, we shall be able to run in tbe way of God's commandments (Isa. xl. 31). Our physical strength is renewed from day to day, by food and rest. We glorify God 'by this fv.ll,er strength. It is not enough to have grace enough to carry us to heaven ; we must abound• in the fruits of righteousness to the praise and glory of God. C.

entries.title: EPH 3:17
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-The indwel.ling of (Jhrist in belie-oers. "That Christ may dwell in your l1earts by faith." Whether we regard this clause of the prayer as representing the result, or the purpose, or the source of the spiritual strength spo~en of in the previous clauEe, it is in very close relationahip with it. Its own meaning 1s perfectly olear. I. THE lNDWELLEB-Cmu.sT. '!'here is a threefold idea suggested by the term. 1. The believer is regarded as a temple or house to be divinely inhabited. It is 01iginally a house in ruins, to be restored as a beautiful temple of the Lord. Judging by the analogy of restoring a ruined house, the first operation is a cleansing out of the rtibbish; the second, an opening of the windows to admit the pure air of heaven, and a kindling of a fire on the hearth; the third is a closing up of all the cracks or openings in the wallil by which the wind or air finds access; and the fourth is the furnishing of the rooms with such articles of convenience as our taste and our means may enable us to 1,rocw-e. Similarly, when the Lord takes up his abode in the sinner's heart, the process, tiiough not successive in point of time, includes, first, the application of the blood of

Christ to" the boa.rt sprinkled from a.n evil conscience;" second, the opcnin~ of the windows of the understnndin~ to displace the tainted atmosphere of man's thouo-hts nnd ths kindling ?f the fire of love Divi~e in_the heart; third, the watchful closing up of t~tos~ avenu~s m the ~oul through which SID so easily finds access; and fourth, the fum1shmg of the sonl with the needed graces of the Spirit. 2. The indwelling is here ascribed to Olwist. It is elsewhere a.scribed to the Holy Spirit t "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" (1 Cor. iii. 16 ). It is likewise ascribed to the Father: "He that dwellcth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him" (1 John iv. 16). 'l'hese varying forms of expression find their solution in the doctrine of the Trinity. He that bath seen the Son bath seen the Father, and be that bath the Son bath the I<'ather; then, again, he that bath the Son bath the Spirit of Christ: "The Spirit of God dwelletb in you. Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his. And if Christ be in you ... the Spirit is life because of righteousness!' (Rom. viii. 9,.10). Therefore, when the apostle speaks of Christ dwelling in our hearts, he refers to the Spirit's indwelling, for Christ dwells in his people by his: Spirit. But there is a distinction in the modes of this indwelling: the Father dwells in us by love (1 John iv. 16); the Son by faith (eh. iii. Ii); the Spirit lies hid in the heart, working the faith in t_he one case and the love in the other. 3. It implies an abiding habit of life.. Christ does not come a.a a sojourner or as a wayfaring man, that. turneth aside to ta.rry for the night, but as e. constant dweller. Herein lies our security for the continuance, the power, the comfort, of this life. II. 'l'HE BEAT OF INDWELLING-THE HEABT. 'l'bis is the true shrine. The word signifies the seat of.religious knowledge as well a~ feeling. 'l'hus Christ sits at the very centre of spiritual life, himself the very Life of that life (Ga.I. ii. 20), controlling all its impulses and movements. 'fhe objects we most desire we treasure in the heart. The heart wearies of many things, but can never weary of this Divine Visitant, who can speak with commanding voice when the. soul is disturbed by suggestions of sin. "If our ·heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart" (1 John iii. 20). The Lord is the supreme. Possessor of the heart "now sprinkled from a.n evil conscience." UI. THE SU11JECTIVE MEANS OF THE INDWllLLING-FAITH. This is not to be regarded merely as the means of our justification, or as the root of our spiritual life, but as its·continuously sustaining principle, according to the apostle's teaching:" I live; yet ,not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life whicl;l I now live in the flesh I live by. the faith of the Son of God" ,(Gal; ii. 20). 'l'his is the faith that worketh by love, that purifies the heart, that overcometh the world. It is the principle of spiritual communion; it is that by which we realize the presence, the excellence, the power, of Christ in us; it is that which radiates alLgrace and peace through the belie'l"er's hee.rt.-T; C. , Ver. 18.-Love, the root (1/f/,d foundatiM of spiritual knowledge. "That ye, being rooted and grounded in love," may comprehend and know the love of Christ. The effect of Christ's indwelling in bolievers is to root them and found them deeply in love-love being the root of the tree of life in the one case, and the foundation of the temple or house in the other; for the soul, ever contemplating Christ within it, is changed into his very likeness. The a.postle means that the Ephesian snints would grow in the knowledge of that love by growing into the likeness of that love. "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.;" "The meek will be guide in judgruent, the meek will he teach his way." The truths of God are by them spiritually discerned. '!'here is a deep philosophy in, this matter. Men cannot understand each other except so far as they have the radical elements of the same experiences in themselves. I understa.nd wha.t you mea.n when you say y:,u are hot or cold, because I luwc bad sensations of hea.t and cold in myself. Thus people of dissimilar tempers, or culture, or opportunities are apt to misunderstand each other. A vulgar man cannot uuJ.erstnnd a man of high refinement. A practical man of the world, who is to-day what he was yesterday, and will be to-morrow what he is to-day, cnn never understand the man of poetic genius, whose spirits come and go like the tides, to-day in the height of sentimental ecstasy, to-morrow in the depths of despair. 'l'here must, therefore, be similarity of temper or experience to promote a real under~tai:idin~. 'Fh_us we can see how only love .can understand lovo. Even in ow: worldly rnt1mac1cs, 1t 1e not quu;kncss of :per- 120 THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. [<lit. m. 1-21.

ception but the force of sympathy or affection that enables us to understand our friends. "Love's quick eye can pierce through disguises impenetrable to a colder scrutiny." Thus it is that the knowledge of God is not t-0 be compassed bv n mere exercise of the int<?lloct; it is to be attained through love: "He that loveth not knoweth not God· for G,.._i. is lc,n" (1 John i.. S). Thus it comes to pass that we can know the lo;e of Ch:-ist realizingly just in proportion as we ha,e that which resembles it in our own hearts s;_1.:. t?at love ~s the~ in virtue of his own indwelling by the Spirit. "The Christ of t .. e Bible mauife,,--ts himself, md, by the law-s of human nature, can manifest himself only to his own image formed in the heart." Thus it is possible to read a new meanina into the bea~tiful sentence of inspiration, " Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neithe~ ha,e entered mto the heart of man, the things which God hnth prepared for them that Io,·e him" (1 Cor. ii. 9). Our Lord has suggesth-ely said, " If any man will do his will he shall know of the doctrine whether it be of God." There are moral as well ~ intellectual conditions in the pathway of all extended knowledge.-T. C.

-2%e comprehension of the love of Ohrist. The true science for llldnt! is " Christ's love." I. CoNSIDEB TBIS LOVE A.S REPRESENTED m THE PASSAGE as to length, breadth, height, and depth. L These dimensions seem to imply infinity, It has been suggested that the apostle speaks as if standing in a centre, himself the object of this love, enveloped by an atmosphere of love which stretches away illi.mitably above, beneath, around. He prays that all saints may stand, as it were, in the focus of the same en,eloping love. What is that which has thus its centre wherever a saint is to he found? The centre of infinite space is wherever we stand; for we carry this centre with us, no matter where we go. So it is with the in.finite love of Christ, which surround.~ the saints with its vast and limitless expanse. Each saint ought to feel that he is in the very centre of that love, as if the sole object of its guiding, purifying, comforting care. Hnman affection has its limits, for it cannot lavish its richest treasures upon se,eral bein,,,"S at the same time. Not so the heart of Jesus, which has room for millions upon millions of saints. 2. But tlu love of Ohrist may be seen in its pre-eminenrefrom tlu st,a:ndpoint of time. Not only does he love millions, but there is a wonderful duration in his affection for us. We think gratefully of the parental affection that shone upon onr life before any time that our memory can recall, and long. before we were conscious of its existence. We value most the friendships that have lasted longest. But what is all earthly love to the everlasting love of Christ, which had us in his heart ages before our birth, and had a kingdom prepared for us before the foundation of the world? But his love is as lasting as it is ancient. Human affection often fails through misunderstanilings, collisions of interests, variations of pursuit, so that there is. often a painful sense of uncertainty 1111 to the future ; but even that affection can hardly follow 115, as to any real succour or comfort, throughout the unknown life that awaits us beyond the grave. There is One, however, who is the same yesterday, to-day, and for e,er; on the coLtinuance of whose love we can securely .count in time and throughout eternity. If he love us now, he will love us to the end. What, then, shall separate UJ:1 from such a Ion? 3. But this lor,e might be regarded fr.am another standpoint : think of m interaity. We measure ib! intensity by its sacrifices, its sufferings, its burdens; yet we must remember that there was more than a mere human BeDsibility beati:1g in the hean of Christ. He plants himself in the very heart of this world's bzra::itude and rebellion and unbelief, exposed to all its hatred, revenge, impurity, profa:iity ; aud dies for this very world, "the Just for the unjust, that he might bring U5 t0 Gud.~ lL lT IS A LOVE DE!ilG.KED TO BE THE OBJECT ALIKE OF COMPREHENSION AND OP KNOW• LEDGE:. The apostle prays that the Ephesian saints may comprehend the dimensions of it an.d "know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge." There is a difference betv,een the two terms. We do not want simply to know about Christ's love, of which the absolute understanding is beyond our reach, but to know it, to realize it as a possession of our own, to have an experimental knowledge of its preciousness. Such love may be darkness to the intellect, but it is sunshine to the heart; too marvellous for us to comprehend, but not too rich for us to enjoy. "In a word, to know the love of Christ-it is might in weakness; it is patience in tribulation; it is strength for OU. OJ. 1-21.] THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. 121

liviog; it is hope in dying; it is heaven bro.ight down to earth; it is heaven dwelLn,., 0 within the soul.'' III. THE GRAND PURPOSE AND RESULT OF THIS REALIZED LOVE. "That ye may be filled with all the fulncss of God." 1. The fulness of God is the fulness which Goel possesses, and therefore incapable of being contractild to the dimensions of a hmunn heart. Yet that fulness-the plenitude of the Divine perfection, which is said to dwell in Christ bodil.v-is the very measure unto which we are to be filled. We are to be perfect as our Father in heaven is perfect ; we arc to come " to the perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ;" we are actually predcstinated to b€ conformed to the image of that Son of God who is the Brightness of the Father's glory, and the express Image of his person. 2. We are to be filled unto thatfulness. The apostle does not say that we shall reach it in this life, or that, if we reach it in the life beyond, the distance between God and us will not still be less than infinite. Plunge an empty vessel into the ocean, it is filled wt of and filled with the fulness of the waters that surround it on every side. That empty vessel is our soul. It can take in the fulness of God in its own measure of self-containment. 'l'he comparison, to be more exact, demands that the vessel in question should be of expansible material, like a sponge, which, lying withered upon the rock, becomes larger and larger as it is sunk in the deep, till it is merged in the very fulness of the sea. Thus our dry and withererl souls, filled with the love of Christ, expand gradually into the very folness of God. 3 .. Effects of this filling unto God's f1.dness. One is that, with a well so full and overflowing, our vessels need never be empty. You may ask too little; you cannot ask too much: for the very fulness of God is ever flowing into you. You cannot exhaust it by any frequency of resort to it. Study ever more and more the love of Christ, which, like an arch, stands all the firmer from every additional stone with which it is weighted. Aoother effect is that, in proportion as you are being filled with God's fulness, there is less room in the heart for sin, or fear, or doubt, or pain. The fulness, like the perfect love, "casteth out fear." As in an exhau::1ted receiver, the more the air is drawn olY the more firmly will the machine clasp the surface upon which it stands, so the more that guilt and fea.- are drawn off from the believer's heart, the more will it cleave to the almighty strength on which it rests. Let our hearts rejoice, therefore, in the fulness of God.-'l'. C.

entries.title: EPH 3:20
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-.A. great doxolo_qy. The apostle had exhausted all the forms of supplication, and now he casts himself upon the very infinitude of God, which was able to supply more than the thoughts or desires of men could suggest in the sphere of prayer. I. TBE THEllil.E OF THE DOXOLllGY. It is no abstract ascription of glory to Gd; it is one full of hope and cheer to the Church-the ability of God to do great things for his people. There is a sort of climax in the language employed : God is able to do what we ask or think; he is able to do above all we ask or think; nay, abundantly above it; nay, exceeding abundantly above all we ask or think; and our thinking is very much wider than our asking. Two things make us strong in prayer-a deep sense of need and e. strong hope of supply. Perhaps we shall hardly venture to ask some blessings, but we ought to consider that we are either to approach God on our own merits or on the merits of Christ. If we pray for blessing on our own merits, we cau hardly be too stinted in our asking; but if on the merits of Christ, we ought not tu disgrace God by asking little things on such a wide basis of encouragement. We have, in fact, got a carte-blanche put into our hands by Christ, saying, "Ask what you will, and it shall be done unto you." We are to ask up to our power of thinking, and far beyon<l it; for "God giveth liberally and upbraideth not." entries.title: EPH 3:1–13
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-7?,e deatk of tM tribal spirit. The apostle, having stated the unity between Jews and Gentiles in the one spiritual temple, proceeds in this parenthesis to state the aspect of the gospel which is thus presented. It amounts, i~ fac~, to th~death .of the tribal feeling, and to the encouragement of that broad cosmopchtamsm which has been fostered by the Christian system. Paul, of course, rejoiced in his Jewish origin and in all the privileges which be had thus inherited .. But since bis conversion unto Chmt, the narrowness had disappeared, and he took his stand before the world as the apostle ar,,i apc,lr,gist of Uie Gentiles, hoping for the same elevation of character for t ~em as fo: h' m5':lf. I. LET C'6 :SOTICB BOW PAUL WAS PREPARED J'OB, THIS CHA!dPIONIIHIP OP THE GE.?-TH,EB. (Ver. 8.) He bad come to entertain a deep humility of spirit. He deemed 1:r:;,,,}f" less than the kast of all saints." In Paul's experience it has been observed ti:iere is a progress. First he speaks of himself as " the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God" (lCor. xv. 9).

Secondly, os in this passage before us, be regards himself not only as hnrdly worthy of the name of an apostle, hut as less than the least of all saints. Having ranked all apostles above himself in the first instance, he now ranks all the saints above him. 'l'hen, thirdly, he puts himRelf below all other sinners, and declares, "This is a faithful saying, aud worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief" (1 Tiro. i. 15). Now, this expresses a <:Qrnplete revolntion in Pharisaic thought. Unquestionably Paul had learned to judge himself severely when he comes to conclusions such as these. Now, Christianity secure~ thi~ apparent moral paradox of esteeming each the other better than himself (Phil. ii. 3). " By humility," as A. Monod has said _in his 'Explication,'" the Christian is led to judge himself severely, while charity comes to his aid in making him judge favourably of another. Each one, besides, reading in his own heart and not that of others, perceives only in himself that depth of sin .which is the worst aspect of it, although least visible, and he can always hope that with others, whatever the appearances may be, this depth, hidden from his eyes, is better than with him." This personal humiliation, then, is the preparation.Paul receives for his great role as elevator of the Gentiles. It is when personally abased that we are exalted in heart and hope, and become the willing servants of mankind. , II. PAUL'S ESTIMATE OIi' BIB OFll'I0E. (Ver. 8.) It was a "grace" given to him to be allowed by God to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ. His notion was that it was the crown and summit of human privilege to be thus placed in charge of such a commission; He magnified his office. Ho saw nothini to bo compared with it in the privileges of men. He woul.d have endorsed the words of a gm1.t modern preacher when he declared to students for the ministerial office," There is no career that can compare with it for a moment in the rich and satisfying relations into which it brings a man with his fellow-men, in the deep and interesting insight which it givts him into humen nature, and in the chance of the best culture for his own character• . . . Let us rejoice with one another that in a world where there are a great many good and happy things for men to do, God has given us the best and happiest, and made us preachers of his truth." Ill. THE HORAL ELEVATION WHICH THE GOSPEL PROPOSES TO DESTOW UPON THE GENTILES. (Ver. 6.) Up to our Lord's time the tribal idea.prevailed. The Jews were a tribe, and their policy was, as their policy would still be, the supremacy of the tribe. Dut Christ proposed not to carry the Jewish tribe up to proud supremacy, but, on the contrary, to bring all other tribes up to their level of privilege, and to weld the world's peoples into one. It was he who first touched the key of cosmopolitan comprehensiveness and bade the narrow tribal spirit,to cease. He talked of many coming from tiast and west to sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. viii. 11). He talked of drawing" all men" unto himself once he was lifted on the cross (John-xii. 82). He spoke.of Jerusalem ceasing to be the single centre of true worship, and of true worshippers worshipping the Father anywhere (John iv. 21-24). All nations were to be discipled by his servants (Matt. xxviii. 20). Into these broad and noble views for mankind the eleven did not very rapidly or fully enter. Doubtless Peter had inauguxated the Gentile Pentecost in the house of Cornelius ; but he reln.psed into narrowness a few years later at Antioch. It was reserved, therefore, for Paul, the most powerful mind of the apostolic band, to c11.tch the cosmopolitan spirit of his Master, and to champion the Gentile against all the prejudice of the Jewish world. It has been suggested that he would not have chosen the appointment had it been left to himself. But, as far as we can judge, he showed no narrowness once he had humbled himself at Christ's feet on the way to Damascus. He there ceased to he the patriot of a tribC', and became, in the widest and worthiest sense, a. citizen of the world nml a clrnmpiou of the rights of universal man. There is surely something grand in this idea of lifting outcast communities into the highest and holiest associntiona. There is no casting of contempt on any tribe, but extending pity and compassion unto all. 'The golden gnto of privilege ill opened wide for every one. The missionary enterprise is the best and noblest policy which men have set themselves in ee.rnest to carry through I IV. 'l'HE LESSON THUS AFFORDED TO THE HEAVENLY WORLD. (Vers. 10-12.) The idea of Paul i8 that the angels on high look down with rapt interest and profit upon what is taking place in the Church. 'fhe movements of men outside the Church hiwe, THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHE~IA...~S. [on. m. 1--21.

of c0urse, their interest ; but it is the bringing of the different peoples of the earth into the glorious unity of the Church of God which so strikes the attention of the heavenly world. The Divine society which is gathering round Jesus is the most instructive exhibition of God's purposes which the heavenly world can contemplate. AsJonathat Edw!irds put it in his sermon upon ver. 10, the angels are benefited by the salvatio1.:. of men, (1) by seeing therein a great and;wonderful manifestation of the glory of God; (2) by Jesus Christ, as God-Man, becoming their Head. We may be sure that the history of the world looks very differently to the immortals from what it does in the pages of mortal history. We see the tramp of armies and of battles upon the graphic page, and an account more or less intelligent of the different and concurrent causes; but with what fuller insight and appreciation must the heavenly world look down upon the vicissitudes of time ! Amid the conflicting policies of different. states and nations, the missionary enterprise appears as the one consistent and uniting policy. The elevation of the world's peoples into one consecrated whole, into one mighty family, into one OI1:,TS.nic whole, is surely worthy of a God. And this is what the Church exhibits; it was for this Paul suffered, it is for this we in our respective spheres must struggle too. -R. M. E. Vers. H-21.-The Ohristian brotherhooil-Paul's second prayer. From the noble idea of the elevation of the heathen to equal privileges with the Jews, the apostle proceeds t.o a second prayer for the Ephesian converts, in which he rises to still greater elevation of thought. Prostrating himself before the Father of all, he contemplates a family unity embracing both heaven and earth, and he prays that his friends at Ephesus may experience such inward illumination and strength as to be fitting members of the mighty family. The leading thought is, then, Christian brotherhood, which embraces angels as well as men. The following thoughts a.re suggested by the prayer:- L C.HBISTUN BROTHERHOOD IS TO BE REALIZED IN DEVOTION BEFORE A COMJll'.ON FATHER. (Ver. 14.) The words" of our Lord Jesus Christ"are not in the most ancient manuscripts, and are rightly omitted in the Revised Version. This clears the ground for the understanding of the family name. The word for" family" (,r111"p1il) is etymologically connect.ed. with ..-,rr~p, so that it is God the Father who supplies the patronymic to "every family in heaven and on earth." All gather round the feet of a common Father, and realize in their devotion the true brotherhood. We do not sufficiently think of how much is accomplished when we get men everywhere on their knees with the Lord's Prayer upon their lips. A1'> we say from the heart, " Our Father, which art in heaven," onr hearts have become really one. However much we ma.y squabble before we proceed to prayer, if onr prayer to the infinite Father be true, we have entered by it in to re.al brotherhood. Contention cannot stand " the light of the count.enance" of tile ~ " Peace-maker." lL CimxsTul; BB.OTHEBJIOOD IS 9ECURBD TBBOUGE TEE INDWELLING OF A COIOION SA.VIOUJL (Vers.16, 17.) For the Holy Spirit, entering into the hea.rts;of God's children, enables them to entertain the elder Brother as a Guest. Christ dwells within each of us. He comes to sup with us and to enable us to sup with him (John xiv. 21; Rev. iiL 20). Christ within us becomes the unifying element. He is the Guest of each and of alL A1'> a Divine Being, he can pervade all the hearts and ensure the brotherhood. The brotherhood is brought about and sustained by an indwelling Christ. Taking possession of our natures, Jesus moulds them to his own gracious purposes and secures the essential brotherhood all round. Ill. CHRISTIAN BBOTEEBHOOD IS INTENSIFIED TEBOUGH TEE GRADUAL COMPBEHEN- BION oF CHRIST'S WONDROUS LOVE,'. (Vers.18, 19.) Jesus' by his indwelling becomes the object as well as instigator of our lol'e. W ~ get "rooted an~ grounded in love:" The selfish, loveless life has ceased, and the lovmg and devoted hfe has begun. This is essential to the comprehension of another's love. As Robertson says, "You must love in order to understand love. . . . One act of charity will teach us more of the love of God than a thousand sermons." Only loving hearts, then, can appreciate the wondrous love of Christ. It passeth the knowledge of natural and unloving men. Love is a revelation only unto love. But now, supposing that the love of Christ has begun within UJI, then his wondrous love becomes a subject of endless contemplation. Its breadth and length, its depth and height, preaent a problem for CR, m. 1-21,) THE EPISTLE TO '£HE EPHESIANS. 125

our holy comprehension, which ca.n never be exhausted. "The believer" says A. Monad "who ha.a been represented j1.1st now a.s rooted and grounded in the lo;e of the Lord, i~ here represented a.s enveloped on all sides by this love, which extends itself in all directions a.round him beyond the limits of vision. Suspended in the very bosom of the infinite love, like the earth in the bosom of space, he looks before him, behind him, above him, below him, to seize the just measure of this love which has saved him, but all ends in demonstrating the impossibility of measuring it. The breadth? On his right and on his left, immensity. The length? Before him and behind him, immensity. The depth? Under his feet, immensity. The height? Over his head, still immensity." Here, then, in the infinite love of Christ there is material for eternal study, and the brotherhood realizes that it has begun an everlasting progress towards" the fulness of God." As we comprehend Christ's love, we find ourselves proportionally" partakers of the Divine nature" and filled with the Divine fulness. This is the infinitely distant goal; this is the straight line to which our hyperbolic orbit is continually making approach, though destined never actually to reach it. And as we approach the perfection and fulness of God, we become the more united in Christian brotherhood. IV, CHRISTIAN BROTHERHOOD REMAINS UNBROKEN BY THE CHANGE OF WORLDS. (Ver. 15.) The family of love, who a.re gathering regularly round the feet of the heavenly Father, cannot be broken up by death or change of worlds. Heaven with its saiats e.nd angels, earth with its suffering and saintly souls, these constitute but one family ci.Icle, and a.re pervaded by the one Christ and the one Christian spirit. It is this thought which robs death of its sting and makes it a.ppea.r but a. sublime emigration. 'fb.e majority are in the Father's house above; it is the minority that are left on earth; and our sainted dead have simply passed over to the majority a.nd are a.waiting us a.mid more perfect associations. "Death, in short," says Ma.rtinea.u, "under the Cbristia.n aspect, is but God's method of colonization; the transition from this mothercountry of our race to the fairer and newer world of our emigration. What though no other passage thither is permitted to a.ll the living, a.nd by neither eye nor ear we can discover a.ny trace of that unknown receptacle of vivid and more glorious life? So might the dwellers in any other sphere make complaint respecting our poor worlcl. Intensely a.s it burns with life, dizzy as our thought becomes with the din of its eager passions and the cries of its many woes, yet from the nearest station that God's universe affords-nay, at a few miles beyond its own confines, all its strong force, its crowded cities, the breathless hurry a.nd ferment of its nations, the whole apparition and chorus of humanity, is still and motionless as death; gathered a.11 and lost within the circumference of a dark or illumined disc. Aad silent ss those midnight heavens appear, well ma.y there be, among their points of light, some one that thrills with the glow of our lost and immortal generations; busy with the fleet movements and happy energies of existence more vivid than our own; where, as we approach, we might catch the awful voices of the mighty dead, and the sweeter tones, lately heard in the last pa.iQ and sorrow, of our own departed ones." V. THE CHRISTIAN BROTHERHOOD IS SUSTAINED BY THE ASSURANCE OP GoD'B SUll- PABSING POWER. (Vers. 20, 21.) In the doxology the apostle adds one other thought to round and complete his glorious theme. He wishes to ascribe glory unto God; Lut what attribute shall form the substance of the doxology? The attribute of power. Not, howevor, the physical power which obtains in the universe of sense, but the spiritual power which obtaiI!s in the "world of mind." And so be looks upward and pronounces the mighty God a.s "able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us." In the world of sense he docs not work up to his full st,?ngth, nor is there a.ny reason why be should. The physical universe speaks of bis "eternal," but not necessarily of his" iufinite" power (Rom. i. 20). It is in the domain of the spirit that he performs his chefs-<i'reuvre. And such a thought ia surely fitted to sustain the aspirations of the Christian brotherhood!- R. M. E.
