Where Christ is not, fu--.d's g1c'ry is not seen. 2. Through Ohn'st man is brought into sympathy with the _clory c:,f God. " God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, ha.th shined in our he.arts, to gi.e the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of J esns Christ.., He it is that inspires, enamours, and transports the soul with the glory of God. Hum.an worship must ever be in connection with Christ. '' He loved us, and gave himself for u.s." IT. In relation to the AGES, "Throughout all ages, world without end. A.men." This implies: 1. That God will be for ever. Were he not to be for ever, worship would not be for ever. He is eternal. "From everlasting to everlasting thou art God.'' "He inhabiteth eternity." "One day with him is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." 2. That the Ohurch will be/or ever. '£he redeemed will never cease to exist. '!'hey a.re to live from generation to generation, through endless ages. 3. That the reasons for praise will be for ever. God's infinite excellence, bis rL.a.emptive and fatherly relation to the Church, and the communications of his love are the grand reasons for praise, and these will be for ever. CoNCLUSION. What a sublime destiny is that of the redeemed I Genuine religious praise is the heaven of the soul It is that in which all the "powers find sweet employ." It is that which brings the whole spiritual man within the glow and the rnnshine of the fatherhood of God. Praise is not the " service of song," as it is called; it is the spirit of life. It is not until all the activities of our being chime in one triumphant and sncce.eding psalm that our destiny is realized.-D. T. Ver. L-" Th£ prisoner of (Jhrist Jesus." St. Paul writes from his Roman dungeon, with the galling constraint.a of his confinement constantly about him. There is a pathos in the situation that must move the sympathy of the reader; and yet there is a dignity and even a glory in it that make us feel the apostle's ocoasional reference to his bonds chiefly a motive for giving the greater weight and solemnity to his persuasive e~hort.ations. I. THE FAITHFUL SERVANT OF CHRIST HAY BECOME A PBIBONEB IN IDB OAUBE, St. Paul was called into the apostleship from a worldly position of great influence and brilliant prospects. He was the most gifted and the most devoted man in the Christian Church. No one laboured more assiduously, and no one met with more marked success. Yet it has all come to this, that the great, honoured apostle lies chained in a Roman prison, his life at the mercy of the "mad boy" Nero. The end might have l)een expected in this form. "A disciple is not above bis master; nor a servant above his lord." If the Lord was crucified, shall we be surprised that the servant is imprisoned? f:itill some are perplexed and disappointed, not at suffering these great hardships, but at haYin:; to bear any cross for Chrut. Christianity is the religion of the cross for the Christian as truly as for Obrist. IL LIBERAL CHRISTI.U."ITY :HAY ENDANGER THE Lll!ERTY OF ITB ADVOOATB. Bt. Paul was a prisuntr "in behalf of you Gentiles." We know, from the history in the Acts, foai it was tr.rough the enmity of Jews that the apostle was accused before the Roman govemmtnt, and that this enmity was roused by the jealousy they felt at hi11 pn,atLirig the gospel to the Gentiles, and advocating the Gentile right to an equality ~itb th Jew. St. Paul was the preacher of the more liberal Christianity of bis day OH, W, 1-21.] 'l'HE El'lSTLE TO 'l'llE EPHESIANS. 141

and thereforo he was most grievously misunderstood and most bitterly opposed. They who feel called to preach more liberal views than arc sanctioned by the prevailin" opin~ons of the age may expcd opposition! b~t may learn the duty of courage and fidelity to truth, and may be cheered by thmkmg of the lonely sufferers in the same cause in bygone days, when the larger views and the freer doctrines were more vigorously opposed than they can be now. The noble champions of liberal Christianity from St. Paul to Maurice, have won substantial victories from which we profit. ' Ill. IT IS DETTER TO BE A PRISONER FOR CHRIST AND LIBERAL TRUTH THA:"I TO BE AT LIBERTY WITHOUT CHRIST AND IN UNCHARITABLE NARROWNESS. After all, the prisoner at Rome is more to be envied than pitied. He was the prisoner of Christ and Chris.; was with him in his bondage. His was the real blessedness of those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake. St. Paul was the champion of freedom as opposed to tbc restraints of Judaism, and this real, spiritual freedom could not be destroyed by bolts and bars. "Stone walls do not a prison make, Nor iron be.re e. cage."

The immortal dreamer had large liberty in Bedford jail when he travelled to the Beulah heights and almost as far as the gates of the celestial city. JV. THE PRISONER WHO SUFFERS FOB A GOOD CAUSE LAY~ GREAT OBLIGATIONS UPON ALL WHO BENEFIT FROM IT. St. Paul quietly appeals to his imprisonment as a ground for prayer (ver. 14) and exhortation (eh. iv. 1). The sufferings of the great martyrs of liberty in the past urge us, who have entered into the heritage won by their toil and death, to be faithful to so great a trust, to walk worthy of it by using our liberty as an opportunity for the highest service of love, and to preserve it from all encroachments and band it down to our children unfettered by new restraints of theological dogma or of official domination.-W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 3:8
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -" Less than the least of all saints." I. HE wno IS MOST HIGHLY GIFTED WITH DIVINE GRACE WILL THmK MOST LOWLY OF mMSELF. St. Paul, the most gifted apostle, is roost deeply conscious of his own unworthiness. We must distinguish between tho endowment of grace and the acquisition of merit. To have much grace is only to bu much favoured. As a man grows in grace be grows in power of spiritual insight; and the result is twofold-be bas more knowledge of bis own true state and a better understanding of the claims of righteousness. Thus the standard is ever rising above bis head in greater heights of holiness, while be is constantly seeing more clearly, freed from all hypocrisy and self-deception, the miserable weakness and sinfulness of his own character. I!, HE WHO THINKS MOST LOWLY OF HIMSELF WILL BE MOST FITTED FOR THE SERVICl'l OF CHRIST. It is not that unworthiness is itself a fitness for service. Both to be unworthy o.nd to think one's self worthy are to be doubly unfit. But as Socrates thought he might be accouuted wise only because be knew he was ignorant while all other Athenians were unconscious of their ignorance, the true servant of Christ is aware of the sinfulness which is common to him and to all others, but others are not so deeply conscious of it. This humble consciousness of unworthiness is helpful for service, (1) because it makes us look for the indispensable grace of God; (2) because it saves us from preaching ourselves when we should be preaching Christ; and (3) because it compels us to give God all the glory of success.-W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 3:8
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-" The unsearchable riches of (Jhrist." Some riches are unsearchable because they a.re inaccessible, like jewels guarded by jealous sentinels, and pearls in sea-caves, and the gold-mines of remote stars. Some riches a.re unsearchable because they are secret, like treasure bid in a. field, and ancient records in undeciphered hieroglyphics ; in this sense an illiterate mim finds the wealth of a library, and an unscientific man the stores of a museum, unsearchable. No doubt there a.re wonderful graces in Christ that are as yet above and beyond our grasp, and deep mysteries tbo.t we cannot fathom, and a spiritual worth in all his blessings that cannot be discovered by the u.nspiritual. But it is not in these senses that the riches of Christ are called unsearchable. The doors of bis treasure-chamber are flung wide that the poorest may enter. '!'here is no 'l'HE EPIB'i'LE TO Tll.E EPHESIANS. [OH, llL 1-21,

wil of mystery tv pre-.ent a little child from seel.ng the beauty within. The riches of Christ are unsearchable simply because they al'e so nbundnut and so various thnt no man c3Il e,er measure the extent, or count the number, or distinguish all the forms of them. For near upon nineteen centuries this great treasury hns been ransacked by friends and foes, by hungering inquirers and by keen-eyed critics, with the result that, like the infinite wealth of nature-which is felt to be more immeasurable in our own ,hy, after the fruitful labours of the most indefatigable natur-.ilists, than ever it was when not one-tenth of what we now know was discovered-these riches of Obrist amaze and fascinate and overwhelm us with an ever-growing sense of their magnificent unsearcba.bleness. • I. THE RICHES OF THB CHA'.ltACTER OF CHRIST ABE UNSEAR0HAllLE, 1. They have been searched into by uncompromi:sing foes, at first by bitter Pharisees _and so.offing Sadducees, later by clever philosophical opponents, such as Celsus and Porphyry,. down to the times of Voltaire's sparkling sarcasm and Strauss's dry criticism. And the. ,erdict of mankind is distinctly against the fault-finders, confessing with Pilate, "I find no fault in him." 2. These riches have also been searched into by adoring disciples, some mth the profundity of St. A~crustine, others with the simplicity of St. Frances; and all types of Christians in every succeeding age unhesitatingly declare that they ne.er weary of won:ihipping fresh wonders in that life of unearthly loveliness. .The n:c:e onr eyes are opened to discern spiritual worth, and the more the character of ('~...,,--t is studied., the more are we astonished and delighted by the vision of infinite 1--:::·-f. .-:.ct:u:i.. . II. 'l'm: RICJIE5 OF THE TRUTH OF CHRIST .ARE ID.'SEA.RCHAllLE. Christ is the Truth ::::c. the Ligbt of tlie world. The ideas of Plato may be measured-the truth of Christ ::c.er. Yet two classes of people deny the unsearchable nature of the riches of this r:dh. 1. Tlwse wl,o say the world has outgrown Christianity. Perhaps they mistake the dogmas of the creeds for the truth as it is in Jesus. The former are necessarily limited, and some of them may have to break up and give place to larger ideas. But the latter is living, infinite, and eternal. 2. Those who are satisfied that they lcnow everything. They are usually the people who know least. A smooth and rounded scheme of doctrine comprehends their universe. Because they have shaped it into logical consistency, they assume that no truth can lie outside it. They have yet to learn that the Word made flesh, like the Word in nature, is infinite. Ill. THE RICHES OF THE LOVE OF CHRIST ABE UNSEARCHABLE. Human love commonly diminishes in intensity in proportion to the extent of the area over which it is spread; family affection being warmer than our interest in the wider circle of friends, and this than general philanthropy, just as the river is deep where it is narrow, but becomes shallow as its banks open out in width. But the grace of Christ, in depth and breadth like the sea, has a l"ast comprehensiveness for all, together with a strong intensity for each. So that in the last great assembly, when some come from distant isles and some from hidden valleys, some from populous cities and some from lonesome deserts, to confess that the grace of Christ has reached them in the fulness of its power, none mll be found so remote as to have been beyond reach, so undeserving as to have been past mercy, or so needy as not to have been able to find the sup:ply of every real want in his great riches of love. IV. TRE RICHES OF THE BLESSINGS GIVEN BY OBRIST ABE UNSEARCHABLE. There is still an unhappy habit among some of listening only to the evil report of the spies who tell of the giants, and turning a deaf ear to the spies who bring the grapes and l ,omegranates. Ko wonder that this habit leads to the painting of the blessing1;1 of Christianity with very dull shades. Rightly understood, the gospel offers a pearl of great price, reveals hidden treasures, strips oil' the rags and brings forth the best 1·obo and the ring. From the first grace of forgiveness to the last grace of peace in death, Christ is breathinu benedictions on the Christian's life, so that when he reflects, he is astonished at what he has already received, and yet learns to accept all thM ail only the earnest of the blessings of light, and strength, and purity, and l)ea'ce, 'that are reserved for his future inheritance.-W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 3:10
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-" The mar: 1/dd wisdom (JI God." I. THE MANIFOJ,D WISDOM OF Gon IB PUT ,::TH nr THY- 1<1::DY-MT"l'If)N OF TITF. WORLD. God is the great 'l'hink<!r, All QUr OH, III, 1-21.] THE EPISTLE TO 'l'HE EPHESIANS. 113

philosophy is the attempt of man to spell ont some of the ideas of God. What wisdom was requisite for the creation of the world and the ordering of all things, from tho movements of a star down to the life of a cell! What wisdom is involved in the government of the world, maintaining life and gladness, developing the latent resources of tho universe, making nil things work together for good, ruling great kingdoms and inclividual lives in justice and mercy I But a higher wisdom is required for redemption. It is more difficult to regenerate than to create, to regain Paradise than to form it at the first. 1. Not only are the power and goodness of God needed for this work, but also his wisdom. Preaching may be foolish, but the gospel preached is the wisdom of God. 'l'he highest intellectuality has been exercised in working ont the world's redemption. 2. St. Paul sees this especially in the breadth of the results-in the inclusion of Gentile with Jew. High wisdom is broad, and liberal charity requires much intelligence. Comprehensiveness shonld not be a matter of vague sentiment. To be effective it must be fortified by ripe wisdom. 3. This wisdom is manifold. God has many interests to consider, many conflicting forces to deal with, and many issues to·provide for. Therefore (1) different men may have different views, and yet all be in the right. (2) Many purposes may be aimed at in redemption beyond what we can see, and thus many processes which to us look meaningless find their cnr1. The water is not taken over the mill-wheel simply that it may find its nearest course to the river;· nor is the Christian led over a broken path because that is the nearest way to heaven. II. THE MANIFOLD WISDOM OP' GOD IS MADE KNOWN THROUGH THE CHURCH TO THE HIGHEST INTELLIGENCES. The Church is the manifestation of a wisdom that was hidden before Christianity appeared. Truth is explained by illustration, and the Church is a concrete illustration of Divine wisdom. It is not in the thinking and teaching of Divine wisdom by Christians, but in their very existence as such, that the wisdom of God is revealed. To be a redeemed soul is to be a proof of that wisdom, just as for one who had been incurably sick to be a healthy man was to be a living proof of the healing power of Christ. This revelation was made to other worlds and higher intelligences. 1. God cares/or other worlds than our own; elsewhere processes of education are being carried on with creatures in whom God takes interest. 2. We are called to minister instruction to other WOTlds. The service is mutual ; angels are ministering spirits to men, men are instructive witnesses of redemptive wisdom to nngels. 'lbus the lowest can help the highest. An angel can learn lessons from a man, as n man can find instruction in an insect. Our lives, then, are linked to other worlds. What happens to us has bearings elsewhere. This thought may help us to face some mystery of life. As in the case of Job, what is humanly unintelligible may be explained when it is seen that the beings of another sphere are being instructed through our experiencu. 3. If the highest intelligences "desire to look into" these things, and see the manifold wisdom of God in them, surely we men should treat the w01·ks of redemption with profound reverence,and regard the study of them as worthy of our highest thouglit.- W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 3:12
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -0hristian boldnus. I. BOLDNESS IS A CHRISTIAN GRACE. The gospel destroys the gloomy old religions of terror. It dispels even the natural fear of guilty souls in the presence of the holy God. It brings liberty and courage. It is essentially the manly faith of the world's adult age. II. 'l'rus BOLDNESS IS MANIF'EST IN OUR CONFIDENT ACCESS TO GoD. The Christian is not to approach God under the circumstances which made the courngeous entrance of Queen Esther into the presence of King Ahasuerus so nobly patriotic. We see Gotl as our Father waiting to be gracious. It is unworthy to fear. Our prayer should not be the cry of the captive for mercy, but the glad request of the child. Note: 1. Christian boldness is wasted unless we use it in ·ccming nearer to God. 2. '!'his boldness is no excuse for irreverence. III. CHRISTIAN BOLDNESS IS EXPLAINED BY OUR RELATION TO CmtIST. 1. Christ dispels our ignorant terrors by revealing the fatherhood of God. We have but to acquaint ourselves with him to be at peace (Job xxii. 21). 2. Christ gives to us the l'erfcct love that casts out fear. 3. Christ reconciles us with God, and so removes all ,;rnund of rc11,5onable alarm. For while we are unreconciled aud unforgiven, courage is 144 THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. [OH. llL 1-21. ------- ---------------------------- madness, and the wildest terror the reasonable condition of those whose consoience is roused and who realize their frightful peril. But through Christ we are forgiven and recc,ncilro t-0 God. It is ungrateful, after being thus blessed, to c!Jerish the old fears. lY. CHRISTIAN BOLD::--,.SS IS ENJOYED THROUGH FAITH IN CHRIST. 1. Faith is llc,-,,,-,;sry in order to bring us into those ,-elations with Ohrist which make our boldntss r:f:JC and just.ifillble. Without faith we are not redeemed, and while unredeemed we l::m:- no grvund f,lt being bold in Christ. 2. Faith is necessary in order to e11able us r..: ~a1ia our free and &lfe condition through Christ. Until we trust Christ we shall :::,,t dllre t-0 approach God with a confidence that is grounded on our relations with Christ. Thus spiritual. CO'l\"aroice is a mark of unbelief. He who trusts most strongly will enjoy mo.st freedom of access to God.-W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 3:14
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-The universal fatherhood of God. I. THE NATURE OF THE PATllliKHooi:. OF Gon. I. God is the Source of our being. He has not only created us as he has created the rocks. We are not manufactured, but begotten by God. He has breathed his life into us. 2. God has formed us in his own image. There is a similarity of nature in child and pa.rent. All spirits belong to the same family and have a common likeness to God. 3. God is closely related to us. Throughout life the father is most nearly connected with his children by nature and consequent claims and duties. God is our Father now; he has not merely called us into being in the past. He always and necessarily bears the fatherly relation to ns. II. THE EXTENT OF THE FATHERHOOD OF Goo. From God "every family in heaven and earth is named ; " then God is the Father of every family. His fatherhood is universal. I. It reaches to aJ1 spiritual beings. Of what orders, how many, and how various they are, are wholly beyond our speculation. But none are so remote, so peculiar, so lofty, or so low as not to come within God's fatherly relationship. 2. It is iuci.ivido.ally concerned with each separate order of beings. "Every family." The families a.re distin,,,cruished and so are their homes. God regards his children with personal interest. 3. It is not destroyed by evil conduct. There are fallen beings, orders, and families that are de,,araded in sin. But these make no exception to the uni versa! fatherhood. In spite of the shameful corruption of some of the families, God is still Father of alL David did not cease to be the father of the rebel Absalom. The prodigal son conld arise and go unto his father. The worst sinner, when he comes to himself, may say, "My Father." This necessarily results from the very nature of fatherhood. The three facts of origination of life, commnnity of nature, and close relationship can never be annihilated. For a father to ignore them is for him to become an unnatural parent. III. THE 00NSEQUENCEB OF THE FATHERHOOD OF Goo. I. In God. (1) He will manifest a fatherly interest in every family. In choosing the Jew he cannot forget the Gentile. In blessing the Christian he cannot overlook the heathen. Christians, liko the Jews, have foolishly thought to appropriate God to themselves. But less enlightened races have not been neglected by God. He has not left himself without witness in pagan lands. All religions, in so far as they contain any truth, are inspired and rest on Divine revelations. God visits all his children. The seeking after God in the dark of remote mq~ers i" r;. vague response to the voice of God heard_ by the~ in the~r consciences.. (2) God has rights over all men, and no one has a right to disown his Father. God ml! judge a.II and jnstly chastise the disobedient children who refused to admit his claims. (3J God desires to bless all his children and will always welcome back the penitents. 2. In w. (1) We should remember that, as spiritual beings, we are related. If men are akin to the inhabitants of other worlds, much more are they very cl06t:ly related to one another. Hence our duties of brotherhood to ~oreign nations and to savage races. (2) We should have boldness and confidence m our approach to God. St. Paul names the universal fatherhood of God iIL the preface of a prayer.-W. F. A. Ven;. 14-19.-Thegreat mystery of the love of Ohrist. The special object of St. Paul's prayer for the Ephesians is that their knowledge may b_e ~nlarged, and the one direction in which be desires for them the increase of knowledge JS in regard to the love of Christ. That is the most wonderful and the mo11t vital theme of Christian meditation; it can OH, III, 1-21.] 'l'HE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. 145

only be rightly contemplated under spiritual a.id; but the true understanding of it will be fruitful in rich blessings. I. T~ OBEAT MYSTERY o_F THE LOVE OF CHRIST, Everything in Christ is wonderful, but nothing more so than his love. The multitude were astonished at his miraculous powers. Keen e.nte.gonists were confounded before his superlative wisdom; but his friends e.nd disciples were above all and growingly touched by the gentleness, the goodness, the sympathy, the self-sacrifice, and the love which filled his life. This "passeth knowledge" in many respects. 1. Character. (1) Disinterestedness amounting to the extreme of self-denial. Christ never sought his own pleasure. He lived wholly for others. Measure his self-sacrifice by the depth of the descent from the glory of the only begotten Son to the agony and shame of the cross. (2) intensity. 'l'he toil, suffering, and fruitful energy of Christ's love reveal this, (3) Endurance. It is sustained by an infinite patience, like God's long-suffering goodness, like " the mercy of the Lord" which "endureth for ever." Christ stands long at the door and knocks. 2. Comprehensiveness. (1) Extending to the whole world. The objects of our affection are necessarily limited in number. Who can understand a love that embraces Jew and Gentile, Greek and barbarian, and every man, woman, and child in the world? (2) Including the most uninviting subjects. We love those whom we admire or those to whom we are drawn by some attraction, sympathy, or relationship. Christ loves the base, despicable, and corrupt men, remote and obscure folk-" the dim multitude" and those who seem even less lovable-the great mass of dreary, uninteresting people. 3. Objects. These are the highest and purest. A low love indulges, pampers, and spoils in weakly trying to please its objects. Christ's lqve often gives pain, demands sacrifice, perplexes and troubles us. It seeks the redemption, the purification, and the highest glory or men. II. THE WAY TO KNOW THE LOVE OF CHRIST. It "passeth knowledge." Nevertheless, though we cannot comprehend, we may apprehend it, as one who cannot see the mountain's cloud-capped towers may explore its base, as one who can never define an illimitable ocean may grow familiar with its home waters and neighbouring bays. Now, such knowledge as we may have of the supreme mystery of the love of Christ is not t~ be got by merely reading the New Testament history, nor by any amount of theological discussion. It is spiritual, sympathetic, inward, and attained through Divine grace. St. Paul prays for the means of acquiring it. They are three, in successive gradations -one leading on to the other. 1. Spirit=l strength. This is to have life, vigour, e.nd energy in the inner nature. For so long as the spiritual faculties are dead, or slumbering, or only move languidly, they cannot rise to grasp great, Divine things. An inspiratiou of God's Spirit, to be measured only "by the riches of his glory," will supply .his strength. 2. The indwelling Christ. The first act of the awakened, energized spiritual nature is to receive Christ through faith. While he is only outside us we can neither• know him nor love him. 3. Our love to Christ. When we by faith receive Christ into our hearts we learn to love him. Then only can we understand his love. It is true that " we love him because he first loved us;" still, the vague, wondering sense of Christ's love that wins our hearts to him is a poor perception compared with what we shall experience when we look at him with the enlightened eyes of love. Only love can understand love. JII. THE SPIBITUAL BLESSEDNESS THAT FLOWS FROM KNOWING THE LOVE OF CHRIST, This is to "be filled unto all the fulness of God." Men have sought union with God by ascetic devotion, by mystic contemplation, by sacramental grace; for all spiritually awakened souls have felt a void which only God can fill. The secret which priest and' pietist have searched after in vain is here revealed. By understanding the love of Christ we are brought into sympathetic connection with him in whom dwelleth the. fulness of the Godhead bodily, and through his mediation we receive the gre.ces and glories of the Divine nature (John xvii. 21).-W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 3:17
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-The real presence. No great delusion could attain wide influence unless it were the counterfeit or perversion of e. valuable truth, and unless it promised to satisfy some deep, natural desire. The doctrine of the real presence is a pathetic witness to the yearning of the soul for personal fellowship with Christ, and t-0 the truth that he does come into the lives of his people. EPHESIANS, I, THE EPISTLE T0 THE EPHESIANS. [err. 1v. 1-32.

I. CB:R='s r=-.:xa IS RU.L. It mnot eMugh thrit. he should be with us only as "the choir iu,is.ible" of the dcp.vted great are near; i.e. in our memory·and in his influenC<'. We are not satisfied with having bis spirlt among us in the sense in which the spirit of Plato and the spirit of Shakespeare are _still with those who read ' Pbredo' aud • Hamlet.' Christ promised to be personally present with his disciples (Matt. xxviii. 20). He ascended up into heaven, not that he might be .removed from us, but that, rassing from the material to the spiritual world, be might come into the closer contact with our souls. II. CHRIST'S PRESENCE IS IN oUR HEARTS. Ho touches us through our thoughts and :iffcctions. There lies our true self, and it is to our true self that he comes. He makes his 11~cse11ce felt by the truths he inspires, the love he rouses, and the strength he infuses,· _i ust as the sun's presence is felt in the seed when it begins to germinate in its dark tomb hcneath the earth. In this way Christ is even more near to us than -he was to Z:icchreus when he sat at the publican's table, or to John when the beloved disciple leaned on his Master's bosom. . Ill. C1rm.H's PRES~CE IS ABIDING. He comes "not to sojourn;" he abides with us. He is mth us when, busy in doing his will, we are not thinking of the Lord himself, a.s the master is among the workmen who for the moment are too diligent to i,x,k at him. He is with us in hours of spiritual night when we are not enjoying C0mmunion mth him, as a friend may be by our side in the dark, near though undisco,ered. He is with us in our weariness when we·have not strength and heart to pray, as the mother watches her sick child while he lies moaning and quite unconsciollll of her gentle nnrsing. IV. CmusT'S PBESD."CE IS E}.';JOYED THROUGH FAITH. He is not in every heart; for there are Christless souls. Nor is he fullr pre~ent with each one of his own people; for it is on behalf of true Christians that' St. Paul prays for' the strength to receive Christ. He is near to us just in proportion as our faith is vigorous to lay hold of him. Yfo cannot put orn fingers in the nail-prints. We must trust the unseen presence. W o must not look for any second sense, any mystical intuition; for that is as much walking by sight as if we saw our Lord with our bodily eyes. Faith is pure trust i!l. that of which we have no direct apprehension. By this faith we receive Christ.-W. F. A.

entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-77te <Jhrutian 'fDalk. " Walk worthy of· the vocation wherewith ye are called." We now come to the practical part of the Epistle, and the first exhortation is a striking one. Paul attached great importance to the element of walk or character. IIe skilfully puts two things in connection with each other--vocatidn on the one hand, and walk on the other. The preceding chapters had shown the wonderful glory of the Christian vocation. The succeeding chapters are directed to secure a correspondingly elevated Christian walk. Two main topics present themselves. 1. Generally, the value of the Christian walk Q7 character. 2. The kind of walk required-" worthy of the vocation," etc. L V ALO: OF CmusTrili' WALK OR CIIARAcmm. 'l'hie may be sh.own in three aspects. Al!. a. r,1ea for Christianity, or evidence of the reality of Christian faith; as a persuasive toward.5 it, and as a pattern for imitation. 1. A plea. Sceptical tendencies of the present ~oe; k,gic not i;ufficien t to meet them. Strongest popular evidence of Christianity is its inherent trnthfulness, its self-commending power. But next in power is the consistent lives of earnest Christians. Men and women consistently following Christ, ·breathing his spirit, and mo,ing heavenwards, show that his religion is not a·sh.am'or a 8.eception, but a great reality. 2. A persuasive. Such lives appeal to the heart as well as tho head. They show re1ia-ion to be, not only a reality, but a great obligation and .a great blessino- • appeal to th; conscience and force it to say," That is what we ought to ho." Men fe~l• they ought to live like such, and certainly they would fain die like them. 3. A pattern. Do we need it? Have we not other and m~re perfect pattc!ns? ~ormon on mount· life of Christ? Yes, but human nature des1dcrates somethrng on its own level-soO::ething visible and tangible, a stepping-stone between heaven and earth; Hence Paul gave thanks that the Thessalonians became followers of him and of the Lord, and be told the Philippians that he and others were given the~" for an ensample." Every Christian congregation should have a number of model Christians fitted to be examples to the rest-the elders a.nd elderly peoplo es~ecially. Men may sneer at model Christians, but they do not sneer at model so~d1ers or . model servants! and certainly every Christian worthy of the name should aim at bemg ae near Christ aa r,0ssible. IL Tm:: KISD OF WALK. "Worthy of the vocation wherewith yo a.re called." We have all an idt-a c,f consistency; inconsistency should be the object of our abhorrence. 'l'he world has a keen eye for inconsblcncies of Christians, and exposes them mercilessly. It takes comrort from them to continue in sin. thought nothing of in the worldly. If wha.t David did in re Uriah bad been done by Nebuchadnezzar, no one would have said anything. A consistent walk is, by God's help, within.the reach of all. It is an impressive sermon to the world, a continual sermon, a.n unanswerable sermon. Let all preach this sermon, though it be their only tine. 'l'he "walk worthy" is a walk of holiness, humility, forbearance, forgiveness, patience, charity. It is also a walk of brightness and beneficence. It seeks to make the world brighter and better. Let us be urged to it by the sins of the world, by the miseries of the world, by the dangers of the world, as regards the soul. In order to promote it, let us be much with Christ, and as far as we can, with those who are like Christ. Let. us study the biographies of Christ-like men and aim at conformity to their example. Let us often pray the prayer of the third chapter of this book, and other prayers of the like tenor. Let us use earnestly our means of grace, praying that each sabbath, each sermon, each sacrament, may serve to make us more worthy of the vocation wherewith we are called,

entries.title: EPH 4:2–6
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -Details of a wal,k worthy of the 110cation. This walk demands-- I. THE PRESERVATION Oll' SOCIAL CONCORD, THROUGH THE QUIET OR PASSIVE VIRTUES, which, having been very characteristic of Christ, are eminently incumbent on all who bear his Name. 1. Lowliness, arising from a chastened sense of our sin and unworthiness. 2. Meekness, which is in speech what lowliness is in spirit. 3. Lrmg-suffering and forbearanee i11 ~'6; in opposition to hastiness, irascibility, impatience, ill temper, which, though often little thought of, are eminently unworthy of the Christian calling. Christian victories are often gained by meekness and endurance-what Milton called "the invincible might of meekness.'' These graces have reference mainly to the ordinary intercourse of social life; what follows has to do more with the public life of the Church. II. THE PRESERVATION OF ECCLESIASTICAL CONCORD THROUGH THE BOND OF PEACE, The concord to be preserved is the "unity of the Spirit "-the unity of which the Holy Spirit is the Author; not mere external uniformity, but inward agreement. It is a fact that there is much inward a.greement wherever the Spirit of God works. It is our duty to preserve, this-to keep it from beiog broken or even appearing as if broken. This unity is to be maintained by the bond which consists of "peace ; " by a peaceloving and peace-seeking spirit, that spirit of which Christ said, " Blessed are the peacemakers:· for they shall be called the children of God." The danger of breaking the unity of the Spirit is great ; readiness to take offence, pride, regardlcssness of the welfare of others, forgetfulness of the vast Christian work and warfare committed to us, are temptations to this, On the other band, the habitual striving after the graces enumerated above, and trying to exercise them habitually, tend to preserve the unity of the Spirit, and to a large extent, too, to preserve external agreement in the government and worship and work' of the Church. III. In connection with this subject, the apostle shows WHEREIN TIIE UNITY OF TITE SPIRIT CONSISTS, AND Wl!EREIN IT IS TO BE PRESERVED. There is a sevenfold unity (sco Exposition). That true believers are one in Christ is one of thoso truths which h[lppily eveu controversy and sectarianism do not C]Uite obliterate. But a moro full, ricb, and constant manifestation of this unity would make a great impression on the world; it. would remove one of tho most common excuses of scepticism; it would tend powerfully both to edify and to extend the cause of Christ; and it would mako tho fellowship of the Church much more delightful, spreading more of the atmosphere of heaven upon earth.

entries.title: EPH 4:7–11
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-0hrist's gifts to his Church. The grand object of the apostle in this section of hill Epistle is to show the ample provision made by Christ for tbo welfaro of his Church. The Church may sing as well ag the individual, " The Lord is my Shepherd; I shall not want." The particular object is to indicato that the gifts conferred by him on the members individually (vers. 7-10), and especially the appointment of the several classes of office-bearers (ver. 10), show the Lord's earnest desire to raise his Church to the highest possible condition of grace and honour; to make her complete and glorious, as the one body of which he is the Ilcad, the one vessel into which ha is to ponr all bis fulnese, the bride on whom he is to exhaust every ornament. 156 'l'HE EPISTLE '1'0 TRE EPHESIANS. toa. IV. 1-32.

The marks of Christ's care for bis Church are innumerabfo; they recede back through nil et.l'rnity i,.nd fonrnrd for evermore (eh. iii. 18, 19). His death marked the climax of his srlf-s~crifice; but e,·on that did not end Christ's service for his Church. For her he 1wt ,mly descended from heaven to earth, but for her too he reascended from earth (() liearen; like the high priest, he went into the holiest of all with his Name on his breastplate, and he only changed the sphere in which his mediatorial office was exercised. But more ; the good Shepherd is ever renewing the miracle of the five loa"es and two fishes; ever saying with reference to his people, "Give yo them to eat;" and ever appointing and qualifying suitable officers to take care of his Church and break among them the bread of life. He is ever qualifying his ministers for rulinu and feeding his flock, for filling the empty soul, speaking a word in season to the .;eary, guiding the perplexed, reclaiming the erring, strengthening the weak, supporting the feeble-minded, and sending on the ransomed of the Lord to Zion, with songs and ever- hsting joy upon their heads. The subject dhides into two-the gift-giving (vers. 7-11), and the end or purpose for which the gifts are given (vers. 12-16). In the first part w-e find: 1. The source of the gifts and the principle of distribution (ver. 7). 2. Connrmation of this from the sixty-eighth psalm (ver. 8). 3. Commentary and inferenoes therefrom (vers. 9, 10). 4. 'l'he special gift of suitable officers. L L Christ is the great Source of grace, including ordinary and extraordinary gifts (" the gift of Christ"). 2. Christ leaves no one out; to every one of us is given grace. 3. The grace was not given in equal measures to all 4. But according to the measnre of the gift of Christ. II. From the sixty-eighth psalm it appears that this proceeding was symbolized when the ark was placed on Mount Zion, when David's victories were celebrated, and a dis- tribution of gifts took place. III. The word " ascended," applied to the Son of God, implied a previous descent; for when he ascended, he went to his own home and seat ; previous to this he came down, and the apostle dwells especially on his having come down to the lower parts of the earth, such as Gethsemane, Calvary, and the grave. His was no holiday visit to earth, to green :fields, or golden palaces; "He was taken from prison and from judgment." Yet even there he triumphed over all his enemies, and now he is exalted " far above all heavens." This last expression is very remarkable, especially in the view of what modern astronomy teaches on the extent of the heavens. It is a marvellous testimony to the glory of the risen Lord. Still higher is the testimony to his glory in the pnrpose for -which he has gone on high-" that he might fill all things." The sun, in the centre of the solar cyst.em. fills that system, spreading light and heat and manifold influences to its extremest limits. All the colours that beautify earth, sea, and sky; all the heat that fosters life and gladdens living creatures of every kind; all the chemical influences that are so manifold in their effects on the economy of nature, radfate from the sun. So Christ is Sun and Centre of the infinite universe, and the universe is filled by him with heavenly influences. There are many sans, but only one Saviour ; there are many systems of worlds, according to our modern astronomy, and even firmaments of worlds, beyond the ken of our strongest instruments; but all are joined by one glorious bond; for not only have they been all formed by one Creator, but all have been "filled" by the one all-glorious Mediator-Lord. What resources does that expression, "that he might fill all things," ascribe to Christ! If he can fill all things, he can fill us ; our hearts are not easily filled; but what can be wanting to us out of such fnlness '/ IV. But from the stars we come back to the Church, and consider Christ as exalted to fill hiB Church. With this view he has qualified and commissioned certain officers to minister to his Church. Of these it is generally allowed that apostles and prophets wero special and temporary; while evangelists, pastors, and teacher~ are ordinary and permanent (see Exposition). Observe that such men are t.o be received (and when needed to be culwi too) as gifts of Chri&t to his Church. It is the Lord of tho harvest who equii- and furnishes labonrere for his harvest. We should not seek ministers of the g'lSpcl, as some do, for onr own pleasure or credit, rejecting them if they do not_ quite ar:iswer our idea; but aa gifts of Christ, in which their great object will be to build up L.is Church and promote the beauty of his bride.

entries.content:

Obrist has a work of perfection on hand. 'l'his denoted by-" for the perfecting of the saints" (ver. 12), and "unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the ful- ness of Christ" (ver. 13). What a high aim with reference to creatures so poor a1,<l needy as the members of his Church! 11. In order to this, the work of the ministry exists; and that work seeks (1) "the edifying the body of Christ;" (2) the promotion of unity of faith and of the knowlerlgc of the Son of God (ver. 13); (3) protection of the Church from childish :fickleness and the arts of men who seek to unsettle her (ver. 14). In order to accomplish these end:;, the ministry is called to speak the truth in love (ver. 15), and especially truth " as it is in Jesus" (ver. 21). 'l'ruth, thus spoken, is the great means of spiritual edification and of progress towards perfection. External rites or ceremonies can profit nothiug except in so far as they are Divine channels for conveying this truth. ill. While ministers are instruments, Jesus is himself the great Source of growth. 1. The growth to be promoted is growth" unto him who is the Head" (ver. 15). All vital, spiritual influence is in Christ. As the woman reasom,d, "If I may but touch the hem of his garment, I shall be made whole;" so if we, by faith, shall come into contact with our living Head, his gracious influence will spread through our souls. 2. The whole Church is articulated with Christ; its parts are articulated with each other, but all are designed to communicate with the Head, and to assist in conveying vital influence from the Head to the members. So it is in the human body ; it is all jo1nted and connected together; but the object of this is to facilitate the transmission of the vital force throughout the whole. All the members of the Church should realize their position as parts of a body connected with the bead, and should regard the measure of energy received by them as designed for the general good (ver. 16). 8. While Christ is the sole Source of vital influence, and ministers are the main instruments of its transmission, the whole body is to be self-edifying, intelligently and consciously moving on towards the grand consummation (vcr. 16). Ministers do not differ in kind from the members. They have got special gifts for the edifying of the body, but Cl'ery part of the body has got some gift for the same end. All ought to conspire harmoniously together, keeping in view the grand consummation. Churches and members of Churches must not be content with any inferior aim, but habitually and earnestly move on toward perfection. And for this the Spirit of love is indispensable (ver. 16). '!'he Church cannot edify itself except in love. Strife and division are sure to arise, and these are not edifying, but disintegrating. One great lesson here is that, as Christ is the Truth, so he also is the Life. The gospel as a system of truth has Christ in the centre; so the Church as a living agency has Christ in the centre. Take Christ from either, and "Ichabod" may be inscribed on the wall.

entries.title: EPH 4:17–24
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Contrasted principles of Gentile and Christian character. We now corne more explicitly to the details of Christian duty. The apostle bad presented a very high standard of Christian privilege in the preceding chapters, and now he presents an equally high standard of Christian duty. What God gives iu the one form is to be given back in the other, and in corresponding proportion. The importance of the subject is indicated by the formula, "This I say, and testify in the Lord." Tho apostle contrasts tbe Christian with the Gentile walk, and indicates wherein the latter is to differ from the former, (1) in what the Christian i8 not to be, and (2) in what he is to be. I. 1. In the vanity of their mind. 2. In tbe darkness of their understanding. 8. In their alienation from the life of God. 4. In their abandonment to lasciviousness. 'fhus even Christia-n converts] need to remember the duty to keep themselves unspotted by the world. There is a world of guilt and godlessness from which it is necessary for them to keep themselves unstained. II. PoBITIVE RULES OF CHRISTIAN LIFE. 1. Their Source. "Ye have not so learned Christ, if so be ye heard him," etc. (ver. 20). The whole tenor of Christ's teaching and influence is against these things. Only make sure that you have come under it. 2. What they are. (1) "Put off the old man," etc. Comprehensiveness of the word "man;" his tendency is to rottenness ,or corruption; the lusts of deceit which are connected with him are pernicious and ruinou8. (2) " Be renewed in the spirit of your IJ1iod." Renewal begins within by the Holy Spirit rousing in you a desire for it, l\lld 158 THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS.

urging you to use the means towards it, Accept aud improve these movements of the Spirit within you. (3) In this way, "put on the new man," and especially encourage and seek t-0 have developed these two features of the new creation-rio-hteousness and holiness. Righteousness, including int.egrity, honest., true, fair open°dealin"' • doing justly out and out, in every place and in every relation-in the house, the" ~arket, the counting-house, the shop, among neighbours, among strangers, everywhere and at nE times. Holiness of truth, including high reverence for God and all that is Divine s_.-;:npathy and congenisJity of he..'\I"t "ith Gvd, cleanness of nature, purity of soW: ,:c•ar:o~ty to the image of Christ, ~ho is the I_n_rnge of the invisible God. No professing umstian ca.n be ~empted from this rule of lite. Nor should any assume too readily that he is thoroughly conforming to it. "Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall." Christianity in its practical relations, is very searching and thorouo-h. It ,iemands a high standard of life and practice. But no wonder, if Christ be the n:ad, the Sonrr,e of all ,ital power, and if there be a complete provision by which the needed rower may be communicated to all the members. Never let it be said to Christians, " What do ye more than others ? "

entries.title: EPH 4:25
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
Ephesians somewhat resembled Joshua the high priest, when standing before the angel of the Lord, and when Satan was standing at his right hand to resist him. Joshua was clothed with filthy garments, and the angel spake to those that stood before him," Take away the filthy garments from him. And unto him he said, "Behold, I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee,and I will clothe thee with change of raiment." Raas uf the old man still hang about these Ephesians, disfiguring their persons and giviI~g them a very different appearance from that which befits the regenerated sons of God. The apostle is giving directions to take away each filthy rag and substitute for it the fair raiment of the new man. And he is doing this under a solemn sense of danger and responsibility, and with the feeling that two great spirits are also interested in the work and acti,ely concerned in it-the one, the spirit of evil, who is trying cunningly but earnestly to spoil the proces.s, and induce the Ephesians to cling to their own garmenu;; the other, the blessed Spirit of God, who in his in.finite love is seeking t-0 clothe the Corinthians in the garments of purity, to seal them unto the day of redemption, so that by the brightness of their appearance they shall be known to be God's in the day when he makes up his jewels. And what makes the whole matter so solemn and momentous is that, unless they are ever on their guard, the subjects of this process are ever liable to give place to the one spirit and to grieve the other; the awful danger lying in this, that the spirit to whom they are prone to yield is the spirit of evil, and the Spirit they are apt to grieve is the Holy Spirit of God. 1. The rags of the old man to be put off are lying, anger, stealing, coarse language, bitterness, wrath, anger, clamour, evil-speaking, and malice (see Exposition). 'l'hree reasons are given, more or less explicitly, why such things should be put away. (1) We are members ono of another (ver. 25), and ought to assist instead of injuring one another (var. 28). (2) We ought not to give place to the devil (ver. 27). (3) We ought not to grieve the Holy Spirit of God. 2. The robes of the new man to be put o_n are tr~t~ful_ness, h~nest industry, edifying speech, kindness, tenderness of heart, forgiveness, rnutat1on of God, and the lovirig walk which becomes his followers. 'fhree reasons are given likewisa wby these robes should be put on. (1) God in ~rist forgave u_s (ver. 32). (2) Christ loved us. (3) Christ gave himself for us, an offenng and a sacri:fice to God of a sweetrn1elling savonr. 'lllis ~ one o~ the most compre~ensive _a°;d ~ea.utiful su:nmaries vf tne C,'hristian life. It 1S the qwntessence of practical Chnstwnty. It furnishes an admirable rule for self-examination, and an admirable incentive to progress in the life of God. It is a passage, not only to be got by heart, but written on the heart. We may wdl Eay, as we read t~ese verses, "This i8 Ch_ristianity; this is the walk worthy of our vocation." If the writer of the hundred and nineteenth psalm had such boundless delight in the Law of God, though it had not to him the delightiul evangelical aroma. it has to 11s, what ought our feelings to be? Under all dispensations of the covenant. the Law is still the rule of our life, thongh salvation is of grace;· and the ·prayer tha~ continually becomes us is, "Incline my heart unto thy testimonies; quicken thou me, tl1at I may keep thy Law." Rags or robes; why should any hesitate between them?

To most men rags are most repulsive. To wear literal rags-to appear shabby, dirty, untidy, is very unpleasant. How much more, in the eyes of God -and the saints and ang~ls, to wear moral rags! Many a one clothed in purple and fine linen wears the filtlnest rags of the old man ; and some, on the other hand, in the plainest and coarsest attire, have put on the beautiful robes of righteousness, and shall be crowns of glory in the hands of the Lord and royal diadems in the hands of their God.

entries.title: EPH 4:1
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -Ethics after theology. The doctrinal part of the Epistle is now finished and the practical part begins. This is the true and natural order. l. IT IS IN THE SPHERE OF THE DOCTRINAL THAT WE FIND THE POWER TIIAT CAB.RIES US THROUGH ALL PRACTICAL DUTIES. In all the Epistles the duties enforced are grounded in the doctrines declared or explained. The doctrines are the reservoir which sends its stream of power down over the human life. The engineer scoops out a hollow space to be filled with water, constructs his machinery, and then lifts the sluice that sets all the machinery in motion. When the doctrines of grace have been fully expounded, the apostle lifts the sluice aud lets on the stream that sends life spinnin~ round and round in a course of holy activity. "I beseech you therefore, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice" (Rom. xii. 1). II. IT IS NECESSABY TO INCULCATE CHRISTIAN DUTIES EVEN IN THE CASE OF CHltISTIANs.· If the apostles did it, we must do it. It is only Antinomianismresting on the doctrines of grace without watchfulness of the walk before God-that contests this principle. An Antinomian Bible would have no place for duties. Christianity includes duties as well as doctrines .. It does not merely hold out a refuge to the guilty, but takes all who accept Christ under it-s supreme and exclusive direction. It evangelizes human life by impregnating its minutest transactions with the spirit of the gospel. But we must be always careful, in :preaching the necessity of good works and iu enforcing Christian duties, to ground them, as the Scriptures ground them, in the doctrines of grace.-T. C.

entries.title: EPH 4:1
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -The obligations of the CJhristian calling. "Walk worthy of the calling wherewith ye are called." I. THE NATURE OF THIS CALLING. It is the Christian vocation. We are called out of darkness into God's marvellous light(! Pet. ii. 9), into the grace of Cl:rist (Gal. i. G), into the fellowship of Christ (1 Cor. i. 9); unto holiness (1 'l'hess. ii. 7); unto glory and virtue (2 Pet. i. 3); unto peace (1 Cor. vii. 15), not only with Goel, but with our consciences and with one another (Acts xxiv. 16; eh. iv. 2). 'l'his calling is o high calling, a. holy calling, a heavenly calling. We may well, therefore, walk worthy of it. II. THE wALK IN HARMONY WITH OUR CALLING. It is emphatically "to walk worthy of the Lord unto all pleosing" (Col. i. 10); "to walk worthy of God who bath called you unto his kingdom and glory" (1 Thess. ii. 12) ; to have a conversation becoming the gospel of Christ (Phil. i. 27). In human society, men are often kept from unworthy courses by a feeling of honour, as gentlemen; how much more ought Christians, to cherish a. sense of honour as disciples of the Saviour and joint-heirs with him of tho kingdom of heaven I 'l'he feeling of family honour is often a. powerful guard against mean or ungenerous actions. It is a profound disgrace to find the descendant of an ancient and noble family forswear all its best traditions. As members of the household of God, as brethren of Jesus Christ himself, shall we disgrace this sublime relationship'? We cannot afford to bring shame upon our profession (Heb. vi. 6), to lose the comfort of our calling (Ps. xix. 11), or to lose its end (Heb. xii. 14). Let us not, therefore, affront our calling by inconsistencies, but walk in a way that will fully harmonize with its nature, glory, and end. It is all the more necessary to do so as the true walk of a saint tends so powerfully to promote the unity of the Church.-T. C.

entries.title: EPH 4:2
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Graces that pl'omote the harmony of the Ohurch, "All lowliness and meekness, with long-suffering, forbearing one another in love." These graces are 'l'HE EPIS'l'LE TO THE EPHESIANS. [OH, IV, 1-3~

specially needful in the Church; for their opposites; pride, irascibility, and impatience do much to create heart-burning and division. I. LoWLINESS OF MIND. 1. Its tuiture. It is that deep humility, as opposed t1, pride, arrogance, and_ conceit, which is produ~ by a right sense of our weakness, 1gnornnce, an~ depe1;1<1ence, and by a due apprec1at1on of the undeserved glory to which we are called m Christ Jesus. Men are made humble and self-dititrustful less by the l..iwwle.:lge that they are weak, ignorant, and mortal, than by the fact that, while striving i,,r_a hii;:her end, they are 11lways coming short of it by their mistakes and their follies, :.:·,~ are ID constaut need of a strength greater than their own. It is thus possible ta ''!::te ::. high aim with a profound humility. 2. Its importance. It is necessary lw,rn:se fu-.d requires it (Micah vi. S); because Christ c-xemplified it (Matt. xi. 29), l't'<'an:se God dwells with the humble (Isa. h-iii. 15); because it is the way to leam wisdom (Prov. xi. 2), to attain grace and holiness (Prov. iii. 5, 6; Jas. iv. 6), and to pre:-en-e unity in the Church (Ja.s. i,. 1). It has many promises made to it. God will respect the humble (Isa. !xvi. 2), he will give them grace (1 Pet. v. 6), he will exalt them (1 Pet. v. 6), and reward them with all good things. Its importance is specially manifest in Church relations. Believers are not to think of themseives more highly than they ought t-0 think (Rom. xii. 3), nor exalt themselves above their degree (2 Cor. x. 13-15), but to esteem others better than themselves (Phil. ii. 3). Let believers, therefore, have a humble apprehension of their knowledge, for" knowledge 1,uffeth up" (1 Cor. viii 1); and humble thoughts of their goo_dness, for we cannot understand all our errors, and need to be cleansed from our secret faults (Ps. xix. 12). Let them "pnt on humbleness of mind," as the brightest ornament of Christian character (CoL iii. 12). 11. Mui.:m:ss. There is a natural connection between meekness and humility, and therefore they are often joined together. 1. Its natwre. It is that disposition which «ioc:, not arraign God and does not avenge itself on man. As regards God, it implies a rc:acly submission to the authority of bis Word (Ja.s. i. 21), and a cheerful resignation to i..Lis proviaence, as opposed to murmuring and fretfulness (Ps. xxxix. 9). As rcf;<.rds man., the meek will have a calm temper under provocations; he will be "slow ,u =th" (Jas. L 19); he will give "the sott answer that turneth a.way wrath" (Prov. :: ,. 1); he will show that ornament of a meek and quiet spirit which adorns more than rnLies (1 Pet. iii. 4). When joined with strength it makes one of the most effective c:,ar-Jcters. It is especially to be esteemed in a religions life. Therefore the apostle says, " Let him show out of a good conversation his works with meekness of wisdom" (Jas. iii.13). It is with meekness and fear that we a.re to give a reason of our hope (1 Pet. iii. 15), and it is in a spirit of meekness we are to recover the erring (Gal. vi. l). It is one of the nine graces of the Spirit (Gal. v. 22). 2. its importance. . See how largely it contributes to the usefulness of Christian life. The meek man has great power with men. See how it contributes to the comfort of life; for it keeps him from the friction of temper that so often detracts from true repose; it brings us nearer and nearer to him who was pre-eminently "meek and lowly of spirit" (Matt. xi. 29); and it has the promise of the earth for an inheritance (Matt. v. 5). Let us, therefore, seek meekness (Zeph. ii. 3). IIL LoNG-oUFFERING. 1. Its natwre. It is the disposition that leads us to supprllSS our anger (2 Cor. vi. 6; Gal. v. 22); and is opposed to that irritability often exvressively called shortness of temper, which is quick to show resentment. This spirit is of great moment in the Church, where there may be frequent collisions of opiruon., or interest, or feeling, and it waits with patience till the passionate or obstinate &:<c: their way to more reasonable courses. 2. Its importance, God commands it (Rom. rii. 17). He exemplifies it (Matt. v. 44; llom. v. 6-8), and !,is Son bas left us a u,ost impre&ive exhibition of it (1 Pet. ii. 21-23). We all fail iu our duty an,J nt:ed to ha\'e due considcrntion made to our failings. We are above all to bear and forbe...r in matters of religious fellowship (Hom. xv. 1). IV. THE SPI.E.IT IN WlflCH THIS LONG-SUFFERING 18 TO DE EXERCISED. " Forbearing one another in love." Christians are not to resent injuries or retaliate for wrongs done tc, them, but are to bear with each other's infirmities, to cover each other's weaknesses, to pity each other's frailties, and to forgive the provocations they injlict upon each other. This is to bi:! done, not from a principle /'Jf merely worldly courtesy or from OIi. IV. 1---32.] THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. 161

contemptuous inuifference, but from that love which" suffereth Ion", and is kind." It is "charity which covercth a muHitude of sins," just as surely as'?, hatred stirreth up strife" (Prov. x. 12). It would be impossible to secure the eq uauimity of life if the principle of forbearance, prompted and guided by love, were not uenerally exercised. The counsel of the apostle in this whole passage pointedly condemns the proud arrocrant, censorious disposition, which tramples, not only on the rules of courtesy bu"t of Christian affection. We owe to others what they require at our hands. There' is much in us they have to allow for, and therefore it becomes us to allow for much in them. Therefore our very manners ought to show true Christian consideration, for the poet has rightly said- "And manners a.re not idle, bnt the fruit Of loyal natnre and of noble mind." T.C.

entries.title: EPH 4:3
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-The unity of the Spirit ana the mode of its keeping. "Endeavouling to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." I. CONSIDER THE NATURE OF THIS UNITY. 1. It is not the unity of the body, the Church. That is an immutable unity which man cannot keep. God alone keeps it. Neither are we commanded to make the unity of the Spirit, but simply to keep it-for it exists, in a sense, independently of man's fidelity; but in the degree in which it is kept in the bond of peace, it will eventually lead to visible oneness. 2. Much less is it a unity of external organization. That unity existed already at Ephesus. It is rather a unity in view of internal differences, w_hich must have existed at Ephesus, as in other Churches which had a mixed membership of Jews and Gentiles. Christ did undoubtedly make both one on the cross, but the apostles allowed a considerable diversity of order and usage to exist in the Churches, according to the dominance of the Jewish or the Gentile element in them. There were Churches that followed the rule of Moses-the apostles themselves holding by the ceremonial law till the end of their lives (Acts xxi. 20-26). And there were Churches that did not observe days nor follow Jewish usage, but took a course authorized by apostolic command itself. If the differences that existed in the days of the apostles did not destroy the unity of the body, it is difficult to see how similar differences in order and worship can destroy it now. 3. The unity of the Spirit is that unity of which the Spirit is the Author. Its indwelling is the principlo of unity in the body of Christ. Man, therefore, cannot make it, nor can he destroy it, though he can thwart or disturb its manifestations. 'l'he use of the word "endeavouring'' implies that it may be kept with a greater or lesser degree of fidelity. II. CONSIDER HOW THIS UNITY IB TO DE PRESERVED.. "In the bond of peace." That is, the bond which is peace, springing out of humility, meekness, and forbearance. Just as pride, arrogance, and contention are separating elemonts, tho opposite dispositions are conducive to unity. The peace which is the element of Christinn society is that to which we are called in one body; for we are called by tho God of peac8, redeemed by Christ who is our Peace, sanctified by tho Spirit whoso fruit is peace, and edified by the gospel of peace, that we may walk as sons of pence. 'l'hus tho unity is preserved and manifested by peace, as it is marred or lost sight of amidst conflicts and jars. The apostolic injunction is very inconsistent with the Darbyite principle that the unity of the Spirit is to be preserved by separation from evil, theological, ecclesiastical, or moraL It is strange that the apostle never hints at such a thing as soparation, but speak0 only of such graces as "lowliness, meekness, with long-suffering," which arc but little exemplified in many of the separations brought about by such a principle. The Darbyite principle is not a bond of peace. It multiplies separations and divides the saints of God. There is uniting power in a common belief or in n common aliec- tion, bnt there is none in mere separation from evil. The common rejection of Arianism can never become e. centre of union for Protestants e.nd Roman Catholics, because they are still so fundamentally apart in tho whole spirit of their theology. The unity of the Spirit which we are enjoined to keep is, therefore, a unity compatible with minor differences, and ought to be the grand means of throwing the unity of the body into a more glorious distinctness before the world.-T, 0,
