"I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord," etc. The ver11011, looked at homiletically, suggest the following truths:- L TluT JLUi's EX7ERNAL CONDITION IN THIS WOBLD IS l'IO TBUE TEST OJ!' BIS BEAL -woBTR. A greater man than Paul, greater in; tru~ thought, l?fty aims, disinter~sted sympathies, self-sacrificing love, Christ-like devotion, and philanthropy, ne'!er lived. He was great in himself, great in his spiritual influence, great in the estimation of all capable of appreciating worth. Yet he was a "pri~oner" and doomed to martyrd?ma condition the most ignominious and painful. This. fact shows : 1, TM corruption o/ OU, IV, 1-32,] THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. 191

liuman society. So blind in moral judgment and so perverse in heart bas civil society been, o.lmost from the beginning, that it has doomed its best men to degradation, suffering, and often martyrdom. 2. T/uJ high probability of a future retributive dispensation. The beheading of John the Baptist, the imprisonment of a Paul, the crucifying of the Christ, proclaim with a. tongue of thunder a coming judgment, a day when "all ungodly men shall be convinced of all ungodly things which they have ungodly committed." II. THAT THE END OF ALL TRUE THEOLOGY IS THE IMPROVEMENT OF CHARACTER. The apostle, after laying down in the preceding chapters the grandest theological truths, begins in these verses an application of these truths to practical life. "I beseech you therefore." "Therefore." Why? Because of the wonder fol things I have stated. Theology, if it remains with us merely as a science, will do us no spiritual service. It may stimulate thought, widen the realm of intelligence, afford scope and incentive to our speculative faculties, and develop our powers of logic and controversy. ,But what boots all this? Devils i.!i depravity and torture arc theologians. lt is only when theological truths pass from the intellect to the heart, and thence circulate as blood through every particle of our being-in other words, when doctrines are translated into deeds-that they really serve us. Theology is bread ; but undigested bread does not impart health, but impairs it, does not invigorate the man, but enfeebles him. A great theologian is often a. moral invalid. Ill. THAT THE PRrvILEGES OF A MORAL BEING ARE THE MEASURE OF HIS OBLIGATIONS, "Walk worthy of the vocation," etc. The Bible teaches us our duty, not so much by written precepts as by principles, either expressed _or implied. Indeed, it seems to me no code of legislative propositions, though its volumes filled the world, could supply directions for the boundless activities of an undying soul. You cannot bring all the obligations of souls into any number of written sentences. Hence we have principles, and often one principle will meet all the possible activities of a soul, determine its duty in every separate act. The principle we have stated is an example. When a real Christian is told to "act worthy of his vocation," he is told everything touching all conceivable obligations, This point supplies us with two genernl remarks. 1. Ghrist iuns are called into a Divine sonship, and their duty is to ivalk worthy of that. The call you have in the fifth verse of the first chapter. "Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will." We are called to be the sons of God, What is our duty? •ro act worthy of our relationship, act as sons ought to act towards such a Father. Give him: (1) Tho highest reverence. Our heavenly Father is not only greatest to us, but greatest to tho universe. 'rherefore reverence him. (2) The highest gratitu<l,e. W o owe everythiLi; to him-being and the highest blessings of being. Therefore to him our profoundest arn! incessant thanks are due, (3) The highest esteem. He is tl.ie best of Beings, the Fountain of all virtues, the Standard of all character, the Totality of goodness. Therefore he should be love,\ with all our soul and strength. (4) The highest confidence. Yield to him a cheerful trust, a boundless reliance. Trust in him for ever. (5) '!.'ho highest attention. lie should occupy more. of our thoughts than any other being, You should study his character, trace his ways, anticipale his wishes, imbibe his Spirit, imitate hie character, 11nd thus become partakers of his nature. When Christians are told to walk worthy of their sonship, what more can be said? It means to livo a pure, useful, elevated, morally royal life. 2. Christians are called into a spiritual corporation, and their duty is to walk worthy of that. When on earth Christ founded a new society, its members consisted. of those who practically accepted him ns their great Teacher, Example, Saviour, Lord. That society, few in numbers at firs~, has been increasing ever since. Millions have gone to heaven, and millions are still on this earth found in connection with all Churches, and not a few in connection with none. This society, though its members are divided by sentiment and ritual and distance, are nevertheless one-one in spirit, purpose, life. They are but branches of ono tree the Root of which is Christ, members of one body the Head of which is Christ. Now, every Christian is called into this grand corporation. And the apostle here states two things concerning onr relation to it. (1) 'l'he grand purpose we should aim at. "Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in tho bond of peace." "Unity of the Spirit," mP.ans the unity of which .the Spirit is the Author, Unity, not merely doctrinal 193 'l'HE EPISTLE 'l'O THE EPHESIANS. [OH, IV, 1-82,

or ecclesiastical, for there may be doctrinal. and ecclesiastical unity where there is spiritual srp..~rntion. It i~ ~he unity of souls in Christ. Now, every one belonging to this corporat!on s_houl~ d1hgently endeavour to maintain its unity. This unity is c[lusonant with d1vcrs1ty; the waves are different, but the ocean is one; the branches arc differe~t, but the tree is one; ~he members ,are different, but the body is one; the stoirs arc different, but the system 1s one. Men s thoughts may be different, but men's loves may be one, and loves are the bonds of souls. (2) The method/or promoting this purpose. Three things arc indicated here. (a) Humility. "With all lowliness and meekness." Pride, arrogance, and haughtiness in all its forms, have ever been amongst the most disturbing elements in Church life. (b) Mutual forbearance, "Forbearing one another." The best members of this Church are imperfect in belief, sympathies, and conduct; hence mutual forbearance is necessary in order to maintain unity. He who feels disposed to quarrel with every fault of his associates may spend bis time in doin~ nothing else. (c) Brotherly love. "Forbearing one another in love." Lo,e is the healer of discords. No hand but hers can retune the discordant harp of Church life. These-lowliness, meekness, long-suffering, loving forbearance-quiet, u:ipretending, unshowy rutues are amon~;; the best means for promoting true unity in t'J.e Church of God. Wbo is the most useful Christian? Not as a rule he who has t'..;e r..1ost t=scendent genins, brilliant talents, and commanding eloquence, but he who has the most of tbis quiet, loving, forbearing spirit. The world may do without :;:s Sia,,,craras, whose thundering roar and majestic rnsh excite the highest amazement of mankind, out it cannot spa.re the thousand rivulets that glide unseen and unheard crery moment through the earth, imparting life and verdure and beauty wherever they go. And so the Cbnrch may do without its men of splendid abilities, but it cannot do without its men of tender, loving, forbearing souls.-D. T. Vcrs. 3-6.-1?!,e unitiu of <Jhristianity· a reason for union amongst <Jhristians. "Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all" These various unities in Christianity are here specified by the apostle in order to enforce the importance and obligation of a loving concord amongst all true Cbristians. By noticing these unities with a little closer attention we shall see how they formed in the apostle's mind an argwment jor a loving union amongst all the di.scip"les of Christ. L All Cbristians are members of ONE SPIRITUAL OBGA.NIZ.ATION. "One body." Thongh t"hey are ,ery numerons and ever increasing, though they differ widely in many morally 1Ulfundamental points, and live in different lands and different worlds, still they are parts of one great whole. The tree, thongh it bas a thousand branches all varying in liize and shape and hue, is an organic whole. 'l'his nnity, though not visible, really exists. To be a Cbristian is to be a branch of the one tree, a stone in the one building, a member of the one body. Now, this fact is certainly a str011,g reason for the cherishing amongst all of brotherly Jove and hearty fellowshlp. " That there should be no schism in the body• but that the members should have the same care one for another. And whether one' member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it." II. All Christians are animated by ONE GBEAT SPmIT. "One Spirit." What the body is to the human :soul, this great organization, this universal Church, is to the Spi:it of the living God. 1. Servant_. As every member o( ~he body i~ th~ serva~t of the 11◊ul every genuine Christian 1s the servant of the Spmt, obeys his dictates m everything. 2. Symbol. A.B the body reveals and expresses the soul by its looks, words, 11nd operations, so the true_ C~ur?h reveals the Diyine Spirit j reveals ~ts quick~ning, redeeming, elevating, sanctifymg mflucnce. 3. Residen<XJ. As the body 1s the re~1dence of the soul even so the Church is the temple for the Holy Ghost to dwell Ill, If there is this one Spirit running through all, guiding, animating, ovem1ling all, should there not be through all a mutual, loving sympathy and interest? IIL All Christians have ONE GLOBIOUB HEAVEN, "One hope." What ie the object of a true Christian's hope? Not happiness. Be whose grand object in life is his own bappirie85 is under the influence of that selfishness which is the essence of sin and the Oil, IV, 1-32.] THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. 1!)3

devil of tho soul. That spirit in Churches which cries, "Oh that I had the wings of a dove ! then would I fly away and be at rest," is discontented selfishness, nothing more. AI11:9 I t~at there should be churches, chapels, and pulpits in England ministering to an m~t1able ave.rice that considers this beautiful world not good enou 6h for its home! But if the objed of a true Christian's hope is not happiness, what then? Morat goodness. Goodness as exemplified in the life of Jesus. To become like Christ, to be partakers of the Divine nature, to be holy even as God is holy,-this is the great object of a true Christian's hope. -And herein is heaven and nowhere else. To be happy is to be good, to be good is to be like God, and this is the grand object of genuine Christian hope. "Then shall I be satisfied when I awake up in thine own ima"e." 0 Moral goodness is the only true Paradise of souls. IV. ,All Christians have ONE SOVEREIGN MASTER. "One Lord." Who is this ono Lord? By the general consent of acknowledged expositors, the one Lord Jesus Christ. "One is your Master, even Christ." There are men in Christendom who assume titles indicating authority over human souls. We have the Pope of Rome, the lord bishop, and the" Primate of all England." Terribly sad it is that in the name of him who had nowhere to lay his head, and who taught that the least should be greatest in his kingdom, there should be found men either so dull or daring as to assume such titles as these. Call no man "master," said this "one Lord." He is the Head of the Church which is his body, the only Head. Is not this also a potent reason for loving conconl among Christians? They have to draw their doctrines from one Teacher, they have to learn their duty from one Master, they have to fashion their character after one Model, to depend for reconciliation to God upon one Mediator. V. All Christians have ONE SUPREME CREED. "One faith." This means, as we have seen, one Object of faith. What is the one creed? Theological propositions put forth as articles of belief? If so, there are many faiths-faiths almost as numerous as there are Christian professors. No two men can perhaps believe the same thing in exactly the same way; the same proposition shapes itself differently to different souls. 'l'he New Testament teaches with unmistakable explicitness that the true creed of a Ohristian is not a propositional manifesto, but a personal life-the life of Christ. In more than thirty passages of one Gospel, the Gospel of St. J oh.n, we find with reference to Christ the expressions, "trusting to me," "trusting to him," or "trusting to the Son." 'l'ake two or three as specimens. "This is the work of Goel, that ye believe on him whom he hath sent." ,Again, "He that believeth on me hath everlasting life." ,Again," He that believeth on him shall not be damned." Again," He that believeth on me, the works that I do," etc. "Do this in remembrance of me." Christ is the one Crce<l. He is, in truth, the Bible. See how this one creed argues the importance of loving union amongst Christians. If our creed is a series of propositions we shall be divided, but if our creed is the personal life of One all-holy, all-loving, all-good, we shall be united. If all the members of all the Churches believed with a living faith in the one personal Christ, there would be a loving concord of souls. VL All Ch1istians have ONE SPIRITUAL CLEANSING. "One baptism." The primary meaning of" baptism" is cleansing. Bct1M"11Tµos is rendered" washing" in several places (Mark vii. 4, 8; Heb. ix. 10). '!'here are two kinds of baptisms or cleansings mentioned in the New Testament-the material and the spiritual, that of water and that of fire. The latter, namely, the fiery baptism of the Spirit, is the great thiug. This undoubtedly is the one baptism, the one cleansing. 1. This is the une essential cleansing. Without this, though we were baptized in all the ri1•ers of the world, ,vu Are not members of that one body of which Christ is the Head. Millions have entered heaven without water baptism, but not one without the spiritual. 2. This is the on& Divine cleansing. It is the Spirit's work. This is the "washing of regeneration" and the renewing of the Holy Ghost. Is not this one essential, Divine cleansing another good argument for unity of love in all Christians? VII. All Christians have ONE ADORABLE Goo. "One God and Father of nll, who is above all, and through all, and in you all." 1. There is but one God. This fact i~ supported by the structure and order of nature; stands in direct antagonism to atheism, fetichism, polytheism, and pantheism; and is accepted as a fundamental truth in all evangelical Churches throughout the world. 'l'ho glorious fact reveals the greatuesc; of the Creator, tho definiteness of moral obligations, the fitness of religion for tue EPHESIANS, 0 194 THE EPISTLE TO THE EPIIBSI.ANS. [cu. xv. 1-32,

constitution of man, and the universal brotherhood of souls. 2. 'fhis one God u 1miversal Father. "Father of all." "Of all and throuo-h .all." "All is not neuter: ,..,t.,.r.,.P," It is true that God is the Author of all nature: is over all nature, and lives through all nature; but the apostle's reference here is undoubtedly to i11tellicrent 0 existences, and it may be that he intends only the members of the true Church. .All the members of the true Church recognize him as "the Father of all over all throu.,.h ~~in~ ' ' 0

CoNCL-c;sroN. Here, then, in the unities of Christianity are the bonds of true union amongst men. Notwithstanding all the discords and conflicts that rage and revel through the world, there lies deep down in the heart of humanity an ineradicable desire J.-,,. ura ity. The greatest e-v-ents that have marked and helped the progress of the human nee are the outcomes of this desire. l\Jankind have tried for this unity in many different ways. They ha.e tried by: 1. Politicn.l means. In ancient times kings and warriors ~ndea¥oured to bring men toget~er ?Jlder one iron sceptre. The Assyrian, ohe Pe=, the Greek, the Roman, each m his turn made the desperate endeavour. In modern times Spain and France and Russia have tried and failed. Far enough are we from denouncing or even depreciating such a grand political purpose. For our own pa.rt, we should like to see what we think will one day appear on this earth-one great cosmopolitan government-a government embracing within its majestic arms of righteous and sanitary law all· the children of men the world over. '.!.'he fact that England now sways her sceptre over India and Australia. shows that neither diversities of race, language, colour, religion, habit, nor rer:µoteness of position from the central power are necessary obstructions to the establishment of such. a 11).le. With such a. government immense and manifold would be the advantages. The liberties of all wonld be secured. The spirit of nationality, the prolific parent .of desolating wars, would find no place. All would be fellow-citizens of one state. All the tyrannies and rivalries of little despots would be played out. The age or standing armies would be over. The markets of the world be open e.like to all. Such a government, I believe, will come. The gradual absorption of the smaller into the larger states, the ever- mnltiplying facilities of intercourse between the remotest parts of the globe and diven.ified races of mankind, and the ever-advancing intellectual, moral, numerical, and colonizing superiority of the .Anglo-Saxon race charm my poor soul at times with the belief that such an empire is in the tenor of things inevitable. But let it come. The real unity for which th6 human soul craves will not be met. Law cannot create love. 2. &cksiastirol means. Religion has made one great attempt to bind the human race into one grand confederation. The Church of Rome sets up one head to which all souls must bow, prescribes one ritual through which all souls must move, proponnds one creed to which all souls must adhere. The object is a noble one; our hearts go with it. But the means, involving priestly assumptions and .the .infringement of the rights of conscience, a.re amongst the worst damnabilities of history. Jlence it has failed in its object. Aiming at unity, it has led to endless divisions. Many 11, peace-loving soul, pained with the controversies .of the sects, has sought refuge in Rome, but has found it a stormy as well as perilous port. 3. Commercial means. Merchandise in this acre 0 is preached as the uniting power. Self-interest fa to be the golden chain to bind all men together. Nothing is more unphilosophic than this. Self-interest is not a uniting but an insulating power. The battles of the market, if not as bloody, are as base and as heartless as those of the field and the ocean. The true principles of union are in the text.. For universal union there TI?ust be universal love, for universal love there must be universal excellence, and for um versa! excellence there must be the universal recognition of the one body, the one Spirit, the one heaven, the o:ie Master, the one creed, the one cleansing, the one God and Father of all.-D. T.

tho work of the ministry, for the edifyincr of the body of Christ: till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge° of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of tho stature of the fulness of Christ: that we henceforth be no more children 1 tossed to and fro, and carried·about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men; and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive; but speakin" the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the Head, even Christ: "from whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth. according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love." The subject is-Moral restorative influence the gift of Christ. The "grace" mentioned in the seventh verse refers undoubtedly to the spiritual influences of God in tho salvation and perfection of man. There are four things in this remarkable passage concerning this grace, this restorative influence. I. Tms G-IFT lS COWIWNICATED BY CHRIST. "But unto every one of us is given grace accord_ing to the measure of the gift of Christ." The expression, "according to tbo measure of the gift of Christ," means, I think, that its bestowment is entirely according to bis sovereign purpose. 1. Some have a higher measure of grace than others. Some have wider and clearer views of truth, a richer experience of Divine love and faithfulness, broader and stronger sympathies, more soul-uplifting hopes and aspirations than others. There are babes in Christ and there are men )n Christ. Somo are qua.ii.fled to be ministers, martyrs, apostles, etc. Some are only fitted for a humble place in bis vineyard. 2. This measure :is determined by the will of Christ. It is according to "tho measure of the gift of Christ," not according to the measure of a man's capacity, merit, or effort. The fact removes all ground for boasting in the most distinguished in his Church. By the grace of God each disciple is what he is. IL THIS GIFT IS COMMUNICATED BY CHRIST AS TllE RESULT OF ms WONDERFUL msTORY.. "Wherefore he saith, When he ascended up on high, he led captivity captive." I. His history was a history oftoonderful triumphs. "He led captivity captive." He achieved the most brilliant victories. He triumphed over " principalities and powers, and made a show of them openly." He triumphed over death, rose from the grave, and beoame the Prince of life. He triumphs over the enmity of the human heart and brings the sonls of the rebellious into captivity to himselt: 2. His history was a histonJ of wonderful changes. (1) It involved the lowest descension. "He descended into the lower parts of the earth." He not only came down to the condition ofhnmanity, but he took his place in the lowest social grade. " He made himself of no reputation," etc. Ho descended even into the grave and Hades. (2) It involved the highc·-t ascension. "He ascended on high . . . ascended up far above all heavens." How many heavens aro .there? Who can tell the height of the lowost? He is "far nbovo" tho highest. He thus descended and ascended in order that "he might fill" 1111 human things with bis spiritual influence, fill• all human souls with his ideas, principles, and aims. III. Tms GIFT IS COMMUNICATED BY CHRIST IN A G-REAT VARIETY OF MINISTRIES. " He gave some, apostles; some, prophets; some, evangelists; and sotne, pastors a.n,l teachers." "Apostles." No ono was au apostle but those immediately appointed by Christ, who had seen him after his resurrection and ouilowed with a special iuspiration. "Prupliets." Those who, being divinely inspired, taught in the name of God. "Evangelists." Probably itinerant preachers, missionaries, such as Philip. "Pastors and tcacMTs.1' .Overseers. and instructors. All; who in any way promote spiritual Christianity in the world, from those who were tho most feeble in power to those ofloftiest -.:apaoity, are the gift of Christ. He calls them, qualifies them, and appoint~ them ~!:ieir respective spheres. IV. THIS GIBT IS COMMUNICATED BY CnlllBT Ili' OBDEn TO PERFECT ms CrruncH. "For the perfecting of the saints, for tho work of the ministry." Spiritual perfection is the grand aim of all. 1. Perfection in service. '' For the work of the ministry." Tho twelfth verse teaches that a perfect ministry implies a perfect cha.meter. Thero is no perfect aervice where there is not a perfect chara£ter. A man must be good to do good. 2. Perfectwn in unity. "Till wo all come in the uuit.y or the faith, and of the know- ledrro of the Son of God." '!'his may mean oneness or harmuuy of mind in rdaliun to the"dQCtrine and spirit of Christ, a common thought and symrathy iu relation to thu 'l'HE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. [cu. 1v. 1-32.

S..,n of God. 3. Pei:ftctt'on in cha.meter. "Unto a perfect man, unto the mensure of the stature of the fulness of Christ." Christ is the Standard of excellence, and porfection of character is conformity t-0 him. His character is the me.asure. To be Christ-like is hi be perfect. 4-. PerffJC!ion in strength. " 'l'ha.t we henceforth be no more childreil t:1ssed to and fro,_ carried about with every win~ of doctrine.'' (1) The strength of firmness. Possessmg power enough to stand agamst all the winds and waves of reli- gious opinions. '!'here are some men at the mercy of every new doctrine. Their souls l1~ve no a~ch~rage; they a.re no_t" rooted and grounde~ in the f~ith." (2) The strength o: determination. " B_v the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness." The ideas seem to be not influenced by the mere contingencies of sentiment nor the craftiness of heretical teachers. 5. Perfection in Church growth. "Speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the Head, even Christ." '!'he two verses teach: (1) That Church growth is an advancing assimilation to Christ. "We may grow up ~nto him in all thin,,CTS, which is the Head, even Christ." '!'he trne growth of the soul is progress towards a perfect conformity t-0 Christ. (2) That Church growth requires the lo-ui,ig exhibition oi truth. "Speaking the truth in love." There is a truth, a roolity in the gospel, and the ministry of this truth in love is necessary t-0 promote the true growth of the Church. (3) That Church growth is in every part dependent upon its Tital connection mth Christ. "From whom the whole body fitly joined together," etc. (4) That Church growth requires the healthy action of all its members. "By that which e,ery joint supplieth," etc.-D. T.

entries.title: EPH 4:17–19
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-_Symptoms of mo-ral, madness. "This I say therefore, and testify in the Lord, that ye henceforth walk not as other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind, hanng the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart: who being past feeling have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness mth greediness." In these verses the Christians at Ephesus are warned against the course of life pursued by the Gentiles, whom he describes as the prey of mental delusion, benighted in intellect, unbridled in licentiousneHs. Our subject is-Symptoms qf mo-ral madness. What is" vanity of mind" in a scriptural sense? Not mere mental fatuity. Ma-ra.r.&T'l]s, vanity, includes moral worthlessness and corruption. Sin is folly, and sinners are justly represented as fools. It is said of the prodigal son, that "when he came to himself" he began to inquire. .A sinner is riot himself. "We learn for the tirst time," says Dr. Arnot, "that the man has been mad by learning that his reason is restored. It is a characteristic of the insane that they never know or confess their insanity until it has passed away: it is when he has • come to himself' that he first discovers he has been beside himself. The two beings to whom a. man living in .,in is most a stranger are himself and God ; when the right mind returns he becomes acqnainted with both a,,,aain. The first act of the prodigal, when light dawned on his darkness, was t-0 con,en;e mth himself, and the second to return to his father." ·we learn from these ¥erses that this moral madness is associated with several things. L Wrm .A1' Th"TELLECT WITHOUT TRUE LIGHT. There a.re two expressions here indicating the state of a sinner's intellect. "Understanding darkened" and "ignorance that is in them." When we say that the sinner's intellect is in the dark, we mean, of course, in respect to the spiritual realities and interests of his being. He may have tho light of poetic fancy and of secular intelligence-the stars of general science may beam on his horizon ; but so far as moral light is concerned, he is in the dark. His eyes a.re blinded. Three things show this. 1. His adoption of the partial to the rejection of the complete in enjoyment. He has sensual pleasures, but these pleasures even in their highest measure constitute but an infinitesimal portion of those enjoyments for which human nature craves and for which it is organized-the pleasures of holy loves, devout meditations, sublime fellowships, and uplifting hopes and aims. Is not the man mad who chooses the partial and rejects the complete? 2. His adoption of the fleeting to the rejection of the enduring in enjoyment. 'l'he pleasures and dignities he strives afu,r are all connected with this life, which in its longest periods is brief and it~ ~urei;t conditions uncertain. ,vhat is our life? "A vapour." All is flowing as a stream, all is transient as a dream. The joys and honours of immortality he practically ;~::,,Jrc;; and rejC:ct,;. ls not this 01adneso? 3. His adoption of the ruinous to tu<;

rejection _of ~he restorative in enjoyment. By the adoption of the partial and the fleeting to the rejection of the complete and permanent, he pursues a course that involves the ruin of himself, the utter loss of all good. Are not these facts sufficient to show the darkness of the sinner's mind and the dense ignorance that reigns within him? II. WITH A SOUL WITHOUT THE TRUE GoD. "Alienated from the life of God." No soul, no creature in the world can live a moment without God. "By him we live, and move, and have. our being." Yet there is a solemn sense in which moral beings can and do live aloof from him, live without him. Sinners are" without God" in the world . ." He is not in all their thoughts." They shut him out from the whole sphere of their feelings, thoughts, and activities. Not only do they practically ignore his presence and his claims, but his very existence. They are without God. Practical atheists. Is not this moral madness? I. Is it not moral madness to shut the eye to the greatest Object in the universe---One compared with whom the creation itself is as nothing? 2. Is it not moral madness to disregard the most absolute Mast~ of our destiny-the one Bein~ in whose hand our breath is; One whose very word can make for us an eternal hell or heaven? 3. Is it not moral madness to have no sympathy with the best Being in existence-the Fountain of all love, truth, and blessedness? III. WITH A HEART WITHOUT TRUE SENSIBILITY. "Blindness [hardness] of their heart." "Past feeling." This insensibility, whilst it has been brought about by moral irrationality and ignorance, reacts, deepens the darkness of the understanding, allll intensifies the folly of the soul. When the man's heart gets so hardened as to be "past feeling," he becomes utterly incapable of taking right views of spiritual things. The impure atmosphere of a corrupt and hardened heart will obscure the vision of the intellect. When the heart is " past feeling," man becomes so stupid in intellect a~ to be utterly incapable of seeing the beauty or feeling the force of spiritual tmth. 1. To be "past feeling" is to be past the power of true improvement. Where there is no feeling there is no pain, and where there is no pain there will be no impulse for the search of a remedy; A bodily diseo.se without pain is the most hopeless, and a moral diseo.se without pain must prove fatal. "Past feeling." The moral heart run to "fat." 2. To be " past feeling " is to be past the power of true enjoyment. There is no pleasure without feeling. IV. WITH A LIFE WITHOUT TRUE VIRTUE, "Given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness." The passage includes two things. 1 . .A voluntary abandonment to sin. "Given themselves over unto lasciviousness,'· etc. Having lost spiritual intelligence, God, and sensibility, the son! abandons itself to moral corruption. It does it voluntll.rily. " Given themselves." 'l'hey are not forced by God or the devil. What a sight !-souls made in the image of God plunging into o. hideous, sunless, lifeless, lawless chaos I 2. .An avaricious appetite for sin. " With greediness." The word "greediness " elsewhere means "covetousness "-o. desire to have more. CONCLUSION. Learn: 1. That a clear intellect requires a clean heart. 2. That a clean heart requires a vital connection with God. Religion is essentio.l to a sound intellect.-D. T.

entries.title: EPH 4:20–24
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-TM true method of studying Christianity. "But ye have not so learned Christ; if so be that ye have beard him, and have been taught by him, as tho truth is in Jesus: that ye put off concerning the former conversation the old mnn, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts; and be renewed in the spirit of yonr mind; and that ye put on the new man, which nfter God is created in righteousness and true holiness." These verses, including those bnck to the seventeenth, contain a general exhortation to holiness. The exhortation takes two forms-the negative nml the positive. 'l'hc negative wo have noticed in our previous homily, vers. 17-19 ; tho positive is now before us. 'l'he subject is-The true method of studying Christianity. Christianity is to be "learned." It is not an inbred knowledge. Man has no intuition~ about 1t. Nor is it a knowledge imparted in any way irrespective of the use of onr faculties nnd means. It corues to a man as tho rrsult of "learning." 'l'he man who iloes not rightly study will never know it. But what is the true method of stndyin<:;? '!'his ie our present question, a question which we shall endeavour to an~wer in tlio light ot' the pnss~ge before us. 19S THE EPISTLE 'l'O THE EPHESIANS. [011. IV. 1-32,

1. THE TRUE JlETHOD OF STUDYING CHRISTIANITY 11.EQUlRES TH.lT IT SHOULD DB STI'DIED IN CHRIST. "Truth . . . iu Jesus." Christianity must be looked upon all seen in Christ, I. Rot as seen. in religww professors. 'l'his would give a false view. :2.. Sot as sm1 in mig,"ous books. This would give a false view. 3. Not as seen in reJ,;.·:"o,rs i..sti:tutions. These would give a false view. There is nothing cold in truth c-~ n,.rn.1 w, as &-en in Jc:rus, but all that is brood, warm, free, sublime. II. TliE T&CE KETIIOD OF STUDYING Cm!ISTU1''ITY 'REQUIRES THAT IT SHOULD DB == tn."DEB THE T=o:s- OF Cmus-r. ,,e are "taoght by him," or, as some trans- late it," taught in him." Christ is the only effective Teacher of his own relicion. If the sun is to be seen it must show itself--all the stars and moons of the uni;erse cannot reveal it ; so with Christ. But ho,v are we to place ourselves nuder his tuition? Three things are necessary. I. We should realize our true 'llioral relation to truth as it is t"n him. Troth in him bas a special relation to us, not merely as men, but as corrupt, guilty, and ruined sinners. We must feel ourselves to be the character'to which it is specially addressed. 3. We must end,ea,vour to identify ottrselves with the :particular class ef character whu;h it indirotes. "Truth in Jesus" has reference to special classes of sinners, such as the worldling, the formalist, tbe hypocrite, the inquirer, the penitent. We must put ourselves in the right class. 3. We must invoke the aid of his Spirit. Christ's body is not in the world,· but bis Spirit is. The bodies and souls of other great men have left the world-Plato, Seneca, ·etc. They are· not with tho students of their works, but Christ is. He is with all his students. Ill. THE TRUE METHOD OF STUDTING CHilJBTIANITY BEQUIBES THAT WE SHOULD STUDY IT IN OBDEB TO BE )[ADE CHfilsT-LIKE. "Which after God. "-that is, God's image-"is created in righteousness and true holiness." It is not to be studied for intellectual, ecclesiastical, secular, or professional purposes, but for moral ends-studied in order to make us like God. The moral transformation is here indicated as consisting of two things. 1. The renunciation of the o1,d and corrupt character. The "old man" is put off. (1) Character is the man. It is moral character that makes the human animal o man. " .As a man thinketh ,in heart so i.s he." His character forms his world, his he.·n-en or his hell (2) A sinful, character is the old man. It is old because it is· the first character we get. This must be put off. Old principles, purposes, habits, motives, thrown away. 2. TM adoption of a new principle of character. "Be renewed in tbe spirit of your mind." Renewed in the central springs of being. 'l'he assimilation of our character to the grandest ideal which after God is created, and so on.-D. T. V ers. 25-32.-The ahjured and the enjoined in Christian life, " Wherefore," etc. In the preceding verses, as we have seen, under the head of The true method of studying Christianity, the apostle exhorted the Ephesians "to put off the old man and to put on the new man." He here proceeds to particularize and urge this the great practical work of Christianity. He abjures the elements of the old man and enjoins the elements of the new. Our subject is the ahjured and the enjoined in the Christian life. • L THE .A11JUEED IT CHRISTIAN LIFE. There are certain things here which are, alas I often fonnd in connection with nominal Christians, and which are therefore too often rezardt<l as identified with the Christian system, which are here abjured in language m(,;;., earnest and strong. What are they? L Lying speech. "Pntting away lying." A lie is a fiiliehood intended to deceive, with an immoral design; it is a misreprosentatic,n of that to another about which he baa a right t-0 kno1v the truth. What, then, is fiction :ind parable, say yon? There is no justifiable_ fict!on that does not agree with fact a!id Serve the cause of reality and morals. Lymg 1s one of the most prevalent sins. The ancient heathens everywhere practised it, and moderns too. All travellers and missionaries bear testimony to this. Heathens are not to be believed -0n their oaths. Alas! the vice is not confined to heathendom; it prevails throughout the civilized world. Lies fill the social atmosphere. Men in every department of life are deceiving an<i being deceived by their fellow-men, and often for selfish and immoral ends. Christianity condemns lies. "Lying lips are an abomination unto the Lord.'' And "liars at last shall have their part in the lake that burneth with fire and brimstone." Christianity is essentially and eternally anta;;onistic to all insincerities end unri•alitio,. Vanity, cowardice, and greed are the prolific factors of falsehoods.

2. Sinful anger. "Be· ye angry, and sin not." We say, "sinful anger," for the text implies _that there is an anger that is not sinful. Anger is the mind in emotional antagonism, and in a world of unreality, sin, and crime there is much to justify the strongest antagonism of the soul. Christ himself looked upon the conduct of the Jews with an~er (Mark iii. 5). Indignation sometimes fired his breast, and "woes" like thunderbolts rolled from his lips. The stronger a being's love for the right, the mightier his indignation for the wrong. The text implies two things concerning sinful nnger. (1) That it is abiding. Hence the command, "Let not the sun go down upon your wrath." Anger should not be allowed to continue in the mind, because it iL painful to the soul; it is a :fire that bums. He who cherishes it could not better gratify the vengeance of an enemy, for he is in agony all the while. The great Creator, in whose nature there is "no fury," never made the human soul for anger. "Let not the sun go down upon your wrath." Do not take it to bed with you; it will break you~ slumber and it will breed the devils of revenge. "Anger resteth in the bosom of fools." 'l'here is another thing here implied concerning sinful anger. (2) It is favourable to the devil. "Neither give place to the devil." An angry soul is just the sphere to which the devil has the freest access and can best work out his malignant ends. All the assassinations, murders, and wars he works through angry souls. Don't give place to the devil. Human souls may keep the devil out. He cannot enter without their consent. 3. Social dishonesty. "Let him that stole steal no more." Stealing in some way or other is a vice as prevalent as lying. Our popular ideas of larceny are not deep or broad enough for Christianity. Englishmen regard those as thieves only whom the law has convicted of pilfering, and who are generally amongst the poor and needy. But in the eye of Christianity he is a thief who takes from another his rightful due. The tradesman who deals in short weights and measures, nnJ overcharges for his wares, is a thief; the servant who does not occupy faithfully in his master's service the hours and faculties for which he is paid, is a thief; the physician who prolongs his visit to his patient beyond what is necessary, in order to get gaiu, is a thief; the rulers who tax the people to pay them enormous salaries for offices inefficiently and often injuriously :filled, are thieves. To all these Christianity says, " Let him that stole steal no more ; " be honest. 4. Corrupt language. " Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth." It is a putrescent language that is here abjured. What is o. foul speech in the sense of Christianity? Not the ungrnm- matio in structure or the inelegant in style. The irreligious speech, which treats sacred things with frivolous profanity and sneering ridicule, is foul and corrupt; the selfish speech, which argues o.nd persuades solely for personal gratification, is foul a11d corrupt ; the malicious speech, which endeavours to undermine the influence, damage the interests, and injure the reputation of others, is foul 11nd corrupt; the sensuous speech, that seeks to influence the animal passions and pollute the pure love of man- kind, is foul and corrupt. All such language-and, alas I it abounds amongst us-is indeed putrescent. As heaps of decomposing vegetable and animal matter send forth gases into the atmosphere injurious to the physical health of the world, all corrupt communicatjons proceeding from the mouths of men impregnate the mental atmosphere with elements damaging to the moral health of souls. 5. The anti-Divine. "And grieve not the Holy Spirit of God." Of course we are not to suppose that the eternal Spirit literally endures grief. He is the ever-blessed God. energy, peace, reputation, life, all to save them. entries.title: EPH 4:1–3
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
- Walki11g worthily. It is touching to see how the great apostle, who had a right to issue co=ands to the Churches in the name of Christ, prefers to beseech his readers with gentle entreaty as "the prisoner in the Lord." 'fhis method i~ as much a mark of his wisdom as of his humility and kindnes.s of heart. For we are all more easily _moved by persuasion and sympathy than by patronage and authority. I. CHRISTIANS ARE CALLED TO A HIGH VOCATION. 1. There is a Divine call. We are not left to drift tb,rough life aimlessly, nor are we permitted to carve out careers for ourselves.. Divine purposes go before us, mapping out our course of future service; and Divine voices in the gospel and in our hearts bid us follow our vocation. 2. The call is lofty and worthy of aH honour. Christians are not saved with a bare and

beggarly deliverance, like shipwrecked mariners flung upon the beach, half drowned and bereft of everything. When we enter the C~ristian life we commence a course of high service, vast enterprise, and splendid aims. 3. The purpose of thi~ vocation is to glorify God and bless the world by realizing the idea of the Christian Church. In the previous chaJ?ter St. Paul has been describing some of the great privileges of Christians, which consist chiefly in their being built into ono great temple and growing together in union. The breaking down of national, ecclesi11st1cal, intellectual, and moral barriers, and the building np of one great family, knit together by love and united throu~h a common union with Christ, is St. Paul's magnificent conception of the fruits that Lhe gospel is to bear on earth. II. IT IS THE DuTY OF CHRISTIANS TO WALK WORTHILY OF THEm mGH CALLING. 1. The responsiln1ity of fulfilling our vocation rests upon us. We are called, not driven, and we can disobey the Divine voice. But though we are free from compulsion, we are not free from responsibility. For God has a right to call us whither he will, aud Christ has laid us under peculiar obligations by his work and sacrifice for us. 2. 'l'his fulfilment of our vocation must be in our daily conduct. We are to'' wc·k worthily." Belief and worship are not enough. The life and the whole work an,l daily occupation are to follow the Pivine call. 3. Christian consistency is sg_W1ring 011r conduct with our calling, Many make much of mere self-consistency; but it is well often to be inconsistent with ourselves, or we can never progress, much less repent and amend. Nor is it enough to make our actions consistent with our opinions, unle:ss both opinions and actions are consistent with truth, with God's will, and with our vocation. Ill. vV ALKINO WORTHILY OF THE CHRISTIAN CALLING CONSISTS CHIEFLY IN MAl:--- TAININO AND INCREASING OUR MUTUAL BROTHERHOOD, Love is the queen of the New Testament graces. Selfishness, moroseness, lack of sympathy, and the like nru sins against the peculiar genius of the gospel. To be zealous in defending the faith, to be pure as white marble in saintly separation from vice, to be strict in integrity, etc., will not be enough; for our cnlling is to o. brotherhood, and our worthy walking must help this. 1. Negatively, we must have lowliness which declines to assert one's stdt before one's brethren, meekness which acts gently to them, nod long-suffering which bears with any provocations they may give us, 2. Positively, we must extend Uhristian unity and tho spirit of peace. The peaceful brotherly spirit must not only be passively harmless, it must be earnest, active, nnd diligent.-W. F. A.

entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-0hristian unity, This is n frequently recurring themo in the Epistle to the Ephesians, and it is always treated with an emphasis that marks its supreme importance, and with a prophetic hope[ulness that regards the higher devclopnwnt of it as one of the grandest features of the i<leal future. 202 THE EPIS'l'LE '1'0 'l'HE EPHESIANS. [cH. IV. 1-32,

I. WHEREIN CHRISTIAN m'ITY CONSISTS. 1. Ea:ternally it comists in tM "one body." Plainly the "one body" is the Church, the community of Christians. It should be clear to an impartial reader of the Ne,v Testament that neither Christ nor bis apostles oontemplated the ideal of the kingdom of heaven on earth as we see that kingdom realized only in a Christendom torn and distracted with the bitter rivalries :rno. mutual excommunications of innumerable sects. The Church of Christ the Church in St. Paul's conception, was to be catholic-one great family, harmocious, mi::ru.aily sympathetic and mutually helpful. 2. lnleNially it ronsists in the "one S: iri:." &, long as there is i::ot oneness of spirit in the Church, the attempt to preserve <"X:c.-:::::-.: .::::iic,::i by force is futile; My, it is po::iti,·e\y hurtful. It is best not to have "':::J.<"~",. semblance of Ullion when at hesrt we ,liffer strongly. But if there is a unity 0f spirit, that should be regarded as the most es...sential thing. History shows that the g-:-<'... te:;, bre:iches of unity have been caused by the illibernl efforts of bigots t.o constrain uniformity. If we want true unity we must dispense with agreement in doctrine, f,mn of worship and ecclesia.stical order, and be content with oneness of spirit. This unity will be realized, not by increasing, but by minimizing, the points of uniformity; in comprehensiveness, not in stringent discipline; with larger charity, never with more absolute authority. II. TowARDS WHAT END CHRISTIAN m.'ITY ts TENDING. The Christian calling points to "one hope." All thin_,as make for final integration (eh. i.10). We fail of our vocation if we are satisfied with a churlish isolation. TLere will be varieties of life in the future, no doubt, as there will be" many mansions." But all Christians will be united in the one city of God, even in the one house of our Father (John xiv. 2). • It becomes, therefore, our manifest duty to heal the breaches of Zion. Controversialists should ask themselves whether they bring the millennium nearer by their pugnacious advocacy of pet doctrines, or drive it further off by deepening the fissures of a sorely divided Christendom ; and ecclesiastical advocates of Church unity should consider whether it is likely they will win over to their side all the divergent sects by standing on the narrowest possible ground and erecting about it frowning ramparts . . III. O:s WHAT ORIGINAL FOm.""DATio:ss ClmIBTIA..>r UNITY 1s BASED. 1. C>ruJ Lord. We all have one and the same Christ, and in him weare one. In proportion as Christian.icy becomes less an affair of theological dogmas and ecclesiastical systems, and more a religion of personal devotion to Christ, shall we be able to realize our true unity. 2. One faith. All Christians mnst experience the same spiritual faith in becoming Chrb--t's, and must walk eqnally by faith. Opinions and rules may differ, but we do not Jive by opinions and rules-we live by faith. Now, faith is the same spiritual act in child and in philosopher, in penitent and in saint, in the shouting recruit of th11 Salvation Army and in the grave Quaker, in the evangelical Methodist and in the devout restorer of media!val theology. 3. One baptism. There is one outward sacrament common to nearly the whole of Christendom significant of the washing li.nd renewal all nctd and all can reeeive in Christ. 4. One God and Father. A common worship mites. Communion with our one Father makes us members of one family.-W. F. A.

entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-MeaJJured grace. I. CimL~TIANB ABE RECIPIENTS OF GRACE. 1. Without 1race we can do nothing. All our attainments will be_ proportion~te to the amoun~ an<l_ kind of grace we receive. We cannot fulfil our vocat10n nor rcahze the grand unity ot 1 he Church by unaided human efforts. 2. But_ grace i~ vouchsafed t~ Christians. It is ,lie peculiar privilege of the New Testament dispensat10n that 1t bnngs the energy of '.:race as well as the light of truth. • ~ ll. CHRISTIAN GRACE IS THE Gll"T OF CHRIST. 1. Grace must be a gift. It would cease to be grace if we could create, earn, or deserve it. All the blessings of the gospel arc free gifts IUI are also our natural endowments. 2. Christian grace comes direct from, (Jhri6t.' His sacrifice won it. His ascension enables him to dispense it (vers. t-10). III. Tms GBACE IS GIVEN TO ALL CHRISTIANS. It is not reserved for high e=clesi- astical 0lficials and select sainta. We are no Christians if we have it not. The Church i,. the body of all Christians, and it is one because the same grace flows through the "l,ole brotherhood. 'l'he gospel is broad and democratic. l\T. Tm~ GRACE IS DISPENSED 'l'O EACH INDIVIDUAL SEVERALLY. Each one receives

the gift. We cannot be blessed by Divine grace in crowds and masses. The Church can only be endowed with grace when her private members are personally blessed. We do not receive grace by becoming part of the grand Catholic Church. But we realize the unity of the Church when we have been first blessed with Christ's grace in our own souls. V. Tms GRACE IS MEASURED OUT IN VARYING PROPORTIONS. In Christ there was grace without measure, In us it is measured. Uhrist has a right to measure it, because it is a. gift which he can withhold or bestow as he pleases. Yet if it is measured there is no stint, for if Christ has first given us himself, we may be sure that he will never keep back any needful lower blessings. 'l'he measure of the grace is detcrmineJ by our spiritnal capacity, our faith, our need, our special mission.-W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 4:9
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -The universal experience of Christ. I. THE ASCE21"SION OF CHRIST IMPLIES THAT·HE HAD PREVIOUSLY DESC]:NDED. 1. It implies that he was low down ut some period. Had he always enjoyed his rightful honours there could have been no act o~. rising to them. The coronation shows that the sovereign had once been a subject.· The grea_tness of the elevation of Christ and the stir and change it produces are significant of the low depth of an earlier state. 2. It implies that he had been highly exalted at a previous period. 'l'he mere act of ascension may not show this, but the spiritual character of it does. All things ultimately find their level. The highshooting fountain is an evidence that its water has come from a great elevation. 3. It implies that by· his deep humiliation Christ merfted his great exaltation. He did not simply deserve it by way of compensation. He earned the high honour of the Ascensio11 by the patient sacrifice of himself in his descent down to a life of lowly service, down to the cross, down even to the dim land of the dead (Phil. ii. 5-11). Thus the last is first, and he who humbled himself is exalted. II. 'fHE ASCENSION AND PREVIOUS DESCEN.DmG OF CHRIST ENABLE HIM TO FILL ALL THINGS. 1. His presence enters into every grade of being. From his awrul primeval glory down to the dread depths of Hades and then up to the throne anJ the right band of God, by the vast sweep and range of his profound humiliation an,l superb exaltation, along every step of existence traversed, Christ comes into personal contact with all life and death. 2. His experience gives him knowledge of every grade of being. . And with this knowledge he hns sympathy for all. Our lack of wide sympathies is chiefly owing to our narrow experience. Christ's sympathy is as universal as h_is experience. In his exaltation he does not forget the scenes that moved his heart in lowlier walk(l. " ... Resting by th' incama.te Lord, Once bleeding, now triumphant for my aa.ke, I ma.rk him, how by seraph hosts adored, He to ea.rth's lowest CM-es is still awake." 3. l<'illing all things by experience, knowledge, and sympathy, he has power over all things. Down even to the spirit~ in prison to whom be preached by the Divine Spirit, and through every rank of life, he has influences to exert, graces to bestow, redemption to accomplish. '!'here is no order of things beyond the reach of Christ. As the great reward of his sacrifice and triumph, of his deepest humiliation nnd his highest exaltation, he fills heaven, earth, and holl with a. presence which, if he is the same now as when he lived among men, is everywhere healing and redemptive.-W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 4:13–16
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-The fall-grown man. The object for which the various gifts that flow from the ascension of Christ (see ver. 8) are bestowed is here described. 'l'hat object is not the mere enjoyment of the gifts themselves. It is practical ancl for a distinct purpose, viz. to accomplish "the building up of the body of Christ." For this same end the offices of the Christian ministry and all other ordinances and institutions of Christianity are now ordained. It is not enough to hold services and gather tocrether decorous con,,recrations. Nor is it oven enough to securo converts. '!'ho final object is to build up the Church itself, by developing its manhood and cementing it~ unity. The end is twofold; a".lJ though the two !)arts of it are as intimately connected in experience as they are hero blended together in the lan~nage of St. Paul, they can be considered separately. The fir~t element in the building up of the THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. [OH. l'\t. l-32,

Church is the development of individual. Christians from spiritual infancy to spiritual manhood; the second is the consolidation of the several megibers of the Church into the one body of Christ-the ~nward growth to the stature of the fulness of Christ, the outward growth of the various parts of that great organism of which Christ is the Head. I. THE INWARD GROWTH OF SPIRITUAL MANHOOD. Individual Christians must grow if the whClle Church is to grow. 1. The characteristics of the growth. It is the gradual attainment of manhood. There are babes in Christ among men who are olJ in years. The work of the gospel is not accomplished till it has made strong men of us. A religion of soft sentiment and imbecile intelligence, such as some would commend as a rebuke to our pride, would find no favour with St; Paul. He "-:\Sa man of robust intellect and vigorous energy. The childlikeness of the Christian !s iar from the childishness of the sen\imeutal religionist. Many of the greatest 1,~r,>es hin-e had a singular childlikeness which has only enhanced the ma.nliness or their li,es. The perfect Christian- is just the perfect man. In particular he must ha,e: (1) Increase of knowl,ed,gB. (2) Stability of beUef; the lack of personal convictions t.hat is so common among us is a symptom of intellectual feebleness. We do not want rigid do.,<Tillatism, but surely as our thinking and experience progress some truths should emerge out of the mist of doubt clear and certain, some gtound should be securely won, though much must still be beyond our comprehension. . (3) Fidelity; "speaking the truth," or rather "dealing truly ; " for this a manly firmness must be acquired. ( 4) Love; "in love," etc. 2. The relation of this growth to Christ. (1) Christ is the object of our gtowing knowledge; we have to grow in" the know- ledge of the Son of God." (2) Christ is the standard of. Christian manliness. "The measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ " is what :we are called to grow up to. (3) Christ is the end of Christian effort. We have to grow " into him." 'fhe <legree of our Christian progress may be determined by our nearness to Christ. Apparent increase of knowledge, energy, etc., is real decline if we are drifting further from Christ. The perfect Christian is at once he who is most Christ-like in character and he who is nearest t.o Christ in living communion. II. THE Ol7TWARD GROWTH OF THE CHURCH. The whole body gtows with the gradual increase of its several parts. But this general increase has a character and a hk--tory of its own. '!'he Church gtows up to manhood. Through all the ages of Ch:ri;;tendom it has been the object of Christ to develop and educate his people till the infant C'nnrch of the first age should become the manly Church of the last. Tnis thought warns us against the foolish Yeneration for antiquity which Lord Bacon repudiated, reminding us that these later days are the truly ancient times when the world has grown old in experience. Doubtless we may learn much by the study of patristic and primitive Christianity. But we shall be ill: error if wo i~crine that all we have to do is to revive the days of the Church's childhood; and we shall be far from the broad. strong, spirit of St. Paul if we timidly shrink from those new advances that make for the increase of the Church's manhood. The Church. as well as the individual Christian must gtow in knowledge; it should also grow in fixity of established faith, in fidelity, and in love. The true growth of the Church will also show (1) more harmony and. unity, of sympathy and co-opera.tion in work--" fitly framed and knit t.ogether;" (2) at the same time more elasticity, versatility, and variety of life and action-" every joint" supplying its own share of work· (0) enlargement in numbers and size-" increase of the body;" and (4) closer wnwr: with Christ-the whole body must" gtow up in all things unto him which is the Head."-W. F. A.

entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-.J.B the truth ia in Jesus. These words describe the method, not the 6ubstance, of Chrifitian teaching ; the latter is adverted to in the ne~t ver~~ '!'he bbt.,rical Lam~, "Jesus," instead of the more common official name, "Christ," indicates t':iat_ thIB,t~ching is given through_ the life _of oar Lord ~n earth. _We_.com~ (u :'-~ ~r,c,,nedge c,f troth by hearing hnn, by bewg taught of him, by secmg 1t as 1t 1s I[; IllIIL.

L THE K:SOWLEOOZ OF TRUTH 18 OF SUPRE)II': B!PORTANCE TO us. The means i.£ prvp<Jrtic,ned tv the end. If the life of Chriot is necessary for the revelation OIi. IV, 1-32,] THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. 205

of truth, the truth thus revealed must be of first moment. Emotion without truth is vapid sentiment; and action without truth can have no moral character, and is as likely to be hurtful as useful. It is a blind man's groping. We can dispense with a superfluity of dogma. We have too many words about truth. But truth itself, the living spiritual reality, is the very breath of our souls. To know ourselves ancl our vocation, to know God, his love and his will, to know the spiritual order of things as far as it touches our own lives and conduct, is of vital interest. II. TRUTH IS REVEALED IN CHRIST. Truth is written on the great book of creation, but in obscure hieroglyphics, for nature is an inarticulate prophet. 'l'ru th has also come through the inspiration of thought and conscience in poets and seers. But then it is always in words; and words make it but a clwnsy garment hidinoits finer beauty and, at best, speaking at second hand. In Christ we see truth intelligible, powerful, touching. It is ravealed in his very self and in his words and deeds as they· are the outcome and signs of his character and nature. Christ is the truth. He has but to be and to be seen and heard for truth to be revealed. Ill, THIS REVELATION OF TilUTH L."I CHRIST IS OF A DISTINCTIVE CH.\RACTEr:. 1. It is human. Truth is seen in Jesus just because he is a real and perfect l\lan. As man is made in the image of God, the very being of a perfect man must be a manifestation of Divine thoughts. (1) Therefore any dogmas that are contrary to humanity are false. (2) Therefore, also, we need not fear truth. Sho has a human countenance. 2. It is liuing. Truth in words is cold and dead, though it may be clear and beautiful. Truth in Jesus is alive, revealing itself in action, putting forth energy, responding to our sympathy. a.- It is spiritual. Truth of religio11 and of conduct is what we see in Jesus, not reminiscences of secular history nor anticipations of material science. 'fhe highest truth concerns God and the soul, duty and the unseen world. 4. It is beautiful. Christ's glory was full of grace and truth. In his face truth has no terrors, but the most winning attractions and the most moving loveliness. IV. Suen A PRESENTATION ·oF TRUTH CALLS FORTH DUTIES ON oun PART. 1. we have to "learn Ohrist." That is the one lesson for our souh We may learn all systems of theology and yet know nothing of the highest truth, if we do not know Christ. They who sit at the feet of Jesus drink from the deepest fountains . .As Christ is best described to us in the four Gospels, these Gospels arc the chief source of Christian knowledge. Yet inasmuch as the apostles interpret the mind or Christ, we may learn Christ from the whole of the New Testament, But we must also come to a personal communion with Christ in order to know him aright. 2. We have to prove how we ha·ve learned Christ by our conduct. This knowledge is to shape our actions. Fidelity, purity, and charity of life must make men see what truth we have found in Jesus.-W. entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-.Anger. I. .ANGER IS A DUTY. 1. It is natural. The man who is never angry is lacking in moral fibre. Christ was sometimes angry (Mark iii. 5). God is angry with the wicked (Ps. vii. 11). 2. It is ;'ust. We cannot rightly rebuke evil without anger. Lies and cruelty should not be treated mildly. Christ would not have been faithful to righteousness if he had not shown indignation in response to hypocrisy. 3. It is useful. We may save a man by first being angry with him. A mild complacency may be the greatest cruelty to a bad man. Even when we cannot rouse the couscience of the guilty by anger we may protect the weak and wronged who claim our first sympathy. II. ANGER DRINGS A DANGER. It is the most perilous of duties even when it is obligatory. 1. It is in danger of being indulged for our own satisfaction instead of the resistance and checking of moral evil. Personal roveugo is l1koly to usurp thu place of righteous indignation. 2. It is in danger of running into excess. It is a 1iaeMion, and every passion tends to irrational extravagance. The angry man must beware of losing his temper. Ill. THE LIMITS OF IlIGHTEOUS ANGER SHOULD DE CAREFULLY MARKED. 1. We must avoid the mingling of wicked feelings with necessary anger. While angry with our brother we must not cease to love him. ,ve may be most angry with those wo 1.Qvo most. But when anger provokes us to wish harm to any one, it degcnernt~s to .!06 THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. [ell, IV. 1-32,

Men may, do fearful harm by the sudden: ebullition of a hasty temper-harm which may be repented of in vain for loner years. It would be well to remember every night that we cannot have God's forgiveness of our sins of the day unless we have fin,t forgi,en those who ha,e sinned agninst us. 3. We must not lose self-control in anger. "Neither give place t.o tbo devil." • IV. THE CHRl::,,'JAX SAFEGUARD A.GATh'ST THE A.BUSB OF ANGER IS LOVE. No man <:an be saiely angry with his brother unless he first love him. It is only they that love much ,,ho can make a wise use of the furious weapon of anger.· If we are "kind one to another, tender-hearted, forgi,ing each other,'' we shall be able to show righteous anger without lowering ourselves to personal spite. . Then our anger will be a pain t.o us and we shall long t.o abandon it for more congenial feelings. entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -Grieving the Holy Spirit of God. I. WHAT IT IS TO GRIEVE THE HoLY SPmIT OF Gon. We are startled at the expression. Few of us would have thought of using it if we had not found it in the Bible. It cannot be a mere figure of speech. It must describe a strange, sad., touching fact. 1. God is a living Spirit. He can be grieved. 2. God is our Father, related t.o us, loving us. It is of the self-sacrificing nature oflove that it lays itself out t.o be wounded when it is· treated unworthily.. We; can always hurt most those who love us most. 3. God is within us. The Holy Spirit is God dwelling in Olll" spirits. Because he is so near he is much concerned with our, charncter and conduct. 1L How WE MAY GRIEVE 'l'HE HoLY SPIRIT OF Gon. 1. All sin is grievous to him, as holiness is hurt by unholiness and love by unworthiness. This should ea ono warning &_,<r.llust oar carelessness in falling into temptation. If we do not feel it, God docs. A child who would not refrain from a bad thing on its own account, checks himseli as he thlnks how it would vex his mother. entries.title: EPH 4:31
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-C'ha.rity tc, tl,e undeserving. I. THE NEGATIVE nu•rrns., "Let all bittcrnc.,, etc., be put away from you." Various influences tempt us to the indulgence·of thf:Se <lark ~sions. 1. Natural d·isposition. Some men appear, to be born with an acrid and mordant temper, as eome plants secrete irritant poisons, 2. Provocation.

Anger rouses anger as fire kindles fire. 'fhe reference to forgiveness shows that St. Paul is especially condemning outbursts of wrath against people who have treated us maliciously. 3. Evil example. "Clamour and railing" are public offences. When many men concur in pouring wrath on a selected victim it is difficult to stand aside from the current of abuse and recognize the unholiness of it. The admonition may be applied (1) to public life, that politics may be freed from the degradation of personal spite ; (2) to affairs of religion in condemnation of the odium theologicum, and also of the odium antitheologicv,m,-why should we hate a man because his opinion is not ours? (3) to social life, since it is better to suffer an injury unavenged than to add a. second injury in return. II. THE POSITIVE DUTIES. Christianity is not satisfied with passive meekness. We must not only turn the cheek to the smiter, we must love our enemies-a duty of positive feeling and action. 1. General kindness. This would destroy the selfishness that is at the root of all revengeful feelings. He who has injured us is our brother. The ties of our common brotherhood that urge us to love him should be stronger than the provocations of his unkindness that would make us bitter against him. 2. Tenderheartedness. This should make us pity the offender for the shame and guilt he bas brought upon himself, and long for reconciliation with him. 3. Forgiveness. The final step for the healing of positive injury is the most necessary, for without it we can have no Divine forgiveness, nor can we truly love our enemy. III. THE GRAND MOTIVE. "Even as God also in Christ forgave you." As we must forgive others before God will forgive us, so when he has forgiven us a stronger reason is added to urge us to forgive those who may in fttture injure us. 1. The Divine for• giveness is the reason for our forgiveness and kindness to others. The parable of the unforgiving servant reveals the gross inconsistency of an unforgiving spirit in Christian men and women (Matt. xviii. 23-35). How can we who simply exist because God has forgiven us deny forgiveness to our brethren? If God who is infinitely above us has condescended to forgiveness, shall we stand more strictly on our petty rights? If God has forgiven us our innumerable, great, and awful sins against him, can we be backward in pardoning the much fewer and slighter sins of our fellowmen against us? Forgiven the debt often thousand talents, how have we the face to exact the debt of a hundred pence? 2. The Divine forgiveness is the patt~n of our forgiveness. It is (1) at the greatest cost-" in Christ," through the gift of God's own Son; (2) covering all sins, the worst and blackest without exception ; (3) perfect, full, and ungrucl,,oing-remembering our sins no more, removing them from us ns far as the east is from the west, burying them in the sea; (4) cheerful and generous-• putting the rin~ and best robe on the penitent ; (5) free, not earned by sacrifice, penance, or good works. Such should be on our forgiveness of one another.-W. F. A.

The fearful prevalence of sensual vice at Ephesus naturally led the apostle to dwell on it empha.tically as one of the worst rags of the old man, a rng to be wholly and for ever cast away. Dut, indeed, there are few heathen communities where sensual vice does not flourish when men have it in their power to indulge in it. It i8 singular how universal sin is in connection with the irregular o.nd disorderly indulgenco of the bodily appetites. It would seem as if God made this a special mo.tter of probation, for when these appetites get the upper hand, they lead into terrible cxcesse~, and,lby bringing disease on both mind and body, avenge the sin to which thoy have impelled. Such precepts and ~nsiderations ha,e a wider bearing than Ephesus and its groves. Sins of the t':esh tlonrish even in Christian lands. , ers. 15-21. - Walk circumspectly, OT strictly. The apostle goes on to urge_ o. circumspect, wise, and earnest life, closely conformed in aH things to the will of God,. fashioned according to that idea of wisdom which is set forth in the proverb, Cl The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom." Nothing is of more value tho.n fixed principles for guiding our life. One settled conviction may be of inestimable value; e.g. the conviction that nothing can come to any good iu the end which is against the will of God. Whenever greatness is achieved in any sphere.of life it is through the force of well-kept rules. Every great author, artist, statesman, has owed his success to certain principles of action to which he has rigidly adhered. It has been remarked that the puritan age was an age of convictions; ours is an a;re of opinions. But what we need is convictions, and pre-eminently the conviction that the only trne, sale, and blessed rule of life is to follow implicitly the will of God. We fin~ here ru,les for a careful Christian life, (1) apart,'.(2) in Christian society. • I. APART. L Walk circumspectly, or strictly, not carelessly. 2. Waik wisely, taking pains to ascerto.in that you so walk as to gain the great end. 3. Redeem the time, or b.:ry back the opportunity (see Ex:pcstion). 4. Understand ; i.e. lay to heart and follow the will of Christ. 5. Avoid intoxic.'ltion and all wild excitemeni and unhallowed pleasure. 6. Be filled with the Spirit, and the holy, blessed emotions which he genders. II. l:s CHBlsTIAN SOCIETY. 1. Cultivate Christian song, and make melody in your heart to the Lord. 2. Let thanksgiving have a special place in your exercises.· 3. Submit yoursel.es one to another in the fear of the Lord. As Christians have not only duties, bot also joys, belonging to their individual life, so they have both duties and joys belonging to their social life. What is most characteristic of the social duties of Christians is mutual 6Ubmission; consideration of one another-of what is due by one to another, and still more of the loving ~ervice which one may be o.ble to render to the other. What is most characteristic of their social joys is the element of thankfulness in which they flourish ; they should,ever live as those who in Christ ho.ve received mercies beyond all calculation; and they sh.ould,make abundant use of song to give expression to such feelings and to .deepen them in so doing. This joyous element goes a long way to give brightness to the social life of Christians ; they will not miss the more carnal delights on which worldly men •set so much store, but will feel that God puts joy in their hearts, more than iu the time that their corn and wine increased.

entries.title: EPH 5:22–33
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Duties of wives and husbands. The Apostle Peter, in his First Epistle, after dwelling on the privileges of believers, strongly urges them to have their conn,ru,ti,,!i hr,r,est or fair among the Gentiles, exemplifying, by the purity and beauty of tbeir life, tl..e excellence of the principles and privileges of the gospel; and then he Lra!ich(;~ c,ut i!itr, thn:e cases or relation.s that afford scope for thi~ mode of life-that c,f subjects to their ruli,r~, that of servants to their masters, and that of wives to their hllbbar,ds ar,d husbands to their wives. 'l'hough Peter aud Paul moved in different orbits, yet, frc,m the stre1ioth of the convictions held by them in common, and the guiilii.nc,; of the llc,ly Spirit in them both, they were led to enforce wonderfully similar CII, V, 1-33.] TIIE EPISTLE TO 'l'l:IE EPHESIANS. 215

applications of the great principles of the gospel. Paul, like Peter, brings forward three relations, the only difference being that, in place of the relation of subjects to their rulers, he has that of children to their parents, and the corresponding duty of parents to their children. We have the clearest proof of its bein"' the purpose of Christianity to purify and elevate the common relations of life. Mu~h of the visible fruit of true religion lies in its making better subjects, better spouses, better children, better servants. Pagans were struck with the excellence of Christian women. The mother.of Chrysostom won golden opinions by remaining a widow from her twenty-first year; "What women these Christians have!" was the exclamation of some. Christian women were wonderful missionaries in the early centuries by their devout, pure, and earnest lives; many was the pagan who, "without the Word, was won by the conversation of the· wife." Such lives are doubly blessed-blessed in themselves, and blessed in their influence on the world. I. THE WIFE'S DUTY. Submission to the husband as to the Lord (ver. 22). Rea.sons for this. 1. The husband is. the head of the wife (ver. 23). 2. '!'here is a parallel between the husband and Christ (ver. 23). 3. Even in respect of Christ's saving power, the parallel holds to a. limited, though very limited, extent (ver. 23). 4. 'l'be parallel is close enough to require the subjection of the wife (ver. 24). II.: TnE HUSBAND'S DUTY. To love his wife. This is enforced: 1. By the consideration of what Christ felt and did for his Church. (1) He loved the Church (ver. 25). (2) He gave himself for her (ver. 25). And the object for which he did so. (a) His immediate object (ver. 26). (b) His ultimate object (ver. 27). 2. By the consideration of the closeness of the relation of the wife to Uie husband as his own flesh. This relation is considered (1) naturally (vers. 28, 29); (2) symbolically (ver. 30). The Church taken from Christ; given to Christ. 'l'be relation of the husband to his wife supersedes (in a. manner) the relations of nature. The relation of the Church to Christ does so too (ver. 31). But the subject is mysterious (ver. 32). Yet one practical obligation is very clear (ver. 33). The constitution of the Church, like that of natural society, involves mutual duties. Nothing can be complete unless each party performs his share. While it is the woman•~ part to be in subjection, it is the husband's part to love. The one balances the other. It is the duty of the wife to be subject even though the husband does not love, and tho duty of the husband to love even though the wife is not subject; but bow hard, difficult, almost impossible, such duties thus become! •If the husband withhold love, be iB wronging his wife, and altogether subverting tho relation between them. Let it ever be observed that, while God has joined husband and wife together, be bas joined the husband's love to the wife's subjection ; what, therefore, God bath joined together, ,et not man put a.sunder.

entries.title: EPH 5:1
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -" Follou:ers of God.''._ This is the high destiny of God's children. I. 'l'HE DUTY HERE COMMANDED. "Be ye imitators of me." It is to do (1) what Guel does ; (2) because be does it ; (3) as ho does it. The special point of imitation here is the duty of showing a for@:iving spirit to ono another. II. WIIY WE SHOULD IMI'l'ATII GoD. 1. Because we are his "dear children." Whom should children imitate but their father? Believers have had experience of their Father's wisdom, love, and power, and it is only an instinct of filial lovo to imitato such !l. Father. 2. Because we were originally made in ltis image (Gen. i. 2G), and though that image has been marred by sin, it is to bo renewctl in the process of I\ Christian experience (eh. iv. 23). 3.
