(1 John iii. 2.) III. MEANS TOWARDS THE FULFil.MENT OF THIB DUTY. 1. Pray without ceasing, especially for fuller measures of his grace, for larger disclosures of bis love, for o. deeper insight into his truth. 2. Live continually as being under his eye. (Ps. cxxxix. 6, 7.) 3. Consider how others have followed him. (1 Cor. xi. 1.)-'l'. C.

entries.title: EPH 5:2
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-The walk of love. We are bound to love one anothor. THE EPISTLE 'l'O THE EPHESIANS. [oa. v. 1--33.

I. Tms WAS THE GREAT DUTY OF THE LAW. cc All the Law is fulfilled in one word even in this, Thou. shalt l~ve th_y n~ighbour as thyself" (Gal. v. ~4). "The end of the commandment 1s love (1 Tim. 1. 5). All our duty to our neighbour is summed up in love. Love supplies the motive-power to all right relations with our fellow-men. II. Tms WAS THE NEW OOMMANDMENT OF CHRIST. "A new commandment give I unto you, that ye love one another" ( John xiii.\34). The .love thus newly enjoined has ceruiin important characteristics. 1. It must be tl1e lot'tl of deeds, fl,Ot words. "Let us not love in word, neither in tongue, but in deed and in truth" (l John iii. 18). 2. It mu.st be ardent. "Above all things have fervent charity among yourselves" (1 Pet. iv. 7, 8). 3. It must be se/,f-sacriftci:ng. cc We ought also to lay down our lives for the brethren" (1 John iii. 16). 4. It oughJ, to be a love well guided and controlled. "This I l:':r~y, _that YO_?r love may abound yet more aud more in knowledge and all judgment" ~~nu. L 9)._ ~- It ought to be a constant love lilre that of (Jhrist. "Having loved ms O'l\"Il which were in the world, he loved them unto the end" (John xiii. 1). 6. It ougl.t fo be a decisire t£st as to our condition in God's sight. "He that loveth his brother abideth in the light, and there is none occasion of stumbling in him" (1 John ii. 10). "We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren" (1 John iiL 14). 7. It must be a love recommended by the highest examples. "God is lo,e." " If God so loved us, we ought also to love one another." We are to •• walk in love, as Christ also loved us." "Let the same mind be in you which was. also in Christ Jesus" (Phil ii. 5).-T. C.

entries.title: EPH 5:2
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-The pattern of (Jhristian love. "As Christ also hath loved us, and hath. given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savour." Jesus was an example of love in his life, for he went about every day doing good (Acts L 38). But it is to his suffering .of death that the apostle points us for •the most sublime and impressive illustration of his love. The words suggest many pregnant though~ . L WHO OFFERED Bll[SELF ? It was Christ, the only begotten Son of God. It was his own volnntary act. " Greater love hath no. man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends" (John xv. 13). "Who loved me, and gave himself for me" (Gal. ii 20). It was love that prompted the gift of himself-eternal, infinite, free. IL WHAT DID HE OFFER? Himse!L Not the blood of ot-hers, much less the blood of bnlls and goats. It was the offering of the body of Christ (Heb. L 10). IlL Fo& "1!0ll? For us, while we were yet enemies (Rom. v. 10). Whether he died in oar stead or merely for o~ benefit is determined by the context, which represents him as giving himself" an offering and a sacrifice." This language marks the distinctly substitutionary character of Christ's death,just as he is himself described elsewhere as" a ransom for many." IV. To WHOM DID HE OFFER HIMSELF? To God. That is, with the design that God might accept the sacrifice. God had pleasure in the death and atonement of his Son. V. IN WHAT MANNER? "As an offering and a sacrifice." The term "offering" 2.pplies to _propitiatory sacrifices, as well as to free-will offerings (Heb. x. 18, 14). The additional word, "sacrifice," marks the clearly propitiatory character of his offering (Heh. vii. 27). VI. WITH WHAT RESULT? "For a sweet-smelling savour." This phrase is applied to propitiatory as well as to free-will offerings, as, for example, ~o the burnt offerings of Noah (Gen. viii. 21). The sacrifice of Christ was well-pleasrng to God, who could henceforth manifest his character" as jll6t, and the Justifier of him who believeth in Jesus." 'l'he whole passage teaches us: 1. The unsoundness of that theology which sees in the sufferin(J's of Christ, not a propitiatory sacrifice, but the love, faith, 3111d submission of God's Son, as an example to man. This view is altogether one-sided. 2. 'Jhe unsounciness of that theology which sees in his sufferings a mere exhibition of lwe, without that element of righteousness which made these sufferings necessary. If lo,e alone could sa"re, why should he have suffered or died at all? It is the atoning 10,e, that is the element of consolation to man. 3. 'l'he unsoundness of that theology whid1 ~s the rt,aeeming power of Christ in his birth rather than in his death, as if the: event rJf Bethlehem were trawicendelitly more important than the event of OH. V, 1-33,] THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. 217

Golgoth11. 4. That there is in Christ's love, not merely a force of argument or motive, but a very rule or measure, of the love which we ought to exercise toward each other in the bonds of the gospel.-T. C.

entries.title: EPH 5:3–5
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -Warnings against impurity of all kinds. The sins here described were common among the heathen, and received no adequate check from their moral guides. Indeed, the old pagan world regarded them as things indifferent. They are, for the most part, sins against ourselves, as the sins condemned in the previous verses are sins against our neighbours. They are to be condemned on many grounds. L Tm;y ABE EXPRESS VIOLATIONS OF THE DIVINE LAW. (Exod. xx. 14.) II. THEY ABE DISHONOURING 'rO GoD AND HIS HOLINESS. The corruption that is in the world through lust is inconsistent with the Divine nature (2 Pet. i. 4). III. THEY THWART THE DESIGN OF THE GOSPEL OF CHRIST, which is" to purify a people to himself" (Titus ii. 14) ; " to cleanse us from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit" (2 Cor. vii. 1). Jesus suffered in the :flesh that we should die to the flesh (1 Pet. iv. 1). , IV. THEY GRIEVE THE HOLY SPmIT, whose office is to sanctify us (eh. iv. 29, 30). "That pure and holy dove will not dwell in a cage of unclean and filthy birds.n V. THEY DISHONOUR THE BODY, which is the temple of the Holy Ghost (1 Cor. vi. 18). They waste it as well as dishonour it (Prov. v. 11). VI. THEY WAR AGAINST THE SOUL in every sense of the term-against its life, its aspirations, its happiness (1 Pet. ii. 11). They even darken the judgment and the understanding (Hos. iv. 11). No sort of sin so hardens the heart. VII. THEY PROVOKE GoD's ANGER. (Col. iii. 5, 6; Jer. v. 7; eh. v. 6.) "For the wrath of God cometh upon the children of disobedience." They subject transgressors to God's judgment, for" whoremongers and adulterers God will judge" (Heh. xiii. 4). And they keep them out of heaven (1 Cor. vi. 9; ver. 5). These sins of impurity are not even to be named among saints, who are to be pure in thought, pure in heart, pnre in speech, pure in life. "Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, that ye should obey it in the lusts thereof" (Rom. vi. 12). 'l'o this end we must: 1 Avoid all the occasions that prompt to impurity: (1) idleness (Ezek. xvi. 49); (2) evil company (Prov. vii. 25); and (3) all other sins (Prov. i. 25). 2. Make a covenant with our eyes (Job xxxi. 1). 3. Watch over our thoughts (Mal. ii. 16). 4. Delight iu God's Word (Prov. ii 10, 16). 6. Continue in prayer (Ps. cxix. 37).-T. C.

entries.title: EPH 5:3–5
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Warning against covetousness. It is singular to find covetousness, which is often the sin of respectability, linked with sins of gross impurity. In reality it springs from selfishness, like these other sins. It has its origin in the same unholy root. I. CoNSIDER THE NATURE OF COVETOUSNESS. It is the inordinate love of riches, manifesting itself in several ways. 1. In the eager anxiety to attain wealth, witbout respect either to God's glory or our own spiritual good. 2. In a sin/ul acquisition of wealth by extortion or fraud. (1 Kings xxi. 2, 13; Prov. x. 2; xxviii. 8.) 3. In a reluctance to use our wealth/or good ends. (1 Tim. vi. 17, 18.) II. How 18 COVETOUSNESS TO DE REGARDED AS "IDOLATRY" 1 Jt is to make a god of our possessions and to give them the homage of our hearts. All the essential elements of idolatry are included in this worldly disposition. The covetous man transfers to riches the love, desire, joy, trust, and labour which God demands for himself. His sin is all the greater because he knows that his god is no god. The warning of the texL is applicable (1) to all whose thoughts run more upon earth than upon heaven (Luke xii. 22, 25, 29); (2) to all whose comfort depends upon worldly successes (Luke xii. 19); (3) to all who grudge the time that is spent in religious duties (Amos viii. 5). 'l'he sin of covetou~ness is, therefore, to be jealously avoided (1) because it is odious to God- " The covetous whom the Lord abhorreth" (Ps. x. 3) ; (2) because it is destructive to ourselves, in turning our hearts from God (1 John ii. 15), in filling our hearts with trouble and care (1 Tim. vi. 9, 10), and in keeping us out of the kingdom of God (ver. 5). Let us, therefore, estimate the world at its _true value, meditate much on tbo fatherly care of our God (Luke xii. 31, 32 ; Matt. v1. 25, 26), act in faith upon the promises (Heb. xiii. 5), and remember the terrible brand of idolatry which rests upon THE EPISTLE TO 'l'BE EPHESIANS. [ CII, V. 1-33.

c0wt<>usness. It is a solemn thought tho.t the most common of all sins is the most serious in God's sight. Yet there is nothing in th& condemnation of this sin that j)1stifies the theory of other-worldliness, or the neglect- of the duties of common i!fc.-T. C.

entries.title: EPH 5:4
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -Wa;rni11g against mibecoming speech. '''Neither· filthiness nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks," J. 'l'HERE ARE TITREE VARIETIES OF UNEDIFYING SPEECH. 1.. "Filthiness:"· This term, tho_ugh_ refcrr!ng to_ acts as much as words, points espec!ally to that obscenity of speech which 1s so disgustrng to the moral sense of man. It 1s proof of a.corrupt heart--for "out-of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh "-and,-more tha1i'anything else, makes the tongue "a fire, a world of iniquity," even "set on fire ·o{ hell." 2... Foolish tai.king." Thi.sis the talking that will have many idle wo_rds to answer for at the day of judgment (Matt. xii. 36). It is more than mere _random gossip; it is the talk of fools which is folly and sin; it includes " corrupt speech'' ( eh. iv. 29), It· i_s aimless, sen.sele..,<s, fri.-olous ulk. Our talk ought to be full of reason and purpose, and bright 'llith happy suggestion. 3. "Jesting." The apostle does not condemn the ple:L-;antry which lends such a grace and joy to conversation, but the wit that is allied to lewdness, brimming over in: doullle entendres, and tending to demoralization. IL TB1i APOSTLE'S JUDG~"T UPON THESE KINDS OF SPEEOH. "Which are not convenient." 1. They a.--e not so in themselves, for the character of impropriety essentin,lly attaches to each of them. 2. They are not so in the speakers, who incur a: still deeper reproach and prepare for themselves a grover jndgment. 3. They are not so for the hearers, who, though they may be amused for the moment; are not profited, but rather debased by such conversation. , • • :• III. THE RIGHT USE OF THE TONGUE. "Giving· of thanks." Christian cheerfulness ought to express itself, not in buffooner:(or levity, but in thanksgiving and praise'. We have much to be thankful for in our daily lot, and the thought of the indulgent. kindness which supplies all our need ought to repress anything like foolish or scurrilous discourse. The langnage of. thankfulness will: minister grace to the hearers.-T. C.

entries.title: EPH 5:6
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Diuine W'T'ath upon disobedience. It was necessary for the apostle to mark the true nature and real end of impurity in all its manifestations. "Let no man deceive yon with vain worcls." ·, L IT IS ~O 'm."'C'SU AL EXPElllE..'<'CE FOR WI=D MEN NOT TO SEE THE WICKEDNESS OF THEIR ACTS. The heathen regarded moral purity as a thing i!1dilferent, and many of their moral guides palliated sorue of the worst features of pagan.sensuality. They argueci, as 50me have argued in modem times with a wicked levity of purpose, that ElllS of imprairy have their origin and their justification in the very constitution of our nature, that thev ace not inconsistent with many social virtues, and that they are not injurious to others. It is one of the blindiDg effects of sin that men do not see their sin u throuuh the iroorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart'' (eh. iv. 18f II. IT IS A ?dL~TAKE TO SUPPOSE THAT THE WRATH OF GOD IS LIBITED TO TflE PilEBENT LIFE, and is merely entailed through the connection established by the Divine government between sin and suffering. 'fhere is such a connection written i11 the physical constitution of man. Sinners often in this life receive in themselves "that recompense of their error which is meet" (Rom. i. 27), 'l'be drunkard is punished here in broken health, in loss of substance, reputation, and happiness. But we arc not to suppose that the laws of Providence which ensure these results exhaust the fulness of Divine wroth against sin. Scripturo tells UR plainly that sins of impurity entail exclusion "from the kingdom of Christ and of God " (ver. 5); that he will judge whoremonger11 and adulterers (Heh. xiii. 5), and that "the abominable, ancl murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall havo their part in the lake that burneth with fire and brimstone" (Rev. xxi. 8).-T. C,

.'" er. 7 .-&paratwn fr(Jffl erm. The apostle counsels believers not to be partakers with siLnr:r;;. That is, in their sins, not their punishment. We are here taught- 1. 'lll.AT lT IS pc,,,~'lllLE FOR BY.LJEVEP.S TO PABTAKl: (J}' Tin 81!\6 OF OTflEilS. 'l'hey OII, V, 1-33,] THE EPISTLE TO 'l'HE EPHESIANS. 211J

may do so by conniving at them, by not checking or punishing them, by not mourning over them, as well as by actually committing them. It is & dishonour to God, a lure to others, a mischief to ourselves, to stand in the way of transgressors. IL THA'l' BELIEVEns OUGHT TO MAmTAIN A VERY SEPARATE WALK IN THE WORLD. They who have named -the namo of Christ ought to depart from iniquity (2 Tim. ii. HJ). 'l'he cry to them ever is," Come out from among them, and be ye separate" (2 Cor. vi. 1 i). There is no co=on standing-room for Christ and Belial in the Church. This does not countenance our separation from society; for Jesus, who was" separate from sinners," was always in society that he might win sinners to God. Our walk is yet to be as i;eparate as it is to be circumspect, that we may stand apart from the plagues that will descend upon a doomed world.-'l'. C.

entries.title: EPH 5:8
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -The darkness turned into light. A.JJ a reason for their not lapsing into vices from which they had escaped, the apostle reminds them of the darkness of their pagan condition. I .. THEY WERE ONCE DARKl.'EBS ITSELF. "Ye were oometimes darkness." The phrase is very impressive, for it indicates a moral as well as an intellectual darkness. A hard he~t is always linked with a blinded understanding. The two act and react upon each other,-bccoming alternately cause-and effect. Men do not care to retair. the knowledge of God in their thoughts, and God, in judgment, gives them over to a reprobate mind. The most eulightened natures of the ancient world were thus "darkness" iLself. Athens, the eye of Greece, inscribed upon an altar the confession of its ignorance. The phrase, •:darkness," suggests three thoughts. 1.- There is fear in darkness-the foar of en!lmies, the fear of death, the fear of undefined agencies. Heathenism was full of fears •. Death was a dark. and terrible spectre. 2. There 1·s discomfort in darkness. Light, its opposite, is the symbol of joy. , 3. There is danger in darkness. Enemie>1 use the nights for their deeds of violence. 'Ne stumble on a dark night; we fall down precipices; . we take a wrong road. How expressive is the term as applied to the heathen I II.. THEY, ARE Now "LIGHT iN THE LORD,"_ Conversion has wrought a radical change in the understanding as well as the heart. Believers are now ligb t "in fellowijhip. with tbeLord".(1 John i. 3). There is tnore implied than the flashing into a human mind the knowledge of the truth; there is the renewing of thut mind into the love of the truth which it knows. Otherwise the light would torment and not comfort. But believers, thus doubly furnished. may well be called "light in the Lord." The light of the sun does not stream down directly upon the world; at least, it comes to the service of men reflected from a thousand objects which receive it upou their surfaces; similarly the world sees the glory of the Sun of righteousness reflected in tho millions of saints who are "lights in the Lord." Ill, THE l>UTY OF BELIEVERS IN THESE CIRCUMSTANCF:S-" WALK AS CHILDREN OF LIGHT." That is, as those in nearest connection with it, 1. .As light signifies joy, believers walk in the foy of an assured hope and a perpetual cleansing. "If wo walk in the light, ns he is in the light, . . . the bloou of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from nll sin" (1 John i. 7). 2. We walk in the day and therefore should not stumble. '"l'he darkness is past, and the true light now shineth" (1 John ii. 8). We ought to keep an eye fixed on the straight path of duty, and avoid the by-paths thnt lead to darkness and ruin. 3. If we walk in the li~ht, u·e ought clecirly to recognize the f,llowsliip of all travellers to Zion. "If wo walk iu tho light . . . wo havo fcllowsbip one with another," \Ve are going the san10 way, inspire,l by the saroo hopes, moctin:c; tho same difficulties, arriving at last nt tho same home.-'f. C.

entries.title: EPH 5:9
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Tl,e fruit of the light. It is shown or seen in nil tho forms of "goo<lncss nnd righteousness nnd truth." Tho goo<l, tho right, tho true, are only to be realized through the light that streams from the Sun of righteousness-" the true light'' that "now shineth." The apostle s11ye the fruit, not the fruits, of the light-as if to show th,u it takes all the three colours to make this light. Christianity would be a very imperfoct manifestation of God if a single one of those elements were missing from the true light. I. GOODNESS. It is spoken of elsewhere as a fruit of the Spirit (Gal. v. 22), aml thorcforo is not mere beneficence, for it hns its Ronrco in religious principle. 'l'hiM 220 THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. [cit. v. 1- 33.

exceJlence, in its T'IUious aspects of kindne.<:S and generosity, is kindled bv the light tb:.t illumin11tes the understanding. • II. R1~HTEOGS..'-~- The light ~h!ch communi~tes a knowledge of righteousness to the mmd also rn~~ a l?Vll _of ngbteon.~ness mto t~e affections. This principle bass due sense of D1vme obligation, and subJects the believer in every relation of life to the guidance of Divine Law. ~II. ·TB= This is a direct _emanation of !he light. It is religious truth, working ultimately to truth of character mall the genmne forms of Christian life.-T. C.

entries.title: EPH 5:10
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -The experimental test of the LortI's will. As the ninth verse is a parenthesis, the apostle states that it is by walking as children of light we are in a position to prove "what is well-plea.sing unto the Lord." l. CoNSIDEB THE TRUE STANDARD OF JUDGMENT AS TO RIGHT A.ND WRONG, The believer is not to discover it in whatever may be well-pleasing to himself, but in what is well-pleasing to the Lord. It is the.Lord Jesus Christ who is Lord of the conscience to regulate all our thoughts and all our actions. He has a supreme lordsbip over our life as well as over our death: "l<'or whether we live we live unto the Lord." He is thus not merely Saviour and Example, but Director of bis people in all the concerns of religious life. In difficult situations, therefore, the true casuistry of life is to ask-'Will this action be well-pleasing to Christ? IL Co:i-smEB THE SU1!.JECTIVE TEST OF THIS DIVINE WILL. Believers are enabled, in the clear light in which they walk, to discover the right path. It is through their being transformed by the renewing of their mind that they "prove what is that good, and accept.able, and perfect, m.1.1 of God" (Rom. xii. 2). Similarly we learn that "if any man will do bis will. he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God" (John vii. 17). Light admitted into the understanding contributes to win the affections, aad, the affections won, open wide the doors for the admission of more light. To know the law yon love and to love the law you know is the best condition in which human beings can be. It is the union of clear light in the understanding with perfect purity of heart which distinguishes the kingdom of redemption in its final practical triumph;-T. C.

entries.title: EPH 5:11–13
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Separation and rebuke the true attitude toward works of darknus. The apostle thus describes the duty of Christians in reference to evil works. L 'l'HE CHARACTER OF THESE WOBKB. "Unfruitful works of darkness." They spring out of darkness, they del~ht in darkness, they lead to darkness eternal. They are not naturally unfruitful, for they are fearfully prolific of result, but, in the light of . God they are fruitless, because most unlike to the fruits of light, which are goodness, :ri,!!;hteonsness, and trntb. '!'hey have " no fruit unto holiness," with an end of eternal life (Rom. vi 22). II. THE DUTY OF 6EPAB.ATION FBOM THEIL This is a negative security. Christians are to stand apart from erery evil work. There must. be no fellowship with darkness. The friendship of the world can only be purchased at the cost of the Father's friendship (J2..S. iv. 4). III. 'IHB DUTY OF BKBUXING WORKS OF DARKNESS, This is to be done with the new of producing a con.scion.mess ~f guilt and evil_ The Chris_ti~n attitude ~ust be aggressive toward all the forms of sm. The rebuke IS to be adrmmstered (1) mth the li~, using all plainness, yet with prudence and meekness, so as to win Gentiles to the truth; (2) with our lives, which, by the~ hol:f ~eparateness, ou_ght to demonstrate the folly and sin of the world. A holy man IS a V1s1ble reproof of sm. IV. THE REASON FOB THIS ATTITUDE Oi' SEPARATION AND REBUKE. The heinousness .of the sins and the necessity of making them manifest to the sinner's conscience. 1. The sins are (1) done in secret, (2) and they are too shameful/or mention. Such sins would naturally shun the light of day, for "every one that doeth evil bateth the light" (John iii. 20), and could not be committed to language without risk of defilement to others. 2. Yet they are not beyond cwre. The light of Divine truth must be let fall iupon them., that they may be corrected. "All things that are reproved are made mani- '.fest by the light." There is a necessary connection in Scripture between truth and holiness, and the truth must first be applied to the ignorant and the wicked, that it may m~kg way for the sanctifying agency of the Spirit. 'l'he sun-glass of truth held IJII, V, 1-33.] 'l'HE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS.

in the hnnd of the rebuker will concentrate the light from heaven upon the conscience of the sinner so that he will sea it full of all nameless lusts, and that very light will kindle a fire to consume them, unless the sinner, loving darkness, should turn a.way from the unwelcome light. 'l'herefore let Christians remember the duty of pious and prudent reproof, which may not only put sin to shame, if not to silence, but lead the sinner from darkness to light, from the kingdom of Satan to the kingdom of God's dear Son.-T. C.

entries.title: EPH 5:14
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -7%e trumpet-call of the gospel. Since it is light that manifests, there must be a rousing voice to awake the sleeper, that the light of life may be poured fully upon him. I. THE PERSON ADDRESSED. "Thou that sleepest." Sleep is an apt figure to describe the sinner. 1. He lives in an unreal worl,d,full of dreams and fancies, q.,ite unconscious of the real world around him. The sinner dreams of safety and peace. He is carnally secure (Rom .. xiii. 10; 1 Thess. v. 6). He may even walk in his sleep. 2. Be is wholly unprotected against danger. If he knew of his danger, he would not be asleep. He needs, therefore, t-0 be roused. 3. His work is wholly suspended. So long as the sinner sleeps in spiritual death he does no good, he gets no good, he cares for nothing. The figure of the text is, therefore, very expressive. II. THE COMM.AND ADDRESSED TO THE SLEEPER. "Awake . . . and arise from the dead." 'l'he first thing is to open the eyes; but we are not to suppose that the sinner bas any power of himself to open them, any more than the man with the withered hand had· power to stretch it forth before Christ said, "Stretch forth thine hand." It is the light which Christ is to shed upon the sleeper that will awake him. Just as the sun in the natural heavens, shining upon the eye of a sleeper, awakes him, so the beams of the Sun of righteousness end the sleep of death. 1. 'l'he cry, "Awake ! " is the voice of love. A mother's love will lull her child to sleep, but if the house is on fire, it will take another turn, and startle the child from it~ slumbers. 2. The cry," Awake I" is tbo voice of wisdom. 'l'he sinner loses much by sleeping. The thief pilfers by night. Tbo tare-sower goes forth in darkness to sow his seed. lf you sleep on till death, you loso everything. 3. The cry is a voice of command. Who commands? It is he who redeemed you with his precious blood. 4. It is a voice you have often heard-in sermons, in sickness, in sorrows, in calamities. III. THE PROMISE TO: THE SLEEPER. "And Christ shall give thee light." The light that comes from Christ can reach even the dead: "The hour is coming, o.nd now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God: and they that hear shall !iv " (John v. 25). The dead are not quickened before they hear his voice, but bis voico causes them to hear and live. Christ will give you light to carry you out of the society of the dead into the companionship of the children of light, because it has already introduced you into the fellowship of the Father and the Son. (1) We have lost much time already (1 Pet. iv. 8); (:!) we do not know how much time yet remains to us (Ja.a. iv. 14); (3) :we ho.ve to girn nn account of all onr time and opportunities. The reason assigned by the apostle is the evil of the days. Time must not be lost if the evil is to be quickly and effectively counteracted. The apostle does not hint. the nature of .the eviL Yet it is allowable to suppose that the days were evil, not in themselves, but by reason of man's wickedness and folly. (1) It is the evil of sin, rather than the evil of. punishment, that is meant. (2) It is pa.rt of the evil that men do not see it at a11. (/3) Itis part of the evil that they do not mourn over it. (4) It is part, of the evil that ,they will do nothing to remove it. There is, therefore, all the more reason for Christians .bestirring themselves in all seasons and spheres of action to counteract the evil of the c;ialys.-T. C.

entries.title: EPH 5:18–21
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-The true antidote to drunkenness. There is n. real contrast here exhibited between fulness of wine and fulness of the Spirit. There is an intensity of feeling produced in both cases. "There is one intensity of feeling produced by stimulating the senses ; another, by vivifying the spiritual life within. The one commences with impulses from without, the other is guarded by forces from within." The one tenus to ruin, the other to salvation. The Spirit-fulness "will keep the soul holy, the body chaste, and render the Christian fit for the service of God on earth and meet for the fruition and enjoyment of God in heaven." The exhilaration ea.used by the Spirit finds a threefold expression. I. IN PSALMS, HYMNS, AND SPIRITUAL ·BONGS. 1. The heathen festivals were remarkable for songs of drunken revelry. The excitement of the worshippers found vent in singing. Christians are likewise to express their exhilaration in songs. "The hearts and spirits of good men arc full of spiritual mirth and joy; they a.re as meny in the Lord as sinners in their lust; it is, therefore, lawful and laudable for them to express their mirth and give vent to their spiritual joy by singing." 2, '!'here is a happy variety in such songs adapted to the various moods of the singers. We have the Psalms of David; we have the hymns composed by pious men like Zacharias and Simeon; and we have the compositions, for public assemblies, of those inspired by tho Holy Spirit (1 Cor. xiv.). 3. There must be a harmony in these songs between the art.istic service of the voice and tho inner melody of the heart. Otherwise the spirit and meaning of the exercise will disappear. 4. Singing has always been a powerful instrument. of promoting the spread of true religion (Reformation, periods of revival). 5. The singing here enjoined was for social intercourse as well as for' tho public assemblies of worship. Christians ought to exercise their gifts of song to spiritual ends. II. IN GIVING OF THANJIS. Tho heart which is filled with the Spirit brims over with thankfulness. 1. To whom thanl,s are to be given. "To God, even the Father." 'l'o God as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and therefore our Father in him. (1) Because it is only from him we have anything that is good (Jas. i. 17); (2) ,bocauso it is only by him we arc preserved from evil (Ps. cxxi. 'i); (3) because he only is good in himself (Luke xviii. 19). 2. How should we give thanlcs to him 1 (1) By humblo confessio!l of our unworthiness (Gen. xxxii. 10; eh. iii. 8); (2) by humble acknowledgment of his mercies (Prov. iii. 6; Ps. cxlv. 1-9); (3) by improving everything to his glory (Prov. iii. 9); (4) by walking before him in all well-pleasing. 3. W11at must we tl1anlc him/or 1 "For all things." (1) For our mercies-for sparing mercy, for recovering mercy, for mercies both received and expected. Yon cannot expect a blessing in them unless you are thankful for them ; and the more thankful you are for mercies receiven the more reason is there for your expecting more. (2) For all providences-for prosperity or adversity, for health or sickness. 'l'he afflictions may be mixed with mercies, and may be the means of quickening our graces (Ps. cxix. 67). 4. How often must we thank him 1 "Alwnys." It must be continuous. The hcnrt must be kept in a constantly th:mkful fmme, and not expend itself at mere intervals in nets of devout thanksgiving. 5. Through whom are our thanksgivings to be made acceptable to God, "In the Na.me of our Lord Jesus Christ." We are authorized to use this Name as our warrant for expecting the acceptance of our services as well as the fullest enjoyment of all spiritual mercies . . Ill. MUTUAL SUBMISSION. The effect of the Spirit's full enjoyment is to produce a humble and loving spirit among Christian people. 1. The duty of mutual submission. This piinciple, which is inconsistent with a perverse egotism or a self-opinionated suveriority, has great and happy effects. It reduces the friction of human life, nnd contributes greatly to its comfort and peace. It has nothing in common with the servile aml obsequious temper which is such a dishonour to manhood. Let us mutually condescend to each other. "In lowline~s of mind let each esteem other better than themselves" (Phil. ii. 3). "All of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility" (1 Pet. v. 6). We ore not isolated units in society. "'fho esscotinl equality of men and their mutual dependence lay tho foundation for the obligation of mutual subjection." 2. The element or sphere in which this duty is to be maintained. "In the fear of Christ." 'l.'his is not terror, but the solemn revorenco with which we bow to the authority of our Divine Lord. Our submission is grounded iu our reverence for him, in our fear of olfonJin:; him by our o.irs of assumption or authority, in our supreme 'l'HE liPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. (CH. V. 1-33.

regard for hi~ holy u-ill. Thus Christi8.ll.ity lifts the commonest dut.ies and civilities and am<'niti,>s of socil\l life into the highest sphere, 1Jy connecting them with the supreme lc,rdship of Christ over his saints.-T. C.

Vers. 22_~24.-.The duti«; of wives._ In enfo_r~ing relative duties the apostle reminds us that religion ~kes hold of all posS1ble cond1t1?ns and callings of men. Religion is the great formative grace for men. We are set m a curiously various scheme of relations, in which the two principles of union and subjection are beautifully blended. The three relations in which these principles are seen in operation are peculiar to family life. The "l'.'i.fe is first mentioned, then the children, then the servants. Religion rounds out the life of the family in a lovely completeness. Consider- !. THE DUTIES OF WIVES. They are all summed up in the one word-subjection. It is singular that the apostle does not command the wife to love her husband as the husband is commanded to love bis wife. Her love is commanded elsewhere (Titus ii. 4), but not here. It has been observed that what is instinctive is not enforced, but only "l'."hat is necessary to hallow and direct our instincts. The husband is to be the head; yet he is not commanded to govern ; but he is commanded to love, as the means of securing subjection or submission on the part of the wife. She, again, loves more naturally and more passionately than man;. her love is no subject of co=and, it is taken for grantei ; and the apostle commands her to obey and honour her husband as tlie besi expression of this love. Jeremy Taylor says, "He rules her by authority, f>he roles him by love; she ought by all means to please him, and he must by no means displease her." Her great· duty, then, is subjection. Let us see what it in,.:ilves. L It is not seroihule. It is not like the obedience of servants to masters, nor even like that of children to parents. It is a submission that recognizes the husband's rule as just, tender, and wise. 2. It is a wise and loving obedience. Wives are "to be obedient to their own husbands" (Titus ii. 5). Sarah is quoted by another apostle as an example of this obedience (1 Pet. iii. 1-6). It wa.s necessary to emphasize this duty at a time when Christianity gave woman a new position of dignity and privilege, and when there might have been a temptation on the part of Christian wives who had unbelieving husbands to assert an authority over them inconsistent with the ori,,,uine.l. institution of marriage. There is to be no dual authority in the family. The gospel made them both" heirs together of the grace of life," as it made" both male and fem.ale one in Christ," yet, even in religious or ecclesiastical matters, she was not to usurp authority over the man, but "to be in silence" (1 Tim. ii. 12). 8. It is an obe,dience wiihin limits, though the wives are enjoined to be subject to their husbands "in everything," that is, in everything within the due sphere of a husband's authoritt, for they are not to obey him in anything contrary to God and his Law. They are to obey God rather than man. 4. It i.s an obe,diencefashumed in its conditions and spirit upr.-n tl.e ruhjedion of t~ Church to Christ. " A.B the Church is subject unto Christ, so let the lriT"es be to their own husbands in everything." This implies that the wife's obediEDce is not to be forced or feigned, but springing naturally out of her affection to her husband, her dependence upon him, and her recognition of the just grounds of his superiority. 5. It implies fear, ur_ ,:ever~.. "Let the wife se~ that sh~ reveren?e her husband" (ver. 83) not desp1Smg him In her heart, as :Michal despised DaV1d (2 Sam. vi. 16), but, like' Sarah, calling her husband "lord" (1 Pet. iii. 6). '!'he chaste conversation of the wife is to be "coupled with fear" to assert its own power. II. THE REASONS FOB THIS SUIIMISSION. 1. The husband's recognized headship in tluJ original institution of ma~e. "_T_he head of the _woman is ~he !°an" (1 Cor. xi. ~). Her obedience therefore, while a rehg10us duty, has its foundation m nature. (1) '!he man was first' formed. "Adam was first formed, then Eve" {l Tim. ii. 18). (2) The man was not created for the woman, but the woman for the man (1 Cor. xi. 9). (8) 'fhe woman was first in transgression. "Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the trans~ession" (1 Tim. ii. 14). (4-) The woman is the "glory of the man," but "the ma;; is the image and glory of God" (1 Cor. xi. 7). 2. Her dependent position. A.B the" weaker vessel," she needs protection, while he far excels her in those qualities which entitle to command. Yet his superiority in the8e re~pccts is consu;tent with his inferiority to the woman in gentleness, patience, sympnt\,y, luve, adicacy of sentiment. 3. The fitness of things. :5hc iH "to be subject to her own OU, V, 1-33.) THE ll;i'1b1'LE TO THE EPHESIANS. 225

husband." . 'l'his_ express!ve phrase points to the closeness, exclusiveness, and specialty of the_ reln.t1onsh1p•. ~t Is thus a great mischief to unsex woman by denying or disregardrng the supenonty of man. 4. The similarity of the relation to that between the Ohurch and Ohrist. "As the Church is subject unto Christ, so let the wives be to their own husbands in everything." As Christ is the Source of authority and direction to the Church, as he exercises both with meekness and gentleness, so is the husband to the wife. She is bound, therefore, to give him the obedience the Church gives to Christ, limited, of course, by the nature of the relation and the authority of God. She is not to ideniify her husband's claims with Christ, as if her Saviour could supersede or weaken the just authority of her husband over her. A religious wife loves and honours her husband all the more from the very intenseness of her love to Christ. Her very obedience, too, fashioned upon the obedience of the Church to Christ, becomes tributary to her influence over her husband. Christianity has lifted woman to a high place, but without unsexing her. The old pagan writer, Libanius, might well exclaim, "Oh what women these Christians have I "-T. C.

entries.title: EPH 5:25–33
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-The duties of husbands. As the duties of wives are comprehended in the single duty of subjection, the duties of husbands are comprehended in the single duty of love. The injunction is significantly repeated three times, as if to indicate that it was essentially needed to correct or qualify his sense of soverei~ty or superiority over her. Consider three points. I. THE CHARACTERISTICS OF A HUSBAND'S LOVE. 1. It is peculiar in its nature, unlike the love of parent or child, friend or neig)i.bour. "He is to love his wife even as himself." 2. It is single, e:cclusive, and undivided in its object; for the husband is to devote to his one wife all the affection of his life. " Rejoice with the wife of thy youth" (Prov. v. 18, 19). This fact is the condemnation of bigamy and polygamy. 3. It is to be considerate and tender, excluding all bitterness. "Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them" (Col. iii. 19). Husbands are "to dwell with their wives according to knowledge" (1 Pet. iii. 7); that is, with a due consideration t-0 their condition as " the weaker vessel," and with a disposition to hide or bear with their weaknesses or infirmities. It is to be a love that will make it unnecessary for the husband ever to command his wife. Tho gos)_)lll counterpart of " Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands," is not "Husbands, command your wives," but "lovo your wives." 4. It is to be mutual. The wife's love is presupposed, though elsewhere it is expressly commanded (Titus ii. 4). 'l'he husband is to love her as she loves him. The rightful confidence and sympathy of married life are impossible without mutual affection. All marriages of convenience or self-interest are thus condemned. Lo e must be the basis of marriage. 5. It is to be constant and lasting, notwithstanding all tho weaknesses or failings of the wife. II. THE METHODS IN WHICH THIS LOVE JS TO FIND EXPRESSION. 1. In providing for the temporal su,pport of a wife. The husband is to "nourish and cherish" his wife. Ho that provicleth not for his own is worse than an unbeliever (1 Tim. v. 3). 2. Ife m?J,St consult her liappi11ess and pleasure; for "he that is married is to caro that ho may please his wife" (1 Cor. vii. 33). 3. He mmt protect her life, her honour, her goo(l name; for she is" the weaker vessel." He must "give honour to the wife" (1 Pet. iii. 7). 4. He is to seek her spiritual welfare. He is to pray for hor and with her, remembering that she is an heir with him of the grace of life, "that your prayers be not- hindered." III. THE REASONS FOR THIS COMMA~"D. 1. The original law of marriage. " For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and the twain shall become one flesh." The union implies such an identification of interest, pr~ perty, and relationship to the world ns to make them n_lmos~ oue person. 2: T~e wife is the husband's other self. She is not only one flesh with h1mse!f, but she _is his v_ery body. "No man ever yet hated his own flesh," except the fanatics of ascetic devotioo. 3. The help, comfort, a11d blessi11g she brings to him. She is given to him as "an help- meet • '' she is his companion. "Yet she is thy companion and the wife of thy cove- nant,; (Mai. ii. 14). 'l'he heart of the hu~band "safely trusts in her" (Prov. xii._ 4). 4. She is the wealcer vessel. A spirit of chivalry ought to surround her w1Lh the shield of protectinO' love. 5. She is "the glory of the man" (1 Cor. xi. 7)-his honour and ornament an°d delight. 6, J]is union with her is typical of the blessed union that exists EPflESIA~S. Q THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. [en. v. t-:,3,

between Ghi·1$t and the Olmrch. All tbe lo,e and self,sacri6ce and service which Christ expended upon the Church supply the t_ype of a husband's duty to his wife.-'!'. C.

entries.title: EPH 5:25–32
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Tlie wmon between <Jhrist and tke Ohurch. The apostle unites, with nn exposition of the duties of conjugal life, a very impi:essive statement of the nature of the union between Christ and the Church. This statement is exceedingly important,• quite irrespectfre ol its supplyin_g; an illustration of the ground and measure of a l,ushand's affl'<:tion for his ~ife. There are three truths hel'e exhibited respecting the ,mion of Christ and his Church. I. CmusT IS THE lIE.U) OF THE Cnuncn .AS WELL AS THE S.AVlOUR OF TIIE BODY. ITe not only saves the Churc11, but goveros it; he not only redeemed it by his atoning death, but is its continuous I're-Ser,cr and Director, his life the very life of his people: "Becans,i I li,e, yo shall live also." II. CHRIST PREP.\RES THF. CHURCH FOR HIMSELF AS BIS SPOTLESS BRIDE. 1. The language implies that ihe Church icas originally impure, in fact, like the foundling infant of the prophet ex.posed on the day of its birth, "to the loathing of its person" (Ezek. :xvi.). If she had not been so, there would have been no need of Christ's glorious cleansing. 2. It was through Ms death that Christ designed to make his people holy. "He ga,e himself" for them (ver. 25). The language is clearly sacrificial. The gift involved a death of unutterable anguish, yet he shrank not from it in his unutter- able love. It is the death which secures our ultimate holiness, for it reconciles us to God and secures to us the gift of the Holy Spirit. We are redeemecl from the curse of the Law, that "we migl1t receive the promise of the Spirit" (Gal. iii. 13, 14). 3. The application ef the atonement. "That lie might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing nf water by the ,vord;" or, rather, "that, havin~ purified it, he might consecrate it." The Church is thus set apart as his bride-" the Lamb's wife." It is thus that Christ sanctifies his people with his blood (Ileb. x. 10; xiii. 11, 12), not merely by way of cxpiati0n, but by way of consecrating them t-0 himself. 'l'he instrumental means of the Church's sanctification is "the washing of \Vater by the Word." This points clearly t-0 baptism, which is elsewhere described as "the ]aver of regener.:tion;" but it is baptiSI!l. inseparably linked with "the Word." What is the spiritual import of this baptism? It neither regenerates nor secures the remission of sins. It is true that it is called "the la,er of regeneration" (Titus iii. 5), and that remission of sins is connected with it. "Arise, be baptized, and wash away thy sins" (Acts Xll.ii. 16). But no more is ascribed in Scripture to baptism than to the Word of God, Baptism cleanses from sin as the Word does. We are saved by the truth, begotten by the truth, sanctified by the truth. But this language docs not imply that the Word regenerates every one who hears it, or that it possesses a magic power to work saving results. " Faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the Word of God" (Hom. x. 17); but many who hear do not believe. Besides, salvl\tion, as in the case of. infants, is not linked inseparably with the Word. Historically, we know from the instances or baptism recorded in the New Testament that faith preceded baptiijm. '111erefore baptism cannot regenerate. We believt', however, that baptism is both a sigli and a seal of the covenant of grace, without believing that it has any regenerating power in itself. The Lord connects the blessin"'s of salvation with ~ bE)lioving reception of baptism, just as he does with a believing° acceptance of thl! Word. For the apostle is here speaking of the effect of baptism on the Church, not upon those who are aliens from it~ blessings. 4c. Tl,e <USign if t}u1, Lord in thi.B purifir,a,tion of t/,e Churcli. "That ho might present it to hims~lf a j!lorious Church, not ha,·ing spot, or wrinkle, or any Ruch thinl,(; liut that it sLould Le hc,ly arid without blemilib." (1) Tl,is refers evulently to t!te time of our Lorai ~,:;:md C/.ITliirtg, when he is to be admin,J in all them that bclic.e. It cannot refer v, the Cil•.ll"ch in this 1.orld, which, even iu its bc.t i;tates, bas many a 1,pot and many a wrinkle. (2) It implfos tl,at tl,e l,(!Td will Mmsel.f present lds Church "as his pur- ,:ha&e,:l J)O"-~es,iun," and he and no other will receive the Church as his bride to himself. (3) Tl,e r,or,rliturn rf the Church will ue one if spotless !llr,ry. f::he will ha,·e neither the spots ,,f sin or error to mar !,er beauty nor the wrinkles of decay, but will be '• h,,\y arid withr,ut blcmi1,h." 5. It v:as love tJ,o,t promz,tcd and directed t!te who~ pru,:,e.~s wl,ich u to liave sw;h a glorious result. "As Chri;;t also loved the Church." III. Cm:Jt;T A::SD nrn Crn.:r.c11 Ar.i,; o::-:r:; Mw,rnr:11s111r. "Fur we are mcmlicn, of hia

body, of his fleeb, and of his bones" (vcr. 30). I. This does not refer to the incarnation, for the assumption of human nature allied our Saviour to the whole race of man. This membership applies to believers only. 2. Neither does it refer, as Romanists say, to the Lord's Supper, in which, partaking of his flesh, we are flesh of his flesh. 3. It signifies community of life, like that which connected Eve in her creation with the flesh of Adam, We are. elsewhere said to be saved by his flesh ( eh. ii. 15), by his blood (eh. ii. 13), by-his body (Rom. vii. 4), by the body of his flesh (Col. i. i2); and his flesh is called our life, and described as· essential to eternal life. "Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you" (John vi. 53, 54). There is, no doubt, great mystery here, and therefore the relation between Christ and his Church may well be called so (ver. 32).-T. C. . Vera. 1-16.-The love and the wrath of God enforeing mO'T'ality. Paul is still working for the unity of the Church and calling for that watchful and pure walk on the part of the Ephesians which can alone promote it. He consequently brings to bear upon them the allied motives of the love and the wrath of God. And here we may remark, in passing, that the moralities which have tried to work themselves without the aid of Divine sanctions have proved practically powerless. No" independent morality" l1as as yet rendered any appreciable service to the world. We still need to be overshadowed by the Divine. Paul, moreover, begins with love, and then passes on to tho fact of the Divine wrath. And- I. THE LOVE OF GoD PATERNAL AND FRATERNAL SHOULD MOVE US TO MUTUAL LOVE (Vers. 1, 2.) The Ephesians :.~e exhorted to follow_their Divine Father as dear children. The constant love of the heavenly Father lights all the children on. their way and rebukes their want of love. The first motive in this section is, therefore, paternal lovo a call to children of God to be loving like their Father in heaven. But the second motive is from the fraternal love of Christ, which led him out of consideration for us to "give himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for an odour of a sweet smell" (Revised Version). The self-sacrifice of Christ, we are here taught, was a very precious offering in the F:i.ther's sight. In the cross the Father for the first time saw perfect obedience carried up to the point and in the a1ticle of death. While in one aspect Jesus realized the Father's wrath on the cross, because the Substitute for sinners, in another aspect he was contemplated by the Father with the utmost complacency. Self-sacrifice is fully appreciated by our Father in heaven. Now, if God regarded with infinite delight the self-sacrifice of the only begotten Son for the sn.ke of his brethren, there is no way in which we can delight our Father so much as by followiug in the Elder Brother's footsteps o.nd being 1"eady to sacrifice ourselves out of love to ti,o brethren. What a spirit this would in ruse into our Church lire! Harless notices that in this passage Christ is really represented as both Priest and Victim. In tho saruo way we may delight the mind of God in being victims and priests in our loving relationi; to the brethren. I!, 'l'llE WRATH OF GOD IS A REALITY TOWARDS THE COVETOUS AND UNCLEAN, (Vora. 3-7.) The idea that God will not be angry with wicked men must bo dismissed from all minds. Righteous indignation against certain fo1ms of evil is an experience' of a most imperative and holy character. We should lose our reverence for a God who did not become angry with sinners. It was the more needful to affirm this truth at Ephesus, since the deities of heathenism were supposed to lm adclicled ,to such crimes as uncleanness and covetousness. Olympus wns filled, by the impure imaginations of men, with a set of men nncl women who were for tho most 1iart fit for penitentiaries and state prisons. Morality received no backing from the mythology. But the thought that a God so loving as our heavenly Father is wrathful with the covetous and the unclean, and allows his wrath to burn against them, is surely calcula~d to wean men from such sins. Thero seems to have been insinuations in Paul's time .that the Diviuo wrath against impurity and covetousness was mythical, just as such insinuation prevails at present. llut surely the frightful punishment which these sins entail in the order of nature speak to the spirit of man about the reality of the Divine wrath. Not all the amcliorntions of science cau bring it about that men can so sin with impunity; the unclean nro cursed in tho very nature of things with a grievous curse, anc\ tho covetous sllffcr of necessity 228 '.l'HE EPIS'l.'LE TO THE EPHESIANS. [on. v. 1-3::1.

in their pinched and miserly souls. (,}od is an angry God against those who love sin, and our only course is to forsake it. Harless and Olshausen believe the word here rendered "covetousness" to mean in this connection "intemperance," the desire, not for gold, but for fleshly gratification-the making a god of the belly, and so an idolat.ry. Of course, if this sense be taken of .-AEov,((", it agrees better with the context and makes more emphatic Paul's appeal for purity. Do we make as much in there days of the Divine wrath as we should? As the love-pain of God as one writer bas called it., it is surely well fitted to enforce morality. ' III. PAR Fr:RTRER SHOWS TH.l.T THE DEEDS OF DABIO.""ESS ABB Ul."'FRUITFUL. (\-ers. ~11.) He tells the Ephesians they were once in darkness, and did these ,:c..<ls of darkness. But they ha,e come into the light which is shed upon our pith by our radiant Lord. They must walk, consequently,' as children of the light, remembering that the frnit of the light (so Rerised Version) is in all goodness and rigoteonsness and troth. 'l.'hus they would prove what is well-pleasing unto the Lord. In so doing they would have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but ·would rather reprove them. Now, in arguing that the works of dark- ness are "unfruitful," Paul is advocating morality on the ground of expediency, -· He has already applied the Divine sanctions, but he does not hesitate to back these up by showing that what God wills is good. Natural law endorses the Divine prece_pts. Bnt this is quite distinct from the position that the natural law can secure obedience when it stands alone. All experience disp:·oves this. Utilitarianism is not a suffi- ciently broad basis for a sound morality. But the expediency of moral rectitude is an important argument in its favour. Sooner or later a man who commits deeds of darkness finds he has made a mistake. IV. BUT IT IS A PURE LIFE WHICH wn.r. REALLY REPROVE 'rHEH. (Vera. 12-14.) It is thought sometimes by superficial people that accurate descriptions of the deeds of darkness will do something to disgust people with them. But this is Satan advising man again to become wiser by eating forbidden fruit. Paul's opiniqn is that it is a shame to speak and therefore to think of what is done by the sinful in secret. All the prurient curiosity which feasts itself like flies on foul corruption is of the devil. 'l'he true plan, therefore, is not to mention such matters. Let them be buried in oblhion, but let Christians awake from all lethargic slumber, and arise from the corruption of spirita.al death, and in the light of Christ live purely. Thus shall the deeds of darkness be reproved. All tbat we have to do then is to carry in the light, and the darkness and its deeds will stand convicted before us. The Ephesians are to indulge in no scandalous conversation under the pretence of defeating the doers of the dark deeds; but they are to walk in the light of Christ and be pure, and lo! the sinners shall hide themselves before them. V. Tnm ]l[A.Y BE REDEEMED BY HOLY LIVING. (Vere. 15, 16.) There he.s been 110me discussion as to the exact meaning of "time" in thjs passage. Harless is clearly of opinion-in which, as in most matters, he is followed by his French disciple, M. Monod-that "opportunity" ( der rechte Zeitpunkt) best expresses ..-dv Ka,pdv. Paul is consequently anxious that in evil days, such as those upon which the Ephesians' have fallen, they should be watchful and wise enough to "buy up eagerly their opportunity," and do the best they can for their age. This is by holy living. There is no other way of understanding the times and fulfilling our course in them. It will thus be seen that Paul appeals to the Ephesians, by both the love and wrath of God, • by the expediency and power of a pure life, to walk worthy of their high calling. In • this way he expects to enlist them in the great army of united and brotherly souls who are gathering round JeaDB our King and Head. May we all respond to his appeal! •-B. M. E.

entries.title: EPH 5:17–21
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Inspiration, spirit= and spiritwJ,. Following up his exhortations about holy Ii.ma-, Paul now proceeds to the subject of understanding the Lord's will. In doing so he ~mes across the necessity which human nature feels for excitement of some kind, and, warning the Ephesians against the low excitement of wine, he ' Upon 'Redeeming the Time,' Saurin bas two sermons in his tome viii. pp. 187-268; e.n 1 Jonathan Edwa1ds has a short discourse on 'The Preciousnes~ of Timo,' founded on Yer. 16.

commends the high excitement of the Spirit, with all its pleasurable manifestations. In other words, he speaks of inspiration, but condemns the spirituous while he commends the spiritual We have thus suggested- !. THE NEED OF SOME BTIMULUB FROM BEYOND OUJIBELVES. (Vers. 17, 18.) Thb is apparent from the fact that every one needs some excitement, as it is called, to keep· him moving-something to "interrupt our quiet and ordinary state of mind with some more lively feeling, which makes us live more consciously and in a manner quicker than we do in common." We all feel this. Now, this goes to show that we are not self-contained, no matter how much we desire to be so, but need a helping hand from without our personalities. Withhold food, and we perish. Withhold all stimulus from us, and we go of necessity to pieces. The whole question comes to be, therefore, where we shall get our required stimulus. II. TBE STIMULUS OF WINE IS ATTENDED WITH DANGER. (Ver. 18.) This is an inspiration which comes through sense. Now, all of us need a stimulus through our senses. Food is such a stimulus. A well-digested meal makes life move faster and quicker than fasting would. But the vinous inspiration leads to "riot" (Revised Version), and is inconsistent with that unity of the Church for which the gospel calls. We should abstain from such a dangerous stimulus as this, for its effect has been hostile to unity of spirit. But we might extend the precaution here to all thos:l excitement~ of a. sensual nature which exhaust and retard the spirit. As Robertsru says, "Wine is but a specimen of a class of stimulants. All that begins froo withQ'IJ,t belongs to the same class. The stim~us may be afforded by almost an::-- enjoyment of the senses. Dmnkenness may come from anything wherein is excessfrom over-indulgence in society, in pleasure, in music, and in the delight of listening to oratory, nay, even from the excitement of sermons and religions meetings. Tho prophet tells us of those who are drunken, and not with wine." Arnold, in the same way, bases upon this passage warnings against excess of bodily exercise, excess of intellectual exercise, excess even in our hours of work, excess, in a word, so far as it militates against Christian sober-mindedness. III. THE INSPIRATION FROM ABOVE OAN HAVE NO ATTENDANT EXCESS. (Vers. 18, 1\:l.)- We may be filled with the Spirit, and no riot result, nothing which will do anything but foster the glorious unity. For, as Arnold shows, the gospel and the inspirntious from God "at once excite and soothe," so that the soul is kept in holy equilibrium, and the inspiration has its natural manifestion. 1. There will be harmony in social song. Poetry and music will become tributary to unity of spirit. The Holy Ghost will permeate by his harmonizing presence social praise. 2. 'l'he praise offered to .he Lord will be heartfelt. It will not be a form of praise, but the very heart ~oing up to heaven. 3. Thanksgiving will be mightily promoted. In the midst of mnnifold mercies our God in heaven looks for constant thankfulness from us. And, indeed, if we understand his love we shall be prompted to give thanks "always for all things," in the N11me of our Lord Jesus Christ. 4. And inspiration will promoto mutuar. subjection in the fear of Christ (so Revised Version). '!'hue it comes to pnss thal an inspired people proves a praising and united people. What harmony the society fille1l with the Spirit realizes! It is heaven begun below. Whnt we need, therefore, is a Pentecost. If the Holy Spirit is pleased to fill ue, then shnll our discords vanish nud our hearts beat in unison. It ii by inspiration that the unity of the Church shall be eecured.-R. M. E.

entries.title: EPH 5:22–33
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
- What husband, and wives owe to Christ. In exhorting the Ephesians to purity and enthusiasm of life, Paul is naturally led to the family institution and the relations to be found there. In the heathen world the relntions between men and women were degrading. As PressenRe says, in his most suggestive book,' La Famille Cluetienne,' "One found in the pagan family neither purity uor love. At the moment when Jesu~ Christ came, it had reached the last degree of degradation, and one can apply to tho family itself those words of the Gospel, 'He has come to seek and to save that which was lost.'" In this passage of Ephesians we havo an insight into what Christ has done for the family. He has made of marriage the choice symbol of his own relation to the Church, and so family life is lifted into n Divine and spiritual light. '!'he consideration of Christ for his people regulates the consideration husband shoulcl show to THE El'ISTLE 'l'O 'l'HE EPHESIANS. [ea. v. 1-33,

wife; and the loyalty of Christ's people to their Master indicates the loyalty the wife should show the husband. Husbands and wives thua owe to Christ the purification of their relations and the sanctification of the home I • • L JESUS LEFT ms HEAVENLY HOIIE '"TO DE UNI'PED '1'0 BIB BRIDE, THE' CHUBOII. (Ver. 31.) It is evident that the parallel between the' son leaving father and mother that he may cleave unto his wife, and Jesus' leaving the bosom of the Father to be united to the bride, the Church, is what is in the apostle's mind.. ;fle says that he speaks of Christ and the Church (ver. 32). And in no·more 1 beautiful way can the self-denial of Jesus in leaving heaven be presented. Heaven had been: :fron:i. all eternity the happy home of the only be~otten Son. •He had lain in the ·Father's bosom and enjoyed ineffable bliss. But thougllts of marri~ae came, and the Father favoured the Son's idea. The morningdawued wheu Jesus must leave the homestead, an'd go forth t..:i win his bride. Angels may well have wondered at the step and doubted its wisdom. But the step is taken. The home is left, &nd never &.,,0'3.in can it be what it once.was, It is to be tenanted in due time with a bride, the Lamb's wjfe, composed of a multitude that no man can number, happy souls, each and all in deepest unity with the Son. We ci.o not sufficiently appreciate the ma.,anificent design of God in the marriage of •his only Son, or the condescension of the Son in forming such an olliance as he has .done. For no condescension in earthly marringes can more than feebly illustrate the condescension 0f the Divine Son in taking a human bride. Princes may marry paupers, but tho difference between poverty nnd princely weruth is as nothing compared with the difference between human nature and what is Divine. But ·besides,the human· nature was not pure upon which he set his love; it was sinful, lost, ruined. Imagine a prince, out of pure as distinguished from passionate love, singling out some poor, abandoned woman, and arra.nging for her education and health and elevation· in thought and feeling, until at last he can fairly marry her and give her share of his.glories and his home ;-this is but a faint image of what Jesus the Son of God has done in selecting as a bride the ruined human race, He determined to win his bride, and so he took sinless human nature on him, and arranged for the union of once sinful, but through grace sanctified., human nature with himself. II. THE CABB OF JESUS FOB THB 0mraCH IS THB IDEAL AT WIDCH HUSBANDS eioULD ADl m CABiliG FOB THEIR WIVES. (Vers. 25-33.) This is Paul's idea in this whole passage. Let us notice the order of the thought. 1. (J/vrist loved the <Jhurch, This sovereign and yet IIl.05t unselfuh love led t;o the whole history of Christ's devotion. His greai heart recognized the po&Sibilities of love when manifested to lost souls, and deiecmi:ned to realize them_ 2. He gaflB himselffur it. Here was heroic love. In the oatore of things husbands cannot give themselves to death for their wives and after.;. 1rarc.s enjoy their confidence. Bnt Christ was able to give himself for the Chmch and then to en.rer into union with it. But it surely shows that a husband who truly turns his wife shonld be ready to die for her. 3. His sel,f-sacrifice wa.a to secure the Church's wndificatwn. The Church was natura\ly polluted., sinful, degraded; but the whole history of Christ's devotion goes to show that he had our sanctification in Yiew. While setting his love on sinful souls, he hated our sib, and provided blood to cleanse our sin away. And the sanctification Christ secures for his bride is to be perfect. She ill to be without "spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing;" she is to be" holy and without blemish." In other words, the sanctification is to be thorough. And is this not to show that husbands who are true to their wives should keep their sanctification steady as a star before them? If a husband does all in his power to 1,roruote his wife's holiness, she can never bCJ the victim of.. any unholy lust, but sanctification will characterize every relation. 4. The love thus lavished on the wife is the love of a man's " bette1' self." To encourage this gallant and holy dCJvotion to women, Paul further shows the compensation. 'l'he husband and wife are one, just as Christ and tho Ci,urch are ot1e. In loving his wife a man is really loving himself. It is self-love as di.,;tingnii;ht:d from selfishness. It is the love of a man's "better self." A man is n0t expected to hate hiB own flesh, but to nourish and cherish it ; self-preservation diet~U:S such a crJurse • in the same way busbandJJ should love their wives, cherishing t::i~P.1 as rc:ally thek" better hah-es," or rather," better selves," and feeling assured tiiai a r:u,r:,.'11 real interests all lie in the direction of ten,ler consideration towards hie "'i1e. It th<.1s a:,r·~a:-.s that Je1JW1 has furni~hed the true id, al of devotion. We go not

to belted knights or tales of chivalry for our ideas about devotion to our wives, but to the foot of the cross, that wo may see in Jesus our perfect Example! Ill. THI!: CHURCH'S REVERENTIAL LOVE TO CHRIST IS THE IDEAL OF WIFELY DEVOTION. (Vers. 22-25.) If Paul would summon husbands up to the heights of consecration by the example of Christ, he would also summon wives up to a corresponding return of reverential devotion. 'l'he Church, in her love and obedience to Christ, is the patter1:1: of wifely devotion. Now, this leads us to consider how Christ rules in his Church. It is not an inconsiderate despotism, but an intelligent, considerate rule oflove. His wishes are expressed with infinite tenderness. There is no fury in his commandments. The Church feels and finds that they are not grievous. And so believers are loyal to the Lord from the heart. Nothing is so delightful as to obey him. Suppose, theu, that such a spirit characterized the wife's relations to her husband; that she saw in his every expressed wish the outcome of love, and obeyed him in the belief that obedience was her privilege as well as duty,-what Edenic homes men and women would possess on earth! And here it may be well to notice a fact brought out in Presscnsc's volume already referred to, and it is this, that the New Testament has evidently enteretl into many more details about the family tlian about the constitution of the Church. The reason is obvious. The battle of the fa.iih is to be won through the family. The family is God's unit. The Church is but a family enlarged; heaven, again, is only a family still more enlarged. God as a Father overshadowd all! If Christianity ensures a holy family; if she wins families from worldiness to holiness of life ;-then she may iadee,l lift up her head assured that redemption is drawing nigh. Christian homes on earth, paradise restored,-these are really the creations which we look for; and beyoml tho shadows a still statelier home arises in 1' the Father's house with its many mansions" prepared for the reception of the bride. The family on earth is sanctified that the family in heaven may be prepared for; the heavenly home is but the perfection of the earthly, if this is Christian to its core.-R. M. E.
