entries.content:
-Wl,at to imitate and to avoid. I. THE IlllTATION OF Gon AND Cnnr;;T. 1. The imitation of God. "Bo ye therefore imitators of God, as beloved children." The force of example is abundantly acknowledged. How much do most of us sufTcr from the lo,v standard of opinion and practico with which we arc surrounded? On the other hand, we havo all felt what it is to como into contact with one who is misc,! above the common standard. By his strength of principle and generous sentiments and noble endeavours he kindles our aspiration. Wo shouhl liko to be what ho is. The wonderful thing here is that God places us (which is of far greater conseque,cce) under the influence of his own example. 'l'his is the only place in which we are distinctly called to imitate God. But the same truth is given expression to by Christ when he says, "'l'hat ye may be the sons of your Father which is in heaven, for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and the good, nnd sendeth rain on the just and tire unjust. . . . Ye therefore shall be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect." P:tn 1 has just exhorted us to imitate God in his forgivingness. This imitation of God proceeds on what was referre(l to before-our being made nfter the Divine image. It proceeds on what is rcferrecl to here-God being our Father, nnd as such communicatiug n kindred naturo to us. Ilut for this kindred nature with God we should have no moro conception of him than the brutes have. "The idea of God, sublime and awful 11s it is, is the idea of our own spiritual nnture purified and enlllrged to infinity. 'fho infinite Light would be for over hidden from us, did not kindred rays d:1wn mHl brighten within us." It belongs to the dignity of our nature (our being pnrtakcrs of tho Divine n-aturo) that there can be proposed to us as our end likenBlls to God. It is de,igued that there should bo a. perpetual unfolding and- enlarging of our spiritual powers and excellences. All our desires, hopes, efforts, nre to be toward this. ,ve 11ro to be filled with the Divine thoughts, replenisbccl with t't111 Divine energy, warmed with the Divine love. Ae a child catches tho very tone of h1,1 father, so aro wo to catch the tone of our heavenly Father. 'J.'here is a reason ,ol•,.,A for our being eager to imitate God. Wo are hie beloved children. Oh, tho lo~u ....,stowecl on usl Sonship forfeited and then restored. What a contrn<liction, to be children reculiarly loved anti not to 6eek likeness to God I But this leads on to tho other thought. 2. 'l.'he imitation of God is also the imitation of Cl1risl. "Au,1 walk in love, even as Christ lllso loved 232 THE EPISTLE TO THE :b:PHESIANS. LcH. v. 1--38

you, iu1<1 ga,..e himself up for ns, an offering and a sacrifice to God for an odour of a s"·e.:t sme:I." C!/;.rist is prese,1ted for imitation in Mi love. We are not to understantl that i"'"e was &n attribute more distinctive of Chriat than of God. For love is the greatest attribute of God. But we are to understand that Christ was especially the manifestation of the lo,·e of God. In Christ's love we see what God's love is. And to imitate Christ in his love is the best way to imitate God. And how does love manifest itself? Selfishness manifests itself in isolation. Love, on the other hand, manifest11 itself in approachableness. And this was the form which Christ's love took. He loved us so much as to come within human conditions-to become one of ourselves. And that (wonderful as it is) was not the extent of his approach to us. For, coming into our nature, he next threw himself into our position, he became our Representative. .And he presented before God for us the offering of a perfect life. He especially, in his death, presented the sacrifice which had full atoning virtue for our sin. And this presentation of himself as an offering and a sacrifice to God (with the love that prompted it) was for an odour of a sweet smell. More grateful than to the sense of smell was the incense that the High Priest took with him into the holy of holies was to the heart of God the incense from his life and sacrifice which Christ took with him into hea,en. It is an incense which continually rises before God with acceptance. The lo¥e which prompted to this and carried it out to completion is here proposed for our imitation. But how need we think of copying such a pattern? All well set down a child to copy a masterpiece of a Raphael or nn Angelo? But let us take these things into consideration. (I) He has made provision for our imitating him. We are to be thankful to God, that, amid many bad examples and imperfect examples of good men, he has gin,n us one perfectly good example.. He has shown us that a life of the bi~ue:-.. unselfishness is not impracticable in our humanity. If that had been all, the e.Icct would only have been to fill us with despair. But the apostle does not encourage us to imitate Christ without pointing to liis sacrifice of atonement. His atonement bring been accepted for us, his perfect life has been accepted too, as that•which with assisting grace we may now hopefully strive after. (2) Compared with the example of God, the example ef Christ is more circumstantial. We know that God is love, but in Christ we see, under many conditions, how love operates. '!'here is much detail upon which we can dwell and from which we can obtain help as to the details of our life. (3) It is an exampl,e easily followed from its familiarity. It was a perfect example; but not in the way of being apart from us, but rather in the way of being so close to us as to be easily understood. It was the time- " When truth, embodied in a tale, Did enter in at lowly doors." (4) It Wall an ezampl,e <WX>mpanied with the strongest incentive to imitation. It was not merely that he taught us the reasonableness of a good life, and exemplified it; but he placed us under infinite obligation in dying for us, and then, having obtained this immeD.se ad,a.ntage, be comes forward and asks us to imitate him. (5) We are to imaate him in his wve by walking in lvoe as he did. This does not imply any tl!l.catural straining; but, in the ordinary walk~ of life, yve_ may fin~ s~fficient sph~re for the exercu;e and growth of love. We are specially to imitate Chnst m the m1ss10nary charactf:I" of his lo.e. We are to feel for sinners as in need of salvation. .And we are to sacrifice much in order that those ends for which he died, and on which his heart is set, may be furthered. Let us, then, choose Christ as our Pattern with the w~ole ene1:gy of our wills. And let us follow him, not as perhaps we may have done, with a famt and yielding purpose, but in the full conviction that in following him we shall best imitate God. IL Tm.NGB TO IIE CONDEMNED. 1. The things that are not to be named. "But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not even be named among you, as becometb saints." The apostle points here to a fact which is sometimes forgotten, that there is a sphere of that which is rwt to be named. There are, for instance, books written, in which blasphemous things are said against the Saviour. There is this reason for not reading these books or not repeating blasphemous expressiono contained in thew, that they stick to and pollute the imagination. So the apoRtle teaches that saints art to be so cultivated in their sensibilities, to have such a delicacy of feeling, OIi, V, 1-33,] THE EPISTLE 'l'O THE EPHESIA~S. 233

that they will not talk about or hint 1Lt things connected with fornication arlll uncleanness. 'l'o take to them in conversation indicates II coarseness of mind, a polluted state of the imagination. That is the proper circle, whether family, or Church, or neighbourhood, from which the very name of such things is banished. We aro surprised that covetousness is classed as it is here among the things which are not to be named. It is a sin about which strange things a.re said in the New Testament. It is said that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. The apostle teaches here that saints are to have such sensitiveness as to be repelled from the very mention of covetousness, as that which would pollute their lips. Think of a community educated up to that state of refinement. 2. The things which are not befitting. "Nor filthiness, nor foolish talking, or jesting, which are not befitting: but rather giving of thanks." There are things, the apostle teaches, which are to be condemned on the lower 1\round of their being improper, or conducing to no good end. By the first mentioned we aro to understand, especially, that which is foul in speech. If we distinguish fooli.•h talking from other faults of speech which are mentioned in this Epistle, we must limit it to what is senseless in speech. Fools have a way of talking in wanton disregard of what is rational, as though their rational powers were given them to be played with. The word translated "jesting" is sometimes used in a good sense. .And Barrow bas shown that there is a wit which is not to be condemned, but which is fitted to minister harmless delight to conversation, to expose things base and vile to due contempt, to reprove some vices and reclaim some persons, to confute errors that do not deserve solid confutntion, to repel unjust reproach and obloquy, ~nd to counterbalance the improper use of it. "It is bad objects or bad adjuncts, which do spoil its indifference and innocence: it is the abuse thereof to which (as all pleasant things are dangerous, an,l apt to degenerate into baits of intemperance and excess) it is very liable, that corrupteth it, and seemeth to be the ground why in so general terms it is prohibited by the apostle." "All profane jesting, all speaking loosely and wantonly about holy things, making such things the matttir of sport and mockery, playing and trifling with them, is certainly prohibited as an intolerably vain and wicked practice." ".All injurious, abusive, scurrilous jesting, which causeth or needlessly teudcth to the dis~ace, dam~gc, vexation, or prejudice in any kind of our neighLonr, is also prohibited." "There ar~ some times and circumstances of things wherein it concerneth and becometh men to be serious in mind, grave in demeanour, and plain in discourse." To what the apostle condemns as not befitting he opposes giving of thanl~s. There is a fitness in thanksgiving at all times (" giving thanks al ways," as it is said in the twentieth verse) ; but wo are to understand that there is a singular fitness in the present connection. Thanksgiving is speech put to the best use (implying both seriousness and joyfulness). Let there be that, the apostle would say, and it will rectify and hallow all speech. 3. The things which are not safe. "For this ye know of a surety, that no fornicator, nor unclean person, nor covetous man, which is an idolater, hath any inheritance in tbo kingdom of Christ and God." The apostle is confident, as declaring what was attested by their own consciousness or practical acquaintance with the kingdom. It is tho kingdom, not only of God, but of Christ and God, that is to say, a kingdom peculiarly associated with the cross of Christ, in which God shows his deep detestation of sin by puuisbiog it in his Son. A kingdom that is ruled over by One who shed bis bloou that siu might be done away, cannot receive into it those who sin and do not mean to give up their sins. By their very antagonism to the whole spirit, law, ends, of the kingdom, they shut the door against themselves. We are surprised again that the covetous man appears in such company, and further here that be is singled out for special remark. "Nor covetous man, which is an idolater." There is idolatry in tl,e other sins, that is, sensual pleasure is put in the place of God. Ami that may bu tho light in which the apostle views the devotees of pleasure as shut out from inheritanco in the kingdom. But the covetous man is put forward as being an idolater by preeminence. Christ had already said, "Ye cannot serve God and mammon." Tho covetous man is not he who values money and seeks to serve God therewith. Ilnt, according to the thought here, he is one who idolizes money, values it in itself and nut for God's ends, sets his affections on it, trusts in it; and, such beiag his ro)ation to it, then it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of e. needle than for him to enter into the kingdom of Gu,!. It is true of tbo covetous man, i;s it ia not true of the oLher,1 THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHJ<.:SIANS. [cu. v. 1-33.

that he can go on .n his sin without incurring the opprobrium of meu, and (pru-tly from the difficulty of drawing the exact line between the-'right nnd the wrong love of gain) without suspecting himself that it is getting a hold upon him, and thiµi (without such checks as the others have) getting hardened in his sin, we can understand how he should be called by pre-eminence the idolater. Warning. "Let no man deceive you with empty words: for because of these things cometh the wrath of God upon the sons of disobedience. Be not ye therefore partakers with them." It would seem that there "·ere apologists for vice, who, by their representations, tried to entice the Ephesian Christians back to Gentile ways. One of their representations was that, besides being ple.'l.Sa.nt, it was safe to do these things. So apologists for vice are ready to say this and many other thlnf:S still. But" let no man deceive you with empty words." Such ,rnrds bave not as their contents eternal truth. "For because of these things cometh the wra.th of God upon the sons of disobedience." The sons of disobedience are those who (m tl:eir lo,e for sin) disobey the gospel of Christ., by which alone there is c.2.iverance from wrath. Refusing God's mercy, how can they escape God's wrath? They are not only lying under ordinary judgments or condemnation now, but they have yet to be dealt with for these very sins. "After their hardness and impenitent hearts they are treasuring up for themselves wrath in the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous jndgment of God.." It is for those, then, who regard their safety (to bring in no higher consideration), whatever apologists may say, to refuse to be partakers with the disobedient. 4. The things that are dark. (1) 'l'hey are in their walk to "be separate from their former state. "Ye were once dark_ness, but are now light in the Lord : walk as children of light." They had been brought up in heathen darkness. It was that in which they lived and moved and had their being. And so, by appro.: priation, it was more or less embedded -in their nature. But now, living and moving and having their being in the Lord, that is, in light (as contrasted with heathen darkness), and being enlightened by him through his gospel and Spirit, they were light. And such being their state, there was a call to walk as children of light We are to walk under the incitement of the glorious fruit of Christian ill-uminatiM. "For the fruit of the light is in all goodness and righteousness and truth." 'fhe philosophic triad is the true, the good, and the beautiful. The Christian triad as given here, and with which we ought to be familiar, is the good, the right, and the true. The good, or excellence of the heart, comes first; for that is first in God. Then follows the right, or regard to conscience, to eternal principle. And, lastly, there is the true, or rcgarcl to reality, not only in fact, but in thought (including the perfect in form). We are gooa in cherishing a spirit of love; we are righteous in doing our do,;y; we are true in conform in a to Divine forms of thouaht. Having these three in us, then it may be said that th~ beauty of the Lord our God is upon us. We are to walk in the -uJay of proving what is wel,l-pleasi11g to Christ. "Proving what is well-pleasing unto the Lord." It is not what the apoloo-ists for vice say; it is what Christ says. It is that which is to.be tested. It is impli;l that we have the means of testing all things in this light. '!'hero are many things which, put to the test by us, we must rejl!ct. _'l'hey are revealed in our Christian consciousness as wrong. There aro other things which we seo to be good, not merely in the convincing light of truth, but in our own blessed experience in tho doina of them we feel that we have the approval of tho Master, we c11n even now hear his .;ords "\Veil done, crood and faithful servant." Our position, then, must be separation from' darlcness. "And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness." The fruit of light is one, a gloiious indivisible cluster. 'l'he works of darkness aro many. The fruit of light is fitted ~o incite 1;1-s. The ~orks of darkness should de~r us. They are unfruitful. They yield nothmg that 1s worthy of the name of fruit, but only shame and death. (2) They are to take an aggressive position toward darl,- ness. "But rather even reprove them." 'l'hcy were not to pass them over in silence or find excuses for them but to hold them up to reprobation to the doers of them. As darkness was a~ive toward them, so were they as light (even for their own 1,afoty) to be awessive toward the darkness. 'fhey were to lift up the Gentiles to their own position. It is added, as showing the clamant need for reproof, "For the thiuns which are Jone by them in secret it is a shame even to speak of." It is added further, a~ ~huwin::; the use or enc!. of reproof, "But all things when they arc reproved a.re made.: n,a::i'.est by tlrn light." "All tho~e secret sins aro laid hare in their real Oll. V. 1-33.] 'l'Irn El'lS'l'LE 'l'O 'l'llE EPHESIANS. 235

moral character, unveiled and brought into distinctness before the moral consciousness, by the light of Christian truth, which is at work in your reproof; by the light, I say, it is made manifest-for, it is added, 'everything that is made manifest is light,' has ceased thereby to have the nature of darkness, and is now of the essence of light." And thus, whether there was amendment or not, they would be making an inroad on the territory of darkness, making dark deeds stand out in the light. (3) They are to take this aggressive position in consistency with the awalcening call of God. " Whereforo he saith, Awake, thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall shine upon thee." The words are from Isa. Ix. 1, 2, and receive from the apostle a. Christian adaptation. (a) It is a call to the child of darkness. He is described as sleeping and dead, that is, in sin. He is insensible to the infinite importance of spiritual and eternal things. (b) It is a call to awake and, arise. "Awake, thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead." He does not let the child of the night alone. He comes to the sleeper and bids him awake, to the dead and bids him a.rise. And in his very summons there is an awakening, quickening power. (c) It is a call to which a promise is attached. "And Christ shall shine upon thee." As if it were said, "The sun is already up, and will pour his enlightening rays upon thee." So while we are sleeping and dead in our sin, it is true that the Sun of righteousness is up shining upon this world of ours, and we must up and catch his rays. Other men are up and doing their work under the light of this Sllli; why should we be asleep and dead in sin ?-R. F.

ZL-Exhortati'c,n to exercise wisdom_ in regard to our manner of walk. "Look therefore carefully how ye walk, not as unwise, but as wise." The object to which we are to look is this-how we walk ; in other word11, the rllnduct of our life. ln regard to this we are to be careful. At cross-roads there are sometimes finger-posts put up to indicate where the different roads lead to, that travellers may be at no loss. By looking carefully at these, they may save themselves much trouble and delay. So it becomes every traveller to eternity to know the road that he is takin~, whether it is tho narrow or the broad. There are finger-posts put up by God(in the Word) by which we may ascertain this and put ourselves right if we have to our grief taken the wron 6 road. But, seeing many do not make use of these finger-posts (do not look at them at all, or only carelessly, and thus exhibit great folly), the exhortation takes the negative as well as the positive form. "Not as unwise, but as wise." 'l'he word translated "carefully" may also be translated" precisely,'' and suggests this, that we are not only to look to the general correctness of our conduct, but to look to it down to the smallest details. It is only by thus going carefully over it in detail, with no foregone conclusion in our mind, but earnestly seeking God to search us and to discover to us what can be altered for the better, that we may be able to bring it out into some beauty of conception as a whole. Tht:re are two things in regard to which we are to exercise wisdom. I. Turn. "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil." The right management of our time is what we are particularly to look to. The exhortation is to redeem tho time, that is, the timo meted out to us on earth, in which to fulfil the Divine purposes. Literally, as given)n the margin, we are to buy up the opportunity. 'fhe idea is that every moment has its own duty assigned to it. By doing the duty in the moment, wo make a purchase of the opportunity, we turn it into a gain. We keep abreast of time; wo avoid subsequent collision of duties. ·whereas by not doing the duty in the moment, we contract debt, we foll behind. Instead of being the free owners of our time, we become slavish debtors to it. We are to be like merchants that seize every vantage that is going. Merchants, that travel about from place to place, do not get a vantage nt every turn. They must lay their account by e.n amount of fruitless toil. But as heavenly merchants, we are in this enviable position, that every moment comes laden with golden opportunity. And we are to make our moments as they pass rich in all the gains of n good life. 1. Good planning. If we would redeem the time in Its day~, then we must anticipate them by wise economical arrangements. Wo must sec them coming, and know how (God willing) wo nro to fill them up. The light that we hnv~ got from past days we are to put into some workable scheme for the <lays to corno. 'lo the excellence of a day-plan it is essential that we rightly proportion between the various duties ofli[o (so that none aro left out or do not get their proper place). We are to keep up the right proportion between our severer and our lighter engagements. It bohovcs every ono to THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. [en. v. 1-33,

have a task, a definite_ task! a ~k that taxes his energies, And if he does not have it bf necessity of .PT?Cunng his daily bread, yet should he have it by necessity of steadying bunself. ~ut lt 1s not g?od for the bcw ~ be always bent, and, if we manage well, we shall find time(and find 1tgood for the domg of our task too) to relax ourselves in social enjoyment.. We are also to keep up the ,·-igkt proportiO'II, between our religious and 001· secular ~utteS. . The latter,. as a general ~rra~ge':°ent, ~ust take up a large proportion of our time. Six to one 1s the proportion md1cated m the command. But in every wel)-pl~ned life there will be found ample time for religious duties. Every day is to bcgm_ with an acknowledgment of_ God. It ~a.y seem utopian to expect morning ,~e,ot1ons of one who has to be at his ~ork at s1:x o'clock. And yet it only requires a little t3ken off sleep or off the previous evemng to secure the necessary time for God. And surely that is not too much to expect of any Christian in the interest of a well-ordered life. Morning devotions alone will not make the day good. Only when these ha.e been conscientiously engaged in there will be felt to be an obligation to make the day's work harmonize with them. The evening may be utilized for self-im- provement and ministries t.o others. And the da.y is to end, as it began, with God. It is only by such planning (in the name of him who is not the author of .confusion), that we can expect to be like merchants accumulating a large fortune. 2. Good p7,anning fallowed up "by decisiveness in execution. There is a reason given for redeeming the time: "Because the days are evil." The very earth bas ta.ken a. complexion from the degeneracy of the dwellers on it. And so our days are evil, and not such as they would ha'i'e been under normal conditions. (1) The days are evil because many of them are lost already. \Ve have known the degeneracy of the days in our own experience. We have lost me.ny a good opportunity. This thought should act as a powerful stimulus to us. The apostle gives revenge as the last a.nd crowning fruit of a. godly sorrow. "Yea., what revenge!" be says. We are to take revenge upon ourselves that we have given so much of our valuable strength and time to our adversary. The workman knows what it is to make up lost time. When he falls behind with his ta.le of work, be bas to work longer hours or to apply himself with double energy when he is at it. So, beca.nse our days have been ill spent in the past (before conversion a.nd after conversion u.o) are we to work with redoubled energy in the future. (2) The days are evil, because c,j the many temptatiom they lYring. In our caim moments (sorrowful for the past) we ti:tin.k of i;pending our time in a cert.a.in wa.y that seems good to us. But circumstances are not altogether with us. In a world where evil has obtained such a hold we must lay our account t.o our being solicited from without more or less urgently to depart from c,nr plan. And what makes the solicitation much to be feared is that we are enfeebled from our past. If we had conqnered obstacles a.s we went along, we should have been in a freer, stronger position to-day. Bnt we have to drag our antecedents with us, like an old debt. We have undigested time, lying like a. burden on our present energies. And though, with repentance a.nd forgiveness, there is a. sense of freedom and hope imparted to us, yet there is that which is to be conquered in evil habit. The only way of conquest is to deal rigorously with all interruptions of duty, as they a.rise, as those who would see the time redeemed, a.nd not its losses added to. (3) The days are evil because they are few. We have time to make up (in the face of i;;reat temptations), and little time to make it up in. Had we a thousand years to live, the case would be altered. That would be a comparatively long period in which to make up what we ba.d lost in thirty or fifty or seventy years. But when the days are evil in this sense that we cannot calculate on a single day as ours, there is surely ur;1;ent reason for m~king up our losses without delay. Were all the interests of life crowded into one moment were we told that upon the use we made of that moment depended our future happin~s or misery,-how urgently should we be called upon to use it aright I What is actuaily the arrangement differs little from that. We really live on from moment to momi::nt, not knowing which is to be our last. How wise, then, to seek to make out ,,r every pa.;;sing moment eternal gain ! Inference in which there is a recurrence to the gerlKf"al e~Jwrt,J.ti,,:m, and a transitwn t<> the sewnd partit;ular. " Wherefore be ye not f,,.-,lish, but underatand what the will of the Lord is." The teaching here is tba.t Christ iE u,rd of our time. He has the sovereign appointment of the time of our coming here a~,,i the time c,f vur going hence. All our undertakings arc conditioned by this: "If th,, u,r<l wilL" He has ~ovcreign rights over our time. 'l'o him we owe the firstfruita

of our time, as we owe the firstfruits of our substance. From Christ we get the whole plan of our life. 'fhe right management of our time, then, is to understaml what the will of the Lord is, what Uhrist would hi.ve us to do. Seeking Christ's mind as to the employment of our time, we may expect that we shall obtain from him the strength necessary to conquer all the obstacles of our time, and to do the work of each day in its day, according as the duty of the day requires. II. WINE. 1. JJissuasive/romfalse excitement. "And be not drunken with wine, wherein is riot." It is evident from the language which is here employed that the wine drank in those times was intoxicating. 'l'he apostolic advice must be regarded as even more applicable to drinks of stronger intoxicating qualities, which are manufactured now. It has its application to the intoxicating cup of the world in every form-to the intoxication of novel-reading, to the intoxication of keenness in business, to the intoxication of political excitement. This advice is not inaptly connected with the previous advice as to the right management of time. For it is when time is not pr~perly filled up, when it is insipid, monotonous, or when it is filled up with wrong-domg, that there is the temptation to go after some form or other of earthly excitement. It cannot be said that the use of wine at all is forbidden by this precept. But there is certainly sounded in connection with it the note of alarm. There is put up beside it the red flag of danger. "Be not drunken with wine." Drunkenness is the feverish desire, the morbid craving,• for drink. The man with his noble powers becomes one huge, ever-seeking, never-satis- fied appetite. It is a vice into which all classes are in danger of falling. If the idle take to drinking to relieve the tedium of existence, the overwrought take to it to make up exhausted strength. The young take to it from a love of excitement, and the aged and debilitated take to it to get new tone to their system. Men of a coarse nature take to it because they are incapable of higher pleasures, and men of fine sensibility tako to it because it is a source of inspiration to the intellect. Men of social tendencies take to it because it helps good fellowship; and the saddest thing is that women take to it in private, because of a peculiarly sensitive frame and inequalities of feeling. It is a vice, then, which must be said to be of a peculiarly fascinating, dangerous nature. And let no one think that he is out of danger. Many of those who have fallen wero not like falling at first. They did not take drink at all for a time, and their friends had hope in them that they would prove temperate men. And when (with other social surroundings in some cases) they began to make any use of it, they seemed to be taking it in a perfectly innocent or needful way, until the liking W!l,S formed, and they could not do without a certain and an increasing amount of drink. Now, let it be observed on what ground the apostle condemns drunkenness, It is in the line of his thought that we are to exercise wisdom as to our manner of walk. Wherein, I ~ says, is ri-Ot. Drunkenness is a madness. There is a form of it to which this description is specially applicable, that which is known as delirium tremens. But even in its ordinary working it has a close resemblance to madness. It takes away from men the guiding power of reason, their self-possession, their self-restraint, and lclltls them to make such exhibitions of themselves as in their calm moments they would be ashamed of. "Riot," which is the word employed in the Revised translation, is defined by Johnson to be "wild and loose festivity." " When his headstrong riot bath no curb, When rage and hot blood are his counsellors, When means and lavish mnnners meet together." (1) The word "riot" points to the prodigal manner of the drur,kard. The drunkanl is prodigal of his means. " So senseless of expense That he will know neither how to maintnin it Nor ceese hie flow of riot." He spends on eelf-indulcrcnce what if saved, would not only increaso tho comfort of his home, but would do mu~h good be;ides. 'l'he drunkar~ is prodigal of hi~ time, and thus violates the previous precept. 'l'he golden opportumty, which ho might employ for informing his mind or instructing his chi\drcn, he ~astes in tho public-h?use. '~'ho drunkard is prodigal of the stuff of which Im frame is made. He wastes his 1ihys1cal THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. [en. v. 1-3S.

l'0wer:,., rnkC'S :rn11y his cleame&- of hcsd, his ste:uiiness of hand, and his general vigour, iu,~u,'t's ,ii,-:ease a?d premature death (:igain violnting the previous precept iu throwing away years that. m the pat.hs oC temperance wouldhavo been his). The drunkard is pl"l.s:iflll ,,f his trorUi to his ft1lo111S, as the temperate mnn is preservative in this respect. \\-hen the lndi111;1 gen~ral row disaster waiting on his country's arms, because, nlns ! in nn emergency his regiments were found besotted with drink, "Call out Havelock's &'lints!" he ex:claimed; "they are nc'7er drunk, and Hnvelock is always ready." The drunkard is prodigal of his better feeUngs. He deadens his home feelincrs. He does not value the society of his wife and children; he does not study their happiness; nay, he can see them want in order that he may be gratified. He deadens his spiritual sensi- bilities. And to liis wife the most dreadful thought may be, not that she is set aside or the children neglected, but that for his idol be is casting off his God. • (2) The word "riot" points to the noisy manner of the drunkard. Men under excitement-are naturally demonstrative, and the drunkard is peculiarly noisy (and in that senseless) in his demonstrations. There is the noise of drunlcen laughter. "As the crackling of thorns under a pot, so [empty and shortlived] is the laughter of the fool." .There is the noise of drunken songs. There is the song ( of its own kind) which goes along with the drink- ing of wine (Isa. x:x:i,. 8). In the convivial song men tell each other vociferously of, their freedom from care, of their good-hearted.c.ess (though there may be the spectres of poverty, of broken hearts, in their homes); or they may go to the lower depth of the indelicate and the profane. But how all such hilarity is out of place! ."I will turn," it is said in the Prophet Amos, "your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation." And there is the echo of this in James: "Be afflicted and mourn and weep, let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to heaviness." 'l'here is tlie nvise of dnrnl;;;n brawls. There is often, under the excitement of strong drink, a combativeness in words and a combativeness in acts. "Who bath contentions? who bath babbling? who hath wounds without cause? They that tarry long at the wine." It cannot be said that the apostle gives a decision in favour of total abstinence. He nowhere counsels total abstinence as a duty in itself or in relation to his times. At the 69.Ine time, he gives no decision ad.verse to total abstinence. And we know that else- where he lays down a principle of expediency which, under certain conditions, makes total abstinence a Christian dr.ty. Many good people think that these conditions exist in onr country at the present time. They feel that the evil of intemperance has risen t-0 sach a height as to be 11. national vice. (threatening our very position as a nation). and they wish to stand as clear of it as they can. They feel· that there are endangered persons in their home, or circle of their acquaintances, or Christian congregation with which they are connected; and they wish to guard them ns well as they can. They feel that they are in danger themselves, and they wish to be on their guard. And· those who for such reasons as these can sacrifice their gratification are dcserv.ing of all honour. Let ns see that (in the discouragement of drinking) our influence is duly on the side of temperance, that we are doing nothing to hinder others in their struggle (often painful) towards virtne and happiness. 2. Pers'IJ,(l,Sive to true ezcitement. " But be filled with the Spirit." The apostle does not ,forbid all exciteine~t,;. rather for the excitement which he ner<alives as false would he S11bstitute o. true excitement. (1) We. can be drunken with wi~e; we are to be filled (never can be d:unken) w~tl1 the Spirit. entries.title: EPH 5:22–23
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Relative duties. I. DUTY OF WIVES. "Wives, be in subjection unto your own husbands." 1. Gr011,nd of subjection. (1) The husband represents Ohrist to the W1.je. "As unto the Lord." The original of the position of husband is to be found in Christ. It is )n this character tha~ he appears in the forty-fifth psalm, i11 the Song of Songs, and tn other parts of Scripture. He is the absolute impersonation of the idea (the Hnsband by pre-eminence); and what we find in the human family on earrh is only a faint copy of the original. It is true, too, that the husband is not in ~e family in his own name. He deri,es his authority from Christ. He is there as represen.:i!lg Christ. He is there as thoagh Christ were there. What, then, the wifd is in .inty bound to render to her hasband., she is not to render to him simply, but to him as representing ChrisL (2) It has its foundation in flature. The natural, relati<mship . .. For the husband is the head of the wife." It is not implied in this that the husband is superior to the wife in all qualities, but only that be is her superior in those qualities which fit him for being head. Especially his superior strength and self-reliance mark him out for taking the leading part. He is husband, or band of the house-what keeps it undivided and keeps it up. He has to come between his wife and the world, to shield her from its glare ~nd its harm. While she is a keeper at home, he has to go out and work for her, that he may provide for her maintenance and comfort, It is therefore fitting that she should lean upon him and be guided by him. The Ohristian unalogy. "As Christ also is the Head of the Church." The headship is a great doctrine for the Church, already taught in this Epistle. As the wife in her weakness and distrustfulness of self leans upon her husband, so the Church in her weakness and felt insufficiency is to lean upon Christ. Worldly powers may be hostile, but she can never be deprived of the protection of her Head. Protected by him, she must be diet at.ed to by none, but must take the law, pure and simple, from his lips. In the analogy t!,ere is an important difference. "Being himself the Saviour of the body." It must very seldom have happened that one bas made a wife of her whom he has rescued from a watery grave or other form of death. But it is true of Christ that he h'ls made a epow,e of her whom he Juu deliveredfr,pn, everlasting destruction. He is Saviour of the body, u. the Church. That makes his headship peculiar (without analogy in the earthly type}, and gives him a peculiar hold on the obedience of the Church. 2. .Manner artd extent of 3Vhjecticn,. (1) Manner. "But" (that is, though Christ is r:..c,re than Protector, is also Saviour of the Chnrch) "as the Church is ~ubjcct to Christ, w, let the ""fres also be to their hu.sbanda." The ideal set before her is that, as thll Church deports herself toward Christ, so she is to deport herself toward her husband. It has this advantage (high as it iB) that, by entering into the spirit of her relationship to Ler husband, sLe i;hould be greatly assisted in subjecting herself (as her husband un<ler home disadvantage must also subject himHclf) to Christ. (2) Extent. "In everything." The necessary limitation here is-in everything that he, acting in the Name of Christ, Las a right to expect of her. If he were laying anything sinful or purely arbitrary and tyrannical upon her, she would be justified in resisting him (appealing from him ClI, V, 1-33.) '!'HE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. 241

lo Christ). But i~ it is within his right, and what he judges important, then (even when she cannot give her approval) she should be willing to fall in with his arrangement. II. DUTY OF HUSBANDS. "Husbands, love your wives." As the husband excels in the governing qualities, so she excels in the lovable qualities. "For softness she, and sweet attraotive grace." If it can be said that he has more power, it can be said that (by her pure and modest feelin~, her deep tenderness and devotion) she has more influence. 1. Manner. Christian analogy. "Even as Christ also loved the Church." We are to think of the love of Ch.rist here only under the special aspect in which the apostle presents it, viz. his conjugal, love, or love of espousals. (1) His devotion to his spouse. "And gave himself up for it" ( or "her," as in the original). "Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept sheep." Years of servitude he had to give for Raebel; yet they seemed to him but a few days, for the love he bore to her. It was a hard price he had to pay for her; but we read here of what was infinitely harder, of One who bad to give himself for his spouse. He had to forget himself in humiliation and sorrow and death for her, and yet, hard as that was beyond all conception, it appeared as though it was nothing, for the love he bore to her. (2) Purpose of his devotion. (a) Immediate purpose (process of sanctification). "That he might sanctify it, having cleansed it by the washing of water with the Word." The language is taken from the ordinance of baptism. The fact is pointed to that the Church needs cleansing. Baptism goes upon the supposition that we are all by nature defiled with sin. It ~ys this, "We are all as an unclean thing." The Church was in this state of impurity when the Son chose her for his bride. 'l'o this the words apply-He loved her foul that he mi~ht make her fair. Washed certainly she must be (as the bride used to be before marriage), to be tit for associating with the highest purity. The blessed fact is also pointed to that; there is what hcu deansing power. "By the washing of water," it is said here. It is the water used in baptism that we are to think of, and that water in what it signifies, viz. the purifying influences of the Spirit. As water washes defilement from vessels, from the person, so the Spirit washes moral defil~ment from our hearts. '!'his washing of water must be accompanied with the Word. For the Spirit cannot purify alone, but only through what the Word reveals, especially that blood of Christ which is said to cleanse from all sin. (b) Remote purpose (result of sanctification). "'fhat he might present the Church to himself a. glorious Church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but tha.t it should be holy and without blemish." By this we a.re to understand that Chl·ist is to have in the Church a bride of incomparable beauty. When the cleansi 1g process has been completed, the Church will be glorious ("all-glorious" is the la.nguagt1 oft-he forty-fifth psalm, and the effect of the description here), more glorious than auy material substance can b~, more glorious than the sun in the heavens. There will not be spot or trace left of her former defilement. 'l'here will not be wrinkle or sign appearing of coming age (such as comes to an ordinary bride). To ma.ke it moro emphatic, it is added that there will not be any such thing, nothing whatever to mar her beauty. But still the ci.escription proceeds; she will be holy. Her beauty (as it will not be imperfect or fading) will not be outward, but will be the beauty of holiness. And she will be without blemish, so trnnscendently beautified that to ad,l to her beauty would be (in things that are less) "To gild refined gold, to point the lily, To throw a. perfume on the violet." At present the Son's bride has many a spot, many a. wrinkle (her cleansing, must still go on, her beauty needs bringing ont), but the time is coming (in the Divine purposl! which cannot fail, in the conception of Christ which must bo realized) wlien sue will be a. fit bride for him. And then it is that, as is said here, he is to present her to himself. He is to leave it to no other (say, angelic attendants) to present her, but he is to take it into his own hand (notwith~tanding the doublo character in which it requires him to act). And this dono (the marriage an nccomplished fact), then, ns is said in the Prophet Zophaniah, he will re_joice over her with joy. He will rest in his love; lio will joy over her with singing. Tliis, then, is the ideal which is put before kusbamls, It J.WllESIANS, B THE EPISTLE 'l'O 'l'HE EPHESIANS. [CH, V. 1-33,

is wbat we could not have dared to ha"o put before us of ourselves. It would hnve H'm11cd profanity to have conjoined things so far apart. llut thus it has been dictated for us by the Spirit of inspiration: "Husb.'\uds, love your wives, even as Christ also kn,i t'.le Church." The husband is to pvsscss, to cherish, and to manifest devoted love t-,wa:--i his mfr·. .And if his is the position of authoritv yet is he (an all-requirincr l,,w being nls,, his) to forget himself in services rendered t~ her. And specially is h; t,n1ght fn.,m the high model that he is not to pamper his wife (or to be careful how to 1•!case his mfe, as Paul puts the case of the married), bnt he is to recrard her as criven i.im for a higher end, :md to seek that she mny possess all spiritual bea;ty. 2. Gr~und. "Even so ought husbands also to love their own wives as their own bodies." The ,;round of the duty is that the wife is one fle_sh with the husband. 'fhere are two points (not immedintcly connected, but brought up :i.fterward) which go to prove this. The first is that woman derived her being from man. Eve was taken out of Adam, and the language was used regarding her by Adam : " This is now bone of my bone, and flesh of my flesh." The second point is that, in the marriage union, man and woman a.re said to become one flesh. "For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife; and the twain shall become one flesh." The wife, then, being one flesh with the husband, there comes into operation (in support of the duty of tl1e husband) the principle of self-preservation. '! He that loveth his own wife loveth himself: for no man ever hated his own flesh ; but nourisheth and cherisheth it." The Christian analogy. "Even as Christ also the Church." Christ bestows a fostering care on the Church; and this is not ·only lovely, but it·is thorO'll,ghly natural. Far: (1) The Church i.s one fle,sh with Christ by derivation. "Because. we are members of his body." Her spiritual being is from Christ as much as Eve's physical being was from A.dam. (2) The Church becomes one fle,sh with Christ in the marriage union. Here the won.ls of the marriage ceremony are quoted with the added comment, "This r::.:yEtery i.s great: but I speak in regard of Christ and of the Church." 'l'he language, '"'one flesh," has a strangeness in its application to an ordinary marriage union, ·but the apostle i.s careful to let us know that he uses it in reference to the mystical, union of Christ and the <Jhurch (by no distortion, for that is the archetype, or original pattern of all marriage, and, we must believe, was in the Divine mind when the words were uttered in Paradise). Shall we think of the Son leaving his Father's house and cleav- ing to his bride in human flesh? But we must not (as some have done) pry too· curiously into it; for it is a mystery, and we must simply lay hold upon the great fact that it points to the union between Christ and the Church being so intimate that he loves her as he loves hi.J.oself. ' III. REcAPITUl,ATION (order of duties inverted). Duty· of husband. "Nevertheless' [i.e. not to press the mystical bearings of the subject] do ye also severally love each, one his own wife even as himself." It is again an idea.I of very difficult attainment. What a fostering-ea.re is conjoined with his authority! And this to be Christ-like (in that fosterin" care which be is now bestowing upon his Church~ and which he will one day bring to~ mature rerult)? Duty of wife. "And let the wife see that she fear her· husband." He may personally be deficient (in comparison with her) in those qualities v.-i::ich fit hlm!for being bead, but nevertheless she i1 to show deference to him in re-"Jll'-Ct c,f the position which he holds. In the precept here it is- rupposed that he has C~--u;tian worth (which is what the representative of Christ should have, what is the w:ormnent of his position). And even when a Christian wife ca.1:IDot IO?k to Christian \,e;rth in her husband, yet must she preserve reverence toward him, while at the samo ~.lILe: seeking to win him over to Christ. Two less(m8 may be learned here. 1. Mar- riatJe i, a Christian ardinance. It is not, indeed, to be raised (as it is by the Roman Catholics) to the rank of a Christian sacrament; bnt neither is it to be reduced to. a mere civil arrangement.. It is here associated with the sublimest Christian thought.. 'fbis, and the presence of Christ at the marriage in Cana. of Galilee, give it a thoroughly • Christian cb.i.ra.cter and throw a Christian ha.lo around it of the brightest nature, ~- It ii 410t to be lightly enwred into, but in a Christian manner. Man and woman ✓ ,j.lust LeloDg to the Lord before they belong to ea.eh other, and are to enter into the ( m..rrie:d state that they may help each other to be more entirely the Lord's. A Christian ';,; not at liberty to marry one who is not a Christian (even in the hope of making him IJC her a Christian). A Christian even among Christians is to seek from tho Lord.

"And now, before the word we spcok That knits the bond mon must not break, Wo fa.in would know tby mind. Lorcl, be the sweet conviction given To both thot thou thyself in hca.ven The hallowed bond host twined." It is in that spirit that it ought to be contemplatecl. Without this there can be no ~ecurity for happiness or for Christ being honoured in connection with the union formed.-R. F.

entries.content:

"But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as bccometh saints; neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which arc not convenient : but rather giving of thanks. For this ye know, that no whoremonger, nor unclean person, nor covetous man, who is an idolater, bath any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Let no man deceive you with vain words: for because of these things com,1th the wrath of· God upon the children of disobedience. Be not ye therefore partakers with them." The subject which we gather from these words is that covetousness is amongst the worst of human crimes. I. IT IS HERE CLASSED WITH CRIMES OF THE WORST OHARACTEB. There are three sins amongst which covetousness is placed in the text: unbridled licentiousness, "fornication," and "whoremongery "-revolting_ indecency; "filthiness," that which is so un<;haste and impure as to awaken universal disgust; and immoral speech-speech that is frivolous, untruthful, obscene, profane. These are sins confessedly of enormous magnitude. All true souls recoil from ·them, all pure minds renounce them as a degradation of the race and an offence to Almighty God. But mark, amongst these covetousness is placed. It is ranked with them as related to them in moral vileness. More than this, it is singled out as worse than these-" a covetous man, who is an idolater." ·what is idolatry? Holding anything nearer to the heart th1m God. 'l'he " covetous man " loves money more than anything else, and money is his god. We here iu England are very zealous for the conversion of heathen idolaters. We create and sustain costly organizations, but thero is no idolatry morti real, more powerful, morn damning, than the idolatry that prevails throughout Engl:i.nd. What god in heathendom is more earnestly and constf)ntly served than Mammon is served in this island? Before tµe introduction of Christianity into this country there were many i<lols here. " In Scotland stood the temple of Mars; in Cornwall, the temple of Mercury; in Bangor, the temple of Minerva; at Maldon, the teD?ple _of Victoria; in Bath, the temple of Apollo; at Leicester, the temple of Janus; at York, where St. Peter's now stands, the temple of Bcllona; in London, on the site of St. Paul's Cathedral, the temple of Diana; and at W cstmillster, where the Abbey rears its venerable pile, a temple of Apollo." But Mammon now has a temple everywhere, a temple on every hill and in every valley, in every church and house. Mammon has said to England, "Thou shalt have none other gods beside me," and England heartily responds, "Amen." I!. lT IS IlEBE CLASSED WITII TIIE WORST OF CRWES, .AS EXCLUDING FROM THE KINGDOM OF Goo. "For this ye know, that no whoremonger, nor unclean person, nor covetous man, who is an idolater, bath any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ aml of God." From this passage may be inferred: 1. '!'bat heaven is a kingdom. Theru is rule and order there. 2. That heaven is a Divine kingdom. "Kingdom of Christ and of God." Christ reigns there. He is in tho midst of the throne; his Spirit animates all; his Spirit fills all with adoring wonder and worship. Christ reigns as God there. BcunAdq.. -roii Xp1<T-roii ,cal e.oii. Christ and God. The heavens are a king- dom managed, not by Divine partncrship,-it is governed by God in Christ. 3. That heaven excludes evil_ characters of all descriptions. How clearly and forcibly this is declared in Scripture 1-" The works of tho flesh are manifest, which are thoso; Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness . . . of the which I tell you beforo, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit tho king- dom of God" (Gal. v. 19-21). "Without are dogs, and sorcerers, an<l. whoremongers, and murderers, 1md idolaters, nnd whosoever loveth and maketh a lie." \Vith the cxcludetl will ba tho covetous man. Y<1s, though he has been a member or a Christian THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. [cu. v. 1-33.

Churc-h, though cultured in intellect, chaste in feeling, and refined in manners, though an elCXJ_uent prl':icher of the go~pel of benevolence, he will find no admission into that world. He ~·ill be "without." With whom? Will he have a pince set apart for himself? No, with the common damned. JIJ. lT IS HERE CLASSED WITH THE WORST OF CRIMES REPUGNANT TO THE DIVINE '?sATTTRE. "For because of these things cometh the wrath of God." Paul so.ys, in his Jetter to the Romans, that " the wrath of God is revealed from heaven aaainst all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men." His deep, settled, immutable n;taaonism to wrong of all kinds is clearly revealed in the gospel of Jesus Christ, But~ there any sin more repugnant to the Divine nature than covetousness, which is idolatry ? What sin has the Almighty denounced with greater frequency and force than that of idolatry? But why should covetousness be so abhorrent to the Almighty? 1. Becaw 6 it involves a mal-approprv1tion of the blessi11gs of Providence. God's will is that whatever a man, either by good fortune or by industry, obtains of this world's goods, should be ~ded for the advancement of truth and the general promotion of human happiness. But the covetous man appropriates all to pamper his own appetites, !!ratify his ov.n vanity, and promote his own sel.lish and ambitious ends. 2. Because it i;,volves a,1 vtw ~-.·an of his men spiritual nature. The powers of the soul are not given to amass material wealth, nor the affections to love it. On the contrary, they were gi,en to gather elements of the highest knowledge, and to love and serve the Infinite supremely in all The soul was made to have God, not money, as the dominant subject of thought and the dominant object of love. 3. Bemuse it inool'l1eS the pr011l-0tion of mi,f,ery in the unir,erse.. Nothing is more repugnant to the heart of the lovina God than miaery. The cause of universal happiness is his, but the covetous man is ;ecessa.rily a promoter of misery in his own soul, misery in his circle, misery through the creation. God's order is that no man should live unto himself, that all should labour for the common weal ; in this way only the good •of the universe can be served, its blessedness advanced, and its order maintained. Every man who sets himself up as his own end in labour and life opposes all the arrangements of God. He does what he can to create discords in its harmonies, miasma in its atmosphere, poison in its streams. No wonder, then, that the "wrath of God'' is against " the covetous man."-D. T.
