entries.content:
-l'hristian. life. "For ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord: walk as children of light: (for the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and troth;) proving what is BCCeptable unto the Lord." These verses present to us the Christian life in its transformation, obligation, and demonm-atwn.. L ToASSFOBXATIO!i. A true Christian is one who has been changed from darkness into light. The figurative language implies: 1. A change from immorality to lwliness. "Darkness" is the emblem of depravity. "They that be drunken are drunken in the night." The ghastly legions of hell win their most terrible victories in the gloom and silence of night. The "light" is a symbol of purity. 2. A change from ignorance to knowledge. Darkness clouds our vision, and hides from us the world in which we live. Man in an unregenerated state is in the moral world as a man in midnight. "Light" is a symbol of intelligence. 3. A_ chan~e fyom sadne88 "! jo'!/. Darkness is dep:e~sin~. Even the irrational creatures feel its deJectmg power. Sm 1B sadness ; true religion 1s joy. We are told that there is "no night in heaven." •It means that there is no immorality, no ignorance, no sorrow there. How great the change that has taken place in a true Christian man I II. OBLIGATION. Two duties are here indicated. 1. Walking in light. "Walk as children of light." Don't go back into darkness. ~ay, don't remain in the twilight of Christian experience, but step farther and farther mto the day. Leave the valleys, scale the hills, and come more directly under the broad beams of day. To walk in the light is to walk intelligently, safely, and joyously. 2. Pleasing God. The ninth verso being parenthetical, the last clause of the eighth verse should be read with the tenth, "Walk as childreo of light, proving what is BCCeptable [well-pleasing] un~ the Lord." "Bt: not conformt<l to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewmg of your mind, that ye may prove what i.s that good, and acceptable, and perfect will of God "

(Rom. xii. 2), The expression "well-pleasing" to God throws a light upwards on God and downwards on man. (1) It reveals God. It indicates (a) his moral susceptibility. He is not indifferent to the moral conduct of his creatures. It indicates (b) his forgiving mercy. Man, though a sinner, can, through his infinite mercy, render himself acceptable to him. (2) ltj reveals man. (a) It indicates the highest end of his being. What higher object can a creature have than to please the Crea.tor? (b) It indicates the highest blessedness of his being. The smile of the Crea.tor is the heaven of the creature. III. DEMONSTRATION. The Christian man develops in his life certain glorions things. "The fruit of the Spirit [light) is in all goodness and righteousness and truth." He demonstrates in his life: 1. Divine beneficence. "In all goodness." He is full of social love, tender, compassionate, self-sacrificing. 2. Divine righteousness. He is a man of inflexible honesty, unswerving rectitude. In him the "righteousness of the Law is fulfilled." 3. Divine reality. His thoughts, sympathies, actions, are in harmony with the eternal realities of being. He is neither a visionary nor a hypocrite. His thoughts are true, his life is sincere. CoNOLUSION. What an infinite boon is the gospel to mankind I How glorious the transformation it effects I how righteous the obligation it imposes I how great the power it confers I-a power to demonstrate in our life the good, the right, and the true.-D. T.

entries.title: EPH 5:11–14
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-(1) Two 1oorlds of one race. "And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them. For it is a shame even to speak of those things which are done of them in secret. But all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light: for whatsoever doth make manifest is light. Whereforu he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light." The text may be regarded as a portraiture of two distinct worlds of men on this earth-the world of the wicked and the world of the Christly. Here we have- I. THE WORLD OF WICKED MEN. The characteristics of these men are here indicated. 1. '.l'hey are worthless. Their works are" the unfruitful works of darkness." Uugo,lly men live in moral darkness. The sun, which alone reveals things as they are in tho spiritual world, shines not in their heavens. All the light they he.ve are the electric flashes of an impure atmosphere. They work in the dark, and their works are " unfruitful." That is "unfruitful" of good. The soil that is sterile as regards it~ capability of producing fruit is often fertile in its capacity to produce noxious weeds and poisonous herbs; so the ungodly soul-it is unfruitful in goodness, but prolific iu crime. 2. They are clandestine. " Which are done of them in secret." Thot' '.ll there may be an allusion here to the abominable mysteries which were celebrated in Greece under the screen of night and secrecy, it describes the general character of a sinful life. All is secret. Sin is necessarily hypocritical ; it speaks in a. false voice ; it works under masks. The more corrupt the human soul the more sneakish anil clandestine. '!'he good alone can afford to be bland and open. 3. They are shamifal. "For it is a shame even to speak of those things." Heathenism has ever abounded and still abounds with nameless iniquities (Rom. i. 24-32). But sin in all its form~ is a shameful thing. It is essentially disgraceful, disreputable, and ignominious. A man has only to think calmly of it in the light of conscience and God, in order to brin_g burning blushes to his cheek. Sin is a shame. 4. They are sleepy. " Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest." A sinful soul is sleepy in a moral sense. It is unconscious of its moral surroundings-it is filled with illusory dreams; it must one day be aroused to a sense of reality. Unlike natural sleep, moral sleep does not refresh and invigorate, but enervates and destroys. 5, They are mortal. "Arise from the dead." Everywhere the Bible represents sin as a state of death. The sinful soul is like a corpse. It is odious and the victim of external forces. Such is the world of wicked men around us. It is worthless, clandestine, shameful, sleepy, mortal. II. THE WORLD OF CHRISTLY MEN. These are represented by the Christians at Ephesus, the men to whom the apostle is writing. This world has a work to do with the other-the dark world of wickedness around them. And it is here indicated. What is it? 1. Separation. "Have no fellowship." It does not mean, of course, that Christians are to have no intercourse or dealings with the ungodly. This conhl not be, and ought not to be if it could. It means that they are to have no spiritual 24G THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. [ea. v. 1-33.

identification with them-no thoughts, purposes, or feelin<rs alike. That, like Christ, they sre to he "S<'f':'rate from sinners." Morally detached"as tho lnmp from the dark- ness. "I have wntten unto you not to kPep company, if any man that is called a bn--ther be a fornicat~,r, or covet.ous, or an idolater, or a railer or a drunkard or o.n ert~rtioner: with such a one no not to eat" (1 Cor. v. 11). :, Wherefore co~e out from among them," etc. (2 Cor. vi. 14-18). 2. Reprehension. cc But rather reprove them." Rel;'ro•~ them by lip. In the n~e of purity and truth expose and denounce their =ckedness. Repro,e them by life. Let the life stand in such a 1rrond contrast to all that is sinful that it may be a standing rebuke. 3. fllumtnaticm. •• All things ~at are ~proved are made manifest by the ligh~" Hold forth the light of the gospel m the m1dst of a "crooked and perverse generation." 4. Resuscitation. "Awake t~on_ that sleepest, and arise from the dead." Thunder in the ear of the sleeper; :speak life mto the heart of the dead. There is living light for all in Christ. •" Christ shall give thee light." "He is the Light of the world." The idea of this verse seems to be that, if Christians will use all their efforts to convert men; they may expect Christ to shine upon them and bless them. The cc light" that comes, from him is a soulqutckening light. "The hour is coming, and now is, when .the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God: and they tha.t hear sha.11 live" (John v. 25). Elijah raised· the deed; so did the apostles. We, a.lso, in God's great Name, can raise the deaddead souls. The ~nrrection of a soul is a far grander work than the resurrection of a body. Let us sound the blast of the gospel trumpet over moral cemeteries~ and the graves will open and dead souls come forth to life.-D. T.

entries.title: EPH 5:15–21
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
---(2) Two UXJT"lds of one roee. " See then that ye wall;: circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Wherefore be ye not unwise, but under.standing what the will of the Lord is. Alld be not drunk 'With wine, 'W"herein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit ; speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, ~aing and making melody in your heart to the Lord; gi:ring thanks ahrays for all things unto God and the Father iu the Name of our Lord Jesus Christ; 61lbmitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God.' All thffie ,erses must be brought in under the same headiug as the verses discussed in our preceding article, viz.-Two worlds of one race. These verses continue to indi- cate the duties pertaining to the world of Christian men. The duties' which we previously discussed were separation, reprehension, illumination, and resuscitation; the duties which we have now to notice are Ohri8tian =istency, holy euitement, and social, worship. • I. CHRISTIAN CONSISTENCY, "See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise." The vereee teach that walking strictly in harmony·with the Christian creed implies: 1. Wisdom. "Not as fools, but as wise." A conduct inconsistent with tho Christian creed we profess is exceedingly foolish. (1) It damages our own moral nature. (2) It misrepresents the gospel of Christ. (3) It insults the omniscience of God. Hypocrisy is in every way unwise. 2. • Diligence. "Redeeming the_ ~1me "- .. Buying up opportnnities.'' How is time t.o be redeemed? . Not by_ regammg any portion of the past. The past is irrecoverably gone. Not by 1noperat1ve regrets conoerning the wrong of the put. Not by mere sentimental desires that the future may be better. How then? (1) By deducing the true m~ral lessons of the past. (2) :1}Y a <leep and devout determination to avoid all the evils of the past. (3) By turmng el"ery circumstance of our life to a right spiritual account. " Because the clays arc eTil," mys PanL The times in which Paul wrote were corrupt; onr times are corrupt. There are several things that make our times evil. (1) A ruling secula1ism. How mercenary is olll" age! (2) Religious formali~: T~e. forms o! rel!!?o~ abound eve_rywhere; the real spirit is rare. The "l~te~ 1s kil!m~ the 'spmt. (3). Sce~tt~al rationalism. The world'11 philosophy, as 1t 1s called, ts for the most part ant1-t~e1st1c, anti-superuatural, anti-Christian. These elements fill the social atmosph~re with 'the moral iungi that make our "days" evil. Because our days are charged with so many evils we should be diligent • we should seize every opportunity to crush the wrong and to promote the right. 3. 'Inqufry. "Understanding what the will of the_ Lord is." G~d has a will concerning us, o:nd it is our duty to endeavour to undcrstanrl it, and f-or this purpose we must inquire into it. ' cu. v. 1- :l3.J THE EPIS'rLE TO THE EPHESIANS.

II. HoLY EXCITEMENT. "Be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess· but be fillc,l with the Spirit." 'l'his verso su!!gests several thoughts. 1. Man hr1s ;n instinctive craving for excitement. 'l.'he words evidently imply this. Paul assumes that his readers must have excitement, in telling them in what they shou~d and in what they should not find it. Excitement ·is a necessity of our nature. 'l'he soul has a deep hunger for it. (1) Observation shows this. Look at society, either as it appears on the pnge of history or as it surrounds you now in all the activities of life, and you will find thnt the love of excitement explains much of all its restlessness, amusements, an,! toils. (2) Consciousness shows this. All are conscious of this impulse. Monotony and stagnation become intolerable. We crave a quicker pulse, a warmer and a fuller passion ... Yes, man has a native hunger for excitement. Hence the popularity of sensa- tional theatres, sports, books, scenes, music, sermons. 2. Man has recourse to improper expedients for excitement. "Be not drunk with wine." "Wine stimulates excitement. It quickens,tbe pulse, it heats the blood, it fires the passions. Hence men like it. 'l.'hey. use it,, uot for the sake of intoxication, but excitement. Wine-drinking is only one of many improper expedients fol" excitement. Drunkenness is here a type of whatever improperly stimulates the senses and enkindles the lusts. (1) There' is sensualism. How many seek excitement in an inordinate gratification of mere animal propensities! (2) There is gambling. What thousands resort to the race-course, the exchange, the billiard-table,·for. excitement! (3) There is immoral literature. Luscious tales, filthy narratives, and sensational romances ;-these are eagerly sought because they make the imagination glow with impure fires. • III. SoCUL WORSHIP. "Speaking to yourselves," etc. These verses (from the nineteenth to the twenty-first) show what is meant by being "filled with the Spirit." 1. High spiritual intercourse with man. "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual·songs." • Speaking to men the highest things in the highest forms of language-poetry. High feeling always runs into poetry. 2. .Devout fellowship with Christ. "Singing nnd making melody in your heart to the Lord." 'fhe soul pouring out its devotions in sweet melodies in the Divine ear. 3. Thankful recognition of Divine favours. "Giving thanks always for all''things unto God." 4. Godly devotion to the common weal. "Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God." All this is implied in being "filled with the Spirit." And is there not sufficient excitement here? To be filled with the Spirit is to be filled with the Spirit's ideas; and what exciting idens are his I With the Spirit's purposes; and what inspiring purposes are his I With the Spirit's love; and what an immensity of stirring impulses is in that lovel-D. T.

entries.title: EPH 5:22–33
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Ideal marriage. "Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord. For the husband is the hcnd of the wifo, even ns Christ is the Ilead of the Church: and he is the Saviour of the body. Therefore ns the Church ie subject unto Christ, so lot the wives be to their own husbands iu everything. Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the Church, and gnve himself for it; that ho might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by tho Word, that ho might present it to himself a glorious Church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy nnd without blemish. 80 ought men to love their wive8 as their own bodies. Ho that loveth his wifo loveth himself. l<'or no man ever yet hated his own flesh ; but nourisheth and cherishcth it, even ns the Lord the Church: for we are members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones. For this causo shall a man leave his father nnrl mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two Ehall be one flesh. 'l.'his is n great mystery: but I speak concerning C!1rist anti the Church. Nevertheless let every one of you in particular so love his wife even as himself; and the wife sec that she reverence her husband." 'l.'he subject of thi~ passage is Ideal matrimony; or, God's idea of the marriage state. As we look into it, our convictions will deepen that the Divine idea is but very partially, if at all, developed in the matrimonial alliances of modern society. What is marriage? It comes not within the limits of our purpose or space to enter into n full discussion of the grand subject of human marriage. Our readers will find a very learned and exhaustive treatment of this question in Dr. William Smith's 'Dictionary of the Iliblc.' Our remarks mus~ be confinc<l entirely to those pha~c~ of the subject which the passage under review 0~ - 24-8 THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. [ott. v. 1--33. - - - - --- ----------------------------- gests. On sll hands it is admitted that marria.,-that is, the union of one man to one woman-is a Divine ordination. Some philosophers see the principle of matrimony running through all nature, not only in the sexual distinction of all animnls, but in the sexual form of all kinds of vegt-table life. But the Bible is our authority. The l1inne institution "f marriage is clearlv tl\ught, both in the Old and the New Testaments. In the opening ~<>es of the~ Divine volume we read these words, "And the Lord God :;;;;id, It is not good that the man should be alone; I "ill make him an help meet for him." _tmd in the New Testament we have these words from the lips of the Son of God himself, "Have ye not read, th.'lt he which made them at the beginning made them male and female, and said., For this cause shall a man leAve father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh? wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder" (Matt. x.ix. 4-6). What does the text teach concerning marriage? It teaches- I. That marriage implies MORAL ROYALTY ON THE PART OF THE HUSBAND. Wives are here commanded to submit themselves unto their husbands "as unto the Lord." The husband is here called the" head, of the wife, even as Christ is the Head of the Church," and the apostle concludes the paragraph by saying, "Let the wife see that she reverence her husband." The idea of supremacy, therefore, on the part of the husband is manifest throughout the passage. But what is the rule to be? Not the rule of superior muscular force or intellectual power. Such a rule would be despotism and nothing less. Tne apostle teaches here that the husband's rulership should be similar t.o that rulership that Christ holds over the Church. 1. The husband is to rule by moral influence. How does Christ rule the Church? Not by force, but by love; by the royalty of his character, the sublimity of his thoughts, the Divine grandeur of his &ims. The Church bows lovingly to his authority, because of the supremacy of his excellence. Thus the husband is t.o rule the wife, for " the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the Head of the Church." It is only as the wife sees in her husband true moral grandeur that she can bow loyally to his sceptre and feel a loving reverence in her heart. 2. The husband is to rule for beneficent ends. (1) The rule is to be restorative. " He is the Saviour of the body." This refers to Christ. The Church is his body; he is to it what the soul is to the body-the ever-present, animating, controlling spirit. So the grand object of the husband should be to save his wife-save her from all that is mean and coarse, from all that degrades the character or pains the soul. Her true elevation, and not the gratification of her vanity, or pride, or lower appetites, should be his master aim. (2) This rule is to be universal. "In everything." It is to extend through the whole of domestic life. Indeed, a true moral rule over the heart will extend to "everything" in the woman's life. (3) The rule is to be self-sacrificing in spfrit. "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ loved the Church, and gave himself for it." The husband's love should be that of the highest chivalry-a love that shrinks at no sacrifice in order to bless and ennoble the partner of his choice. It must be of the same kind as that which prompted Christ t.o give himself for the salvation of the world. Ay, and he must have the same grand object, too-viz. the perfect cleansing of hie bride from all that is morally corrupt. Christ loved the Church, and gave himself for it; what for? "Th.at he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washin~ of waw by the Word, that he might present it~ himself a glorious Ch~ch, not he.yin~ spot, or wrinkle, or any 6Uch thing; but that 1t should be holy and without bleIDJsh. h is sud that the glow-<rorm never shines after it has become a parent. Some women iuse the lu.,.re o! 2oll delicacy and refinement under the influence of men whom they call ti:ieir hU6band!i. The aim of the true husband should be to make the character of hie v.i.fe a •• gloriOUJI" character, "without spot or blemish.'' Behold and admire this l.Ji,ioe picture of a true husband! The marriage in which there is not such a husband is no tnui marriage. It is an impious mockery. When a woman in the marriage ceremony of Ch1lrcbes is called upon to obey a man smaller in intellect, narrower in sympathies, and iDferior in moral character to herself, she is called upon to do violence to her nature-to do that, in fact, which the eternal laws of mind forbid her in sincerity and truth ever to perform. Who can admire the contemptible? who can reverence the , m<:an? The man should appear as a morally royal man iu her eyes, or he is no true husband at alL IL That marriage implies HORAL LOVABLENESS ON THE PART OF THE WIFE. ., So Ci:I, V, 1-33.] 'I'Hl<: EPISTLE TO TIIE EPHESIANS. 249

ought men to love their wives as their own bodies." If the wife is to be loved, she must be lovable, for it is as impossible for the human mind to love the morally unbeautiful as it is to believe a mathemntical contradiction. There are women who are morally hideous, and from whom all manly natures must revolt with disgust. What is the truly lovable in a wife? Personal beauty? This may fascinate the eye for a short time, but it has no power to generate moral esteem. Brilliant genius or sparkling accomplishments? No; these may charm the fancy, but never evoke the true germ of manly love. What is the lovable? The text suggests two of its element~. 1. A vital sympathy with the spirit of a true husband. "So ought men to love their wives as their own bodies. He that loveth his wife loveth himself. l<'or no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the Church." 'rhe true husband we have described: he is a royal man, who rules by moral influence for beneficent ends in the spirit of self-sacrificing love; and the true wife must have such a vital sympathy with that high moral spirit of his as to make the "twain one flesh." His aims are elevated, his spirit is Christ-like, and her whole heart being in vital accord with his, they are "no more twain, but one fle.~h." God, not priests nor hireling registrars, has joined them together. 2. A love-ctntralizing power of character. There must be that fascination and bewitchment of moral spirit about her that will draw the affections of her husband from all the dearest of other objects, and centre them on herself. "For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh." He should discover in her virtues so numerous and strong as to draw his sympathies even from the nearest of his other relations and centre them on her, feeling -that he can repose in her his utmost confidence and bestow on her bis choicest love. CoNCLUSION. It is obvious that the world abounds with spurious marriages. The popular idea of marriage is a legalized union of one man to one woman. Though the union may be formed by mere sensual impulses and selfish considerations, it is still called a marriage. Though it be formed, not only without any relative fitness between the parties conjoined, but with a painful discrepancy in temper, age, health, education, it is still called a marriage. Though it be formed without any element of moral excellence as a foundation, and without mutual love for virtue-simply because no mutual virtuo exists-still it is called a marriage. The woman may be destitute of every high quality, immersed in sensuality and pride, still at the altar the man pledges to her his love; and the man may be a little soul, in every respect inferior to the woman, yet at the altar she pledges him reverence and obedience. Nothing is more baneful to a country than the corruption of the marriage institution. The law of England, alas I unites brutes and fiends together as well as saints. "For marriage is a matter of more worth Than to be dealt in by attorneyship : For what is wedlock forced, but a hell, An age of discord and continual strife? Whereas the contrary bringeth forth happinHI, And is a pattern of celestial bliss." (Shakespeare.) D.T.

-.. Imitators of God." L How IT IS POSSIBLE FOB. us TO BE IMITATORS OF Gon. It is vain to try to imitate God if all resemblance to God is beyond our reach. But this is not the case. While speculative theology is fatally successful in magnifying the distance between man and God, practical revelation is ever bringing us nearer to God. 1. We are like God by nature. God is spirit, and we are spiritual beings. As Channing taught, all spirits are of one family. God made us in his own image. It is our work to revive that image where it ha11 been obscured and to carry it up to higher resemblances. 2. We can imitate God in very small ways. Decauso be is infinite nu<I we are finite we are not to infer that all common likeness is impossible. The smallest pool may bear a perfect image of the sun. 3.. We are susceptible of indefinite growth and improvement. Because we are sadly unlike God now 1t does not follow that we may never resemble him. "It is not yet made manifest what we shall be. We know that, if he shall be manifested, we shall be like him" (1 John iii. 2). God has rlJ'lltaied. 250 THE EPISTLE TO 'l'HE EPHESIANS. [en. v. 1-33.

himself to us. We cannot imitate what we do not know. Mysteries of the Divine nature must <'Ve.r lie beyond our sight. Ne,·erthcless, something real about God we <',o know. For we b:u·e seen Christ, nnd he who sees Christ sees God (John _xiv. 9). II. I:s WHAT RESPECTS WE ARE TO BECOME IllITATORS OF Goo. \Ve cannot attain fo his almighty energy nor to his unfathomable wisdom. Yet we may imitate the me~bc,d of t.lie,,ie Didne attributes in the e:i;:ercise of corresponding human qualities. Ft:t the re;embhmce to G,:,d that is both most important and most attainable is moral ,,::o.l spiritual likene,:s in cbancter and conduct, Consider especially in what points wo ;11,J:,-t need to bo like God. 1. Purity. 2. Truth. 3. Generous giving. There arc men who are s.lways grasping for themselves, and others who distribute abroad. 'fhe btler arc like ~ who is ever raying out blessings. 4. Forbearance. In nothlng do we more need to 1ruirote God than in his gentleness with sinners, his long~sufferincr patience, and his forgiving mercy. 5. Love. This is nearest to the heart and very being of Go<l, for God is love. He who loves his kind most widely and warmly is likest God (see ver. 2). III. WHY WE SHour.o llE IllITATORS OF Gon. 1. It is our natural duty. Nothing short of tbis will satisfy the claims of right. It is not enough that we follow ,the best men and conform with the utmost propriety to the pious fashions of the times, nor even that we obey our own consciences. \Ve have to make our conduct agree with God's conscience. Duty is infinite-a ceaseless climbing to higher and yet hlghcr regions of holiness. We cannot reach the pinnacle of perfection at once, and we are not guilty for not doing what lies beyond our present powers. But we are blameworthyif.we,aim at less than perfection and if we ever rest contented with any lower stage of. progress., "Ye therefore shall be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect"·(Matt. v. 48). ,2.. 1Ve are under obligations of gratitude to become imitators of God. The word" therefore" calls our attention to these obligations. It points back to the previous words, wherein we are exhorted to forgive one another, even as God also in Christ forgave ,us. 3. Our i,i,;hest blessedness will be found in our resemblance to God. He is ever blessed. E~·erything ungodlike mnst be ultimately a source of pain and death. Though the imit.ation of God begins in toil and sacrifice, it grows into the: deepest peace and the richest gJ.arlness. IV. BY WR.AT :IIElllS WE l[AY llECOKE IMITATORS OF Goo. 1. Worship. Heathen gods are objective representations, and even monstrous exaggerations, of the.natures of their devotees. Such gods can have no good moral influence. But God, as ,he is revealed in Christ, is infinitely above us, and full of wonderful beauty and ·attraction. As we gaze upon his glory in rapt devotion we arc changed into his likeness. We all imitate, consciously or unconsciously, what we admire .. •When we see a ~reat picture we wish to paint; when we enjoy good music we desire t<;> produce it; when we see noble deeds we are fired to emulate them, 2. Meditation. As St. Francis is said to have received the wounds of Christ on his own person by ~ntense meditation on them, we may receive the spiritual likeness of our Lord-a more profitable resemblance-by contemplating and dwelling in the spirit of his life. 'l'hen also ~e shall hav:e the likeness of God. He who is nearest to God in prayer and- communion grows likest God. 3. Obedi.ent action. We must do Divine deeds of holiness and charity if we woul<i ba-:-e the character that a habit of such deeds begcts. All this God will supplement a~,c rivify by the in.b-piration of his Holy Spirit breathing his own life and likenes11 i:Jv, DI!. . Y. Ix ll"BAT SPIE1T WE ABB TO BEOOHE DDTATOBB OF Goo. "As beloved children." LL•..;s h,-t·ed children venerate and imitate their parents. Here is no room for spiritual pricie. For when we l05e the childlike spirit we fall away from the imitation of God. entries.content:
-Tl,e sacrifice of Ghrist. I. THE !IAOBIFICE OF CHRIST WAB VOLUNTABY1 He gave himself. He said he had power-right as well as ability-to lay down his lifo (John L 18). Had the sacrifice of Christ not been the free giving of himself, it would have been like the human saerificcs of the heathen-BI fearful deed in, those who slew him and of no import to any one elRe. The esscir.ce,ofthe sacrifice, all that gavo to it

propHiatory efficacy, was the willingness of the Sufferer who offered himself. God is not pleased with pain 1rnd death. What be ie plenscd with is the devotion, fidelity, nnd love tbnt endure pain and death in the fulfilment of an unselfish and noble mission. II. THE SACRIFICE OF CumsT WAS Ol'FEBED TO Goo. Christ was not simply a Mnrtyr to truth, nor only a Suffcrrr in the cause of humanity. The cup that he drnnk was given to him by bis Father. His persistence through mortal agony was in submission to the will of God. Gethsemane interprets Calvary. It reveals an essential element of the sacrifice of Christ that has been too much neglected in our theologies-the obediei,cc, of Christ. St. Paul saw this when he said that Christ became "obedient unto death." Thus the cross was an altar and the crucifix.ion an offering to God. IIL T1rn SACRIFICE OF CHRIST WAS WELL-PLEASmG TO Goo. ln primite language it it is said, tbat when the smoke of Noah's sacrifice went up to heaven "God smelled a sweet savour"-literally, "a savour of satisfaction," i.e. it was acceptable to God. So Christ's sacrifice is described as "•an odour of a sweet smell." Such an act of fidelity to God and love to man could not but be pleasing to God. 'I'hus the sacrifice become,; a propitiation; it becomes the means through which God looks favourably on those for whom it is offered. IV. THE SACRIFICE OF CHRIST WAS MADE ON OUR BEHALF. "For us." Men had often offered sacrifices for themselves-to ex.press their own devotion and to expiate their own sins. It is customary now for people to talk of makiog a present sacrifice in order to secure a future adV'llntage. But Christ's sacrifice was not for his own interests. It was the Shepherd giving bis life for the sheep, the Friend laying down his life for his friends. His was the pain, ours is the gain ; bis the cross of death, ours the crown of life. V. THE SACRIFICE OF CHRIST WAS OCCASIONED BY ms LOVE TO us. "Christ also loved you." 'l'here was no necessity that Christ should die. Ordinary duty would not have required the sacrifice, for, though fidelity and obedience entered into it, these elements were consequent on the free undertaking of a work of love by Christ. Chri~t as a man was possessed of a great love of his kind tbnt constrained him to die for the world ; Christ as the Son of God and "the very Image of his substance" (Heb. i. 3) died because he was full of the love of the Father for his Jost children. VI. 'l'HE SAOBIFICE OF CHRIST SHOULD LEAD us TO WALK m LOVE. 1. In return for his love. Love should inspire love. If it does we shall show our love to Christ by loving our brethren. 2. In breathing his Spirit. Christianity is not merely nppropriating the fruits of the work of Christ. It is followin~ in his footsteps. Christians nre called to be imitators of God, especially as he is manifested in Christ. An imito.tinn of God must therefore consist chiefly in nn exercise of love like tho.t of Christ. llis love to us led him to submit to crucifix.ion. He asks us simply to walk in Jove.- W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 5:14
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-.Awake/ I. A DESCRIPTION. A particular kind of man is hero addressed -" thou that sleepest;" "the dead." 1. The mnn is aslrep. His sleep is spiritual indifference. Whether or no he bas an abstract belief in religion is not of the slightest moment. He mo.y be an a.theist or he may be orthodox of the orthodox. So long as he is sleeping it matters little what he might have been doing hnd be been awake. 'l'he sleeper may have his eyes open to secular interests; he may have e. quick intellect in epcculation or a vigorous energy in business. Yet angels who see that he is uncon- Hcious of the greatest realities must regard him a.s o. dreamer or at best as o. restles~ sleep-walker. 2. This sleep is a sign of death. It is more than sleep. It is unnatural and impossible to a soul in full energy. Spiritual perceptions must have been dullc,l nn<l spiritual powers paralyzed to admit of this blindness and stupor in regar<l to Diviuc things. ll. A 0ALL. Awake! Up! Arise) A loud voice disturbs the sleeper. 1. Gu,l calls, sometimes (1) in providence, rousing the careless soul by the shock of sumc sudden change; and often (2) in the gospel, for it_ is the duty of the prench~r to speak in trumpet-notes, uot merely to teach the nttent1 vo .but also to rouse the listless. '.l, It is impo1'tant to respond to this call; for sleep is (1) a sinful neglect of duty; (~) a foolish loss of blessings-he who sleeps till the full day never sees tho glory of the stm- rise; and (3) n dangerous condition-the longer n man sleeps the mNe difficult will it 252 THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. [oa. v. 1-33,

be to awake, and meanwhile death and judgment may be upon him. 3. It is possible to atM-~Y. The i;piritual i;leep is partly ,oluntary and semi-conscious. As a man rometimes knows that he is dreaming so he may be made aware that he is spiritually asleep and may rouse himself if he will. There is rousing power, too, in the Divine ,-,,ice. It vexes a r:1an to have his rest disturbed, but as one who wakes the sleeper when his house is on fire it comes for his deliverance and he will do well to bestir hi:nself. III. A PROMISE.. "Christ shall shine upon thee." There is something to wake up for. Christ is the Light of the world. His people are now "light in the Lord." He hrings to the waking soul truth, purity, and joy. When the storm rages and the dark night lingers, and to wake is only to take up a.,crain the burden of sorrow and grope in the hopeless gloom, a man has some excuse for sleeping. Despair may sleep, But the Christian finds a bright morning responding to his opening eyes. We are not to wake only to kindle a poor light for ourselves. We are rewarded for waking by the cheering brightness of Christ. We must rouse ourselves, however, to enjoy it. The people that sit in darkness see the great light only when they awake and arise from the dead.-W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 5:15
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -The "alue of time. I. ALL TIME Is oF HIGH VALUE. They who kill time destroy one of the best talents God has given them and rob him of a sacred trust ho has lent to them. L Time ,·s nol our own pruperly. We are servants and have to account to our Master for our use of his hours. 2. Great roncerns have to be attended to. .Kot only is art long while life is short, but duty is great, the claims of service are many, and the wants of our fellow-men are numerous. In this world of toil and strife and sorrow e.ery moment is of value for some good deed of mercy or some solid work of rruth. 3. lhst time is irrerovera.ble. We cannot redeem the time that has been wasted. A repentant diligence may bring back the inherit.a.nee that was squandered away in enra.agant folly; careful attention may bring back the wasted health; but time once gone is gone for ever. 4. Time may be made of increasing '1alUll. An hour is worth more in the use of one man than a day with another man. II. SPECIAL OPPORTUNITIES .All.E OF SPECIAL VALUE. St. Paul nrges us to buy up "the seasons." All time is not of eqnal value. There are moments of peculiar precious- ness. Woe to him who, through heedlessness or wilful negligence, lets them slip I The moment when the rope floats by the drowning man it must be seized or he dies, Strike the iron while it is hot. Sow the seed in the spring if you would reap the harvest in the autumn. 1. Youth has its golden opportunities that belong to no other age. Young men especially shonld make the most of their own season. 2. Manhood has its time of vigour for work that will be beyond the strength of old age. The wise man will watch for occasions of usefulness that his word may be "in season." III. TBE TRUB VALUE OF Tll[E CAN ONLY BE OBTAINED AT A COST, We have to buy it np before we can make use of it. 1. We must spend thought in considering how we can best UBe our time and in watching for right opportunities. For want of due con- 6i.deration there is a frightful lack of economy of energy and time. 2. We must sacrifice our own plea.sure in giving np time that we are tempted to expend on ourselves, our amusement or our rest, to the service of God. He who only gives to God his leisure moments, when he is worn and jaded with his own selfish work, makes but a poor offering. 3. We must put out gT«zter emrgy in order to make our time of more .-alue. Few of us work on the highest subjects at full pressure. The busiest might do more good if, when they cannot as yet find time for serving Christ, they would make time.-W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 5:18
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Drunkennes, and it, antidote. I. THE SIN. It was the mistake of some of the earlier advocates of temperance to dwell too much on the economic ari!:Uments against drunkenness, to the neglect of those which are supplied by religion. That dis• sipation wrecks a man's position in the world is plain and sad enough. But it is not worldly self-interest that is chiefly outraged thereby. The sin of drunkenness is its great condemnation. It is a sin against God and man. 1. It desecrates the temple of the Holy Ghost. 2. lt unfits a man for his mission in the world. 3. It occasions brutal unkindne.Ba to others, robbing the family of daily bread for the sake of gross

self-indulgence, bringing poverty and gloom, wretchedness and terror on the home, and giving to children a hideous inheritance of disease and constitutional tendencies to the same vice. 4 .. It opens t?e doo:r for other vices. Instead of pleading intoxication as an excuse for a crime committed ID the madness of drink, a man should be made to foci that the wickedness of putting himself into such a condition was 00 a"[!Tavated by the terrible results. II. THE TEMPTATION. In order to remedy the fearful evil we must consider how it arises. 1. From customs of sociability. Drinking has been regarded as an almost necessary accompaniment of friendly intercourse. 2. From lack of mental ~upation. Men spending hours together of a. winter's night without any education to supply food for the mind resort to the glass as the one available relief from the tedium of doin"' nothing. 3. The craving for nervous stimulation. This is the real thirst of the exces~ sive driuker. What is called "low spirits," resulting from general ill health, or nervous debility, or trouble, or as the natural conseque:i.ce of previous indulgence, creates the craving for stimulants. Early in the present century, Lord Jeffrey quoted a statement of a physician of Liverpool, respecting some of the most prosperous merchants of that town. "He informs me," said the lord advocate, "that few of the richer sort live to be fifty, but die of a sort of atrophy. They eat too much, take little exercise, and, above all, have no nervous excitement." This condition tempts to indulgence in nerve-stimulants. III. THE ANTIDOTE. We must have an antidote if we would remedy the evil. Mere negative abstinence without anything to support and encourage it is impossible on a large scale and in the worst cases. St. Paul, by a flash of inspiration reveals the cure. "Be filled with the Spirit." 'l'hese are old words. Yet they read strangely in the present connection-so little have they been heeded by zealous but unimaginative and unspiritual social reformers. We are to pray for the Spirit or God which Obrist assures us will be given to all who ask for it (Luke x.i. 13). How is this to counteract drunkenness? 1. It counteracts the craving for nervous stimulation. It is itself a pure and vitalizing spiritual stimulus, infusing at once restfulness and energy. 2. It supplies interest and occupation. For the Spirit of God is the inspiration of thought and power. 3. It purifies and elevates social intercourse. They who aro filled with the Spirit will find that "singing and making melody in their hearts" is a more congenial accompaniment of social intercourse than drinking strong drin.ks.- W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 5:19
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-0hristian worship. We have here, not only an intereoting picture of worship as it was conducted in the early Church, but also apostolio directions for Christian worship tho.t may be applied to all times. Consider some of the chief fea'l;ures of this worship.· I. IT IS PURE. The context shows that this point was of especial interest under the circumstances that obtained when the Epistle was written. The pure and simple observances of the Christian assembly at Ephesus must have stood in striking contrast to the riotous orpes that characterized the heathen festivities. In those pagan ceremonies intoxication and licentiousness were recognized accompaniments. Instead of indulging in drunkenness, the Christians seek to be filled with the Spirit; abandoning immoral practices, they occupy themselves in social worship by singing and ma.king melody in their hearts. Pagans separated morality from roligion. To Christians neither is possible without the other. Christian worship must be offered up in tho beauty of holiness. Christian conduct is purified and elevated by the inspiration of worship. II. IT Is SPIRITUAL. We are to make melody with our "heart." The heart stands, not for the feelings only nor chiefly, but generally for the inner lifo. Worship must begin here, or the richest music and the sweetest song will be an empty mockery. Whatever be our forms of worship, we have constantly to remember that the spiritual God can only be really worshipped in spirit, in inward thoughts and feelings of devotion, III. IT IB EMOTIONAL. Religion is not all feeling. It is based on convictions, and it develops into actioas. But religion does not dispense with emotions. It touches our whole DAture-tht1 emotional part with the rest. It makes great use of feelings as 25-! THE EPISTLE TO 'l'HE EPHESIANS. [cu. v. 1-33.

Instead of gloomy rites and bloody sacrifices Christians have music and song in their worship. 'l'hey are living under a gospel and should echo'.back the gla_d tidings of God's love. They are coming _to a Father and should approach J11rn with happy home-confidence. They are fol\owmg Christ, who gives his joy to his people (John xv. 11). . "."· IT IS voc.u.. It begi~s in the heart, but it doe_s ~ot remain hidden there. Deep we~g naturally wells out m strong utterance. Religious emotion is encouraged and , s,i;:tcd by adequate expression. Of all pa:·ts of religion thanksgiving should be least ~-c;:ern"<l. ,L IT IS llUSIC.U.. "Making melody." We cannot make the service of praise too k':'.:a_tiiul, because we should offer to God l'.hat is best in form as well as in substance, :1:id ~use the music of sc1ng assists the feeling that it expresses. Slovenly sinaina 0 is a mark of indiJierence and irreverence. "'

vIL Ir IS OONGREGATION.U.. "Speaking one to another." This is probably an allusion to antiphonal congre,,"11.tiona.l singing. But whatever be the method adopted, and though a choir may take its part in the service, it is plainly the intention of St. l'aul that all the people should sing, and that thus one should exhort and encouracre another. We cannot praise God by proxy. "' VIII. IT IS ADDRESSED TO Goo IN CHRIST. "To the Lord." Pliny writes how tho Christians in his time met in the early morning to sing hymns to one Christ. We are not to sing simply for our own delectation or spiritual culture, or merely to attract and interest others, but mainly as addressing God and Christ in praise and communion.- W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 5:20
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Thanksgiving. There are three points in this exhortation to thanksgiving thn.t arrest our attention, viz. the time, the objects, and the method. I. TBE TIME FOR THA.NKSGIVI50. There is a time for everything. When, therefore, is tha.nks~ving seasonable? Always. Ail we should pray without ceasing by linng in constant colll.!D.unication with God, so a spirit of gratitude should pervade our whole life and express itself by the brightness and colour that it gives to every.action (Ps. xx:xi,. 1). If the conteKt limits the application of St. Paul's words to public worship (,er. 17), the breadth of their incidence is still very significant. Every Christi.an a:ssembly sh011ld be joyons with praise, in every prayer supplication should be mingled mth thanksgiving (PhiL iv. 6). There are tim~s when this i&..difficult, e.g. in trouble and in moods of spiritual depression. But the difficulty would be diminished if we thought 1658 of our own feelings and more of the gifts_.and deeds of God's; goodness. Modern religion is too subjective, and thereforo it fluctuates with our varyinp; phases of experience. Thanksgiving should call us out of. ourseLves. to contemplate and praise God. Under the darkest cloud a thankful heart will see innumerable co.uses of gratitude. But let our thanksgiving be honest." If we do not feel grateful, do not let us try to force the expression of gratitude. , IL THE OBJECTS OF TH.U"KSOIVINO. "All things." 1. Personal blessings. While we thank God for common gifts to all mankind, our gratitude would be warmer and more genuine if we reflected on the special proofs of his goodness in our own lives. 2. Jt':resh bleEsinga. If thanksgiving is to be perpetual it must constantly find new food for gratitude. This, of all parts of worship, should not be a mere repetition of old, worn thoughts. Our ideas on this point are too narrowed by conventionality. If we art careful to say grace before me.at, why should we not be equally ready to thank God for a good book, a cheerful visit, or a refreshing walk? 3. Thing, that we ca,nnot see t.o be bleui'fl{Js. Gratitude for troubles is difficult to realize. lt is only possible through faith. But if we believe that God is blessing us in them we should thank him aa one would thank a surgeon for e.en amputating a limb to save his patient's life. lIL 'IHl! METHOD oY TBANUOIVING. 1. It. should be offered to God our Father. It is a direct speakin 6 to God. Ail he is the Father of mercies, his fatherhood should be the attribute that is most in our thoughts when we praiso him. fore, be no cringing abjectness in our worship, It should be cheerful and confident. 2. The thanksgiving is to be given in the Name of Ohrist; i.e. (1) in recognition that Go,l's blessings come to us through Christ; and (2) as receiving and appreciating them in the ,;pirit of Christ.-W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 5:22–33
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -Husbands and wives. I. CHRISTIANITY CONSECRATES AXD ELEVATES THE UNION m' BUSllAND AND WIFE. 1. Christianity sanctions marriage. St. Paul, though an unmarried man, casts no slight on marriage. It is trne that he discourages it under temporary trying circumstances (1 Cor. vii. 1), but it is also true that ~he plainly teaches, not only the lawfulness, but especially the dignity of Christian marria"o in itself. The ascetic view of celibacy as a more holy state than marria~c is not foui7tl iu the New Testament. "Let marriage be had in honour among all" (Heh. xiii. 1). 2. Christianity elevates marriage. St. Paul compares it with the union ot' Christ with his Church. He does not take the marriage relation to il!ustrato that uuion-an illustration that was familiar with the prophets in explaining the relation of God to Israel. Ho makes the comparison in the opposite way, taking the union of Christ aud the Church as the true and perfect union, and therefore as tho type of what marriage should be, viz. (1) close union and (2) spiritual union. Further, it is to be observe,l that Christianity elevates marriage (1) by giving women a religious equality with men -men and women have equal privileges in the gospel; and (2) by inculcating purity, justice, gentleness, and unselfishness. I!. THE filGB CHRISTIAN IDEA. OF HARRIAGE LAYS GREAT RESPONSIBILITIES ON HUSBANDS AND WIVES. Care and effort are necessary to realize so magnificent an ideal as a human copy of the mysticnl union of Christ and the Church. Ca.re should be given in particular to the following requisites :-1. Mutual sympathy. It is not riaht that husbands and wives, in dividing the home life into separate departments, should fail to take interest in one another's cares and works. The husband should show sympathy for the wife's domestic -hopes, and fears, and joys, and troubles, and t.he wife for the husband's schemes and achievements and disappoiutments. 2. 11Iutuc1l confidence. 'l'his is essential to mutual sympathy. 'l'here shoulJ. be no secret between husb:rnd and wife. Surely it is a mistake for a husband to hide his trouble from his wife out of a desire to spare her pain, and equally so for tho wife to do the same in regard to her husband. The separation thus caused is a more serious evil than the pain that is prevented. 3. Mutual forbearance. Each must be prepared to meet with faults in tlrn other. But·each would be less provoked by those faults if the husband would think rather of what his wife has to endure in him than of what he may be annoyed at 'n her, and if the wife would re~ect in the same way on her own failings. 4. The consecration of marriage through union with Ol1rist. Such a truly Christian marriage is safe from shipwreck.. It is sad to see how rarely the Christian idea. of marri11ge is realized; but little better can be expected till men and women are aimin~ throughout at a higher life than what is now prevalent in society-a. lifo of spiritual union with Christ.-W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 6:1–4
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Duties of children and parents. It must havo been an interesting day in the Church of Ephesus when it was known that a pastoral letter would be rnad iu the public assembly from the beloved and venerable apostle whose labours hud been attended with such a blessing. Whether the meeting was held in eo.rly morning or late in the evening, every effort would be made by every Christian to be present, antl even as they were walking towards the place of meeting, a certain briskness of manner and eagerness of expression would show that something beyond tho common wa iu 0

expectation. Those who had to pass the great temple of Diana would cast no lingering look behind, nor think of the contrast between that magnificent shrine of idolatry and the very humble building where the true God was worshipped, by whom nil things were made. Even the children would not linger to peep at the gorgeous glory of the temple, for their parents would have told them that at their meeting fL letter was going to be read from the great apostle, now unable to come to them because wicked men had imprisoned him, but still remembering them all, o.s his letter woul<l show. Remembering the interest which, like his Master, the apostle had taken in tho young, it would be an interesting question whether the letter to be rentl would not contain some passage for them, and, if it did, what would be its tenor? Perhaps tho most attentive of them would be beginning to feel weary as five-sixths of the letter was read, but no word yet for them. But at last the message comes; and when it comes it appears that it is not only about them, but addressed to them ; the apostle looks them full in the face, and says, "Children." And when the children's morsel is brought out, it is perhaps not quite what they expected, It is not a sugared morsel, nor is it particularly affectionate in its terms. It is not a nice little story or a poetical allegory, carrying them to the realms of dreamlo.nd ; it is just a simple, practical requirement-" Children, obey your parents in the Lord." Possibly even the ohlcr hearers were rather surprised, and certainly there are many now who would havo expected a more spiritual counsel. 'l'hey would have expected him to say something to the children about Jesus, or about prayer, or about trying to tench the heathen nround them; but he speaks on none of these things. He probably coun,ed that, if the children were right with their parents, other things would follow; if they obeyed their TEIE EPISTLE TO THE EL'IlESlA.NS. [cH, VI, 1-24,

R-~nts. an,i their p.~nts bronght t.hem up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord, ln.,i.'s b!,,,:sing would mit on their efforts and all wonld he well. But if the npostle did nN ~!'<'-'lk to children in the modern fushion, it is all the more importnnt to notice an,i. p,,:ider t.he m=-"6-.e which he actually gives them. I. l)UTY OF CHILDREN. 1. 7b obey. 2. 1'o honour their panmts. The reasons nre- (1) it is right; (2) it is a commandment; (3) it is the first of tho commnndments with a promise; (4) that promise gives expectation of long life and prosperity. In ,,uc of t-hc best books of the early Church, written by one of its greatest men-' The C0nfessions' of St. Augustine-there is a chapter in which he humbly confesses his disob~~ience as a ~y, in neglecting his lessons, and going to see games and sights in oppos1tion to the wishes of his parents. Long after, when he came to be a Christian, the thought haunted and distressed him until, confessing it, and laying it on Jesus, he obt.ained the mercy and forgiveness of God. Long life among the Jews was a token of the Divine favour, and it seems to have been an emblem of the life to come. We need not count in all cases on a literal fulfilment of the Jewish promise; but we may rest assured that a spirit of honour to our parents tends to make our earthly lot better and brighter, and will have some recognition likewise in the life that is to come. II. DUTY OF PAREn"S. 1. Negativdy. Not to provoke or irritate their children. But : 2. Positively, to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. In the Old Testament, Samuel, and in the New Testament, Timothy, are samples or chilJ.ren so brought up. The Lord's command is," Bring up this child for me, and I will pay thee thy wages." What infinit-ely precions results depend on the execution c,f these rn-o precepts! E,ery well-trained Christian household is a nnrsery or all that .en~ to bie;,s the world; while disorderly and unchristian families are hotbeds of vice :me. ffil. The prayer of the hundred and forty-fourth psalm is never out of date : " That our sons may be as plants grown up in their youth; our daughters as cornerswnes, polished after the similitnde of a palace. . . . Happy is that people that is in such a case; yea, happy is that people whose God is the Lord."

entries.title: EPH 6:5–9
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -Duties o/ servants and masters. I. DUTY OF BEBVAN'l'II. Recognized as constitnrnt members of the Church, and, however little esteemed by man, as greatly regarcied by God. In Christ all are brethren, for all are brothers of Christ, therefore of one another. I. The duty of servants is obedience. Qualities of the obedience. (1) With fear and trembling (see Exposition); (2) in singleness of heart; (3) as unto Christ and not to men; (4) not with eye-service, but as servants of Christ; (5) doing the will of God from the heart; (6) with good will. 2. The reward of good service. Whatsoever good you do, yon shall receive of the Lord,; he will repay you. We are apt to be jealous of this doctrine. It seems to undermine free grace. But no; sal,ation is wholly of grace; but one feature of grace is that, when you receive it a~d act on it, it begets, as it were, another !Aft of grace. entries.title: EPH 6:10–20
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -Tlie Olll'istiam, warfare. Even in common parlance we speak of ".the battle of life." Even for ordinary purposes we have to fi"ht ac,ainst indolence, ovil l_u~ts, ~ishonest tendencies, nnd many other things in o~rselv~s; and ngainst oppo~1t.1on, 111 _treatl!lent, temptation on the part of others, and the depressing effects of trml and d1sappomtment. All hard work is II fight; we have to fi~ht against the sense of monotony, against the feeling of weariness, against the longincr for ease; and when we nre sick, or feeble, or depressed, it is often hard to bold on the straight path of hard duty and turn away from the allurements of pleasure. 'fhe ring of the hammer, the blow of the shuttle, the housewife's active step from dawn to dewy eve, often tell of baltles and victories in quiet spheres, that without the eclat have much more real glory than ordinary wars. But much rr.ore is the Christian life a battle. The chief enemies here are unseen. It is impossible to pursue an aimless, careless life and be a Christian. " If any man will come after me," said Christ, "let him deny himself, and take up his cross and follow me." Not only to be a Christian, but such a Christian as this Epistle delineates; to walk worthy of the vocation with which we are called ; to be ever reaching forth toward the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ; to be growing up into Christ toward that condition in which we shall be without spot or wrinkle or any such thing; to be advancing thus in spite of hosts or spiritual foes, working unseen, sapping and mining our Christian life, trying to entangle and enslave us in every way ;-this can be no easy task; it is a veritable battle, demanding constant vigilance and incessant care. It may seem strange that we shoulJ be exposed to such enemies. Is not our blessed Lord exalted far above all principality and power and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come? Has be not spoiled principalities and powers, making a show of them openly? Is he not Head over all things to his Church? Why, then, does he not crush all her foes? Doubtless because he bas purposes of discipline to carry out in connection with these enemies, because, while he is willing to fight in and through his people, he does not see it right to crush bis foes without their instrumentality; in this way habits of vigilance and prayer and activity must be kept up by them; but all the greater will be their joy when at last the victory is gained, and they get the reward of "him that overcometh." In the Middle Ages, certain coarse means were employed to arrest attention to the formidable foes that beset the Christian soldier. Fre~coes were painted on the walls of churches and other ecclesiastical buildings, representing souls which were sometimes seen coming out of dying bodies, while angels on the one side, and devils on the other, were striving to get them. 'l'he devils were grotesque, hideous, revolting monsters, more absurd than terrible. It was the way or that age to emJ,oJy truths which in our material age are apt to be thought as ridiculous as the demons or the Italian frescoes. Dut there are spirits of evil hovering about us, trying to obscure and pervert the truth, to blind us to the fruits of sin, to dazzle our eyes with the glory of earth, to entangle us in subtle temptations, to fill our minds with doubts and fear~ and evil forebodings, luring us to the edge of the precipice, an,! ready, if they shon!J get their way, to burst into their bitter scornful laugh, as they beholJ us, through their wiles, woltering in the gulf of despair. Let us observe: 1. 1'he true Source of strength: "In tho Lord" (ver. 10). 2. The true armour to seek. "The whole armour of God " ( ver. 11 ). 3. The true enemies to be overcome. (V ers. 11, 12.) "The wiles of the devil," and other unseen spiritual foes. 4. The true employment and attitude of the Christian warrio-r: "Withstand ... and stand" (vor. 13). 5. The various pieces of the armottr, and their use. (Vers. 14-18.) "Who is she that looketh forth ns the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?" An army consists of men who not only have armour, but havo been trained to use it. An unarmed army can only be food for the enemy's artillery, materinl for a dreadful rnassacro. Let professing Christians see that they are armed, and that they are making a good use of their armour. Nature cries out for an easy life, for n truce with the world, the devil, nn<l the flesh. In this sense our motto must be war, not peace; for in this scnso Christ came, not to send peace on earth, but a sword.

entries.title: EPH 6:18–20
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-" Praying always." Hera is n part of the Christian's armour which had nothing corresponding to it in the panoply or the Roman soldier. Prayer comes in without any figure. ,ve are taught that, even when overy spiritnnl wc,\pon is prepared 264 'l'HE EPIS'l'LE TO TRE EPHESIANS. [on. VI. 1-24,

and direct«! ~"1\inst the spiritual foe, all is in vain without a direct appeal to God. When Jacob, looking for an attack by E1111u, had completed his arrangements of hie family and flocks, the most important part of his preparations remained-another warfare had to be carried on, he must wrestle with the angel for his blessin.,.. So in the Christian conflict, even when the loins are girt with truth, the heart proteoted by the b.esstplate of righteousness, the feet shod with peace, the head crowned with the he,met of ssh-ation, the perron protected by the shield of faith, and when the bands :-i:-,, g~ping and wielding the sword of the Spirit, there is another duty which is quite indispensable-prayer: "Praying always with all prayer," etc. This is in accordance with the whole t.enor of the Bible : Enoch, walking with God ; Abraham, interceding for Sodom; Moses, pleading on the mountain ; Elijah, praying for rain ; David Hezekiah, Daniel, Simeon, Anna, our blessed Lord in Gethsemane,-all show us that fighting men ought always to pray and not to feint. The soul is thus strengthened and encouraged; it reaches the promises and rests on them ; it feels that God is with it; " They that wait on the Lord renew their strength; they mount up with wings as eagles; they run, and are not weary; they walk, and are not faint." The prayer required is marked by six features. 1. Manifold. With all prayer and supplication; all kinds- secret, ejaculatory, domestic, social, public. 2. Incessant. At all seasons: (1) at all times or periods of life, youth, manhood, age; (2) in connection with every employment, recreation, trial, mercy, undertaking, both great and small ; (3) as a constant habit of the spirit, thinking on God, depending on him, working for him. 3. Spiritual. "In the Spirit "-in dependence on his aid and inspiring power, in opposition to the ruere form or rhyming of" paternosters." 4. Wutchful,. (See Exposition.) 5. Persevering (see Exposition). 6. Comprehensi,flf.. "For all saints," and especially for God's .;er.ants in the gospel. the men who are bearing the burden and heat of the battle. :Yen may ridicule prayer; they may scoff at a praying man, a praying family, a praying DJlticm ; but the spectacle is really sublime. When Pere Hyacinthe, lecturing o::i the pahlic immorality of his country, made the aisles of Notre Dame ring with bis eloq:ie::ice., he did not find ea.use to scoff at prayer. He said that it moved him to find England and the United St.ates not a.shamed to pray in the time of calamity, and to gi.e thanks in the hour of deliverance. God, after all, is the Ruler among the nations, and his rule of good will stand true. " Them that honour me I will honour, but they that de.spise me shall be lightly esteemed."

entries.title: EPH 6:21
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:

He was unselfish, unworldly, unambitious; it were a blessing for the Church if the rank-and-file of its undistinguished ministers and other workers were like him. Great importance of the closing benediction in public service; tendency to think of it u a mere closing form. It contains the very essence of all blessing.
