And it was not an object which kept them from flagrant irregularities in the pursuit of it. The object which the Christian combatant is to have before him is not to have mere romance, but truth, binding truth, in it. That truth may be said to be connected with Christ's tomb, but not in a mere realistic way. It is imperatively demanded, now that Christ bas conquered on the cross, and that conquest has been attested by an empty tomb, that in his Name souls everywhere should be delivered. And the Christian combatant does not gird himself to get possession of some sacred place or of some sacred relic, but to help men who are in the present guilt and tbraldom of sin toward their deliverance. 2. The breastplate. "And having put on the breastplate of righteousness." The idea in righteousness is that of a right relation to the Law of God. Righteousness worn as a plate over the heart is to be understood rather as the mind conscious of right. The Ubristian combatant is to be jealous over himself with a godly jealousy. He is to have nothing to do with insincerity, but is to _study reality. He is not to have selfish motives, but is to be thoroughly disinterested. He is not t-0 have feelings of grudgiug malice, but is to be just and compasrionate. He is to be especially fired with a desire to glorify God. The man who is conscious of this may be said to have righteousness as a breastplate. 3. The sandcds. "And having shod your feet with the preparation of the gospel of peace." The Christian combatant, having girded himself in the cause of truth, and being conscions of no unworthy feeling, is next to put on the gospel sandals. It is that by which he is enabled to carry the good message. For that also belongs to the work of the battle-field. He puts on his shoes for the holy war. But in that war ho is not always closing with his adversary. '.l'here are times when he has to follow up an advantage. Nay, bis great business may be said to be to get ~is message delive_red, ~o cry aloud so that Satan's captives may hear. The message which he has to deliver 1s a message of peace. He fights, not for fighting's sake, but that the times pf peace may be ushered in. And as he thinks of his message, and enters into tho spirit of it, his sandals become promptitude, alacrity (according to the idea hero); he becomes swiftfooted and speeds on with bis message. 4. The shield. "Withal taking up the shielcl of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the evil one." As the Cbristian warrior runs swiftrfooted with his message of peace, there arc fiery darts thwwn at ]Jim. When any one is eminent in the ChriHtian coDflict, Satan is likely to r<1i6': u 1, a 6aini;t him traducers. Those who do not believe in disinterestedness arc ~ut 11, r:.ah 'JUt that he is serving himself. ']'hose who do not believe in earnestness ;, rd:'.0~J :c.r,, f.·1m ttJ circulate evil r~portB of him. It is worse when, in the very ,:_·.,,r.,:t:;- di,::; £;,idual feeling, he is laid open to wmr,tatione from his lusts. Or it ~:.;,y r,<; tha: L, •,<;ry rn= Jaye him open to the temptation of 11piritual pride. So 1: ."'.-~ v.:r.~. n Le wi:.,, ::,ad bcsc:n \'ic:t(,rious in many a sr,iritual eunflict was tcmptc,\ (it ie t.<:'1 fr;,t ~atan rrov,,ked him) to number the people. An,\ the dart thrown at him

took effect, and was fiery enough in its consequences. What the Christian combatant is to do, when he is thus assailed, is not certainly to under-estimate the force that is brought ag~inst him, but it is also by faith rightly to estimate the force that is placed at bis service. What can he do against the principalities and powers and the fiery darts they send out for his destruction? If he look to himself, he can <lo nothing. Ilut he looks away to the power which placed Christ above all the principalities and powers, and he places it as a shield between him and the fiery darts, and in it their fire is quenched, their force is lost. 5. The helmet. "And take the helmet of salvation." The helmet is not, as in 1 Thess. v. 8, the hope of salvation, but salvation itself, i.e. salvation enjoyed. 'l'he Christian has an important piece of defensive armour in the assmance of salvation. The Lord rebuked Satan, and encouraged Joshua the high priest (Zech. iii. 2), by pointing to him as one of his saved ones. When one can think of grace going out toward him in the changing of his position to all eternity, he can feel triumphant; he has salvation as a helmet on his head. 6. The sword. "And the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God." The Bible is the sword of the Spirit. Furnished it is by the Spirit; for it was under the inspiration of the Spirit that the Word was written. And, as the Spirit inspired men to write it, so it is only he who can enable men to make a right use of it. To this we may apply the words of the hymn- "God is his own interpreter, And he will mo.ke it plain." In the temptation of our Lord, what Satan did was to misrepresent the character of the Father, to put a gloss upon Scripture. And what our Lord, in meeting the temptation, did was to confront him with the pure truth, and the truth opposed to his deceptions. And he was so skilful in the use of this sword that he could fix upon the particular Scripture that suited the occasion. And the Christian combatant, too, must not only see the truth, but the truth for the occasion, the truth that slays his doubts, that exposes the fallacies with which Satan would compass his destruction. And he must bo able to do this in connection with some sure, incisive word of Scripture. That is the offensive weapon, the weapon which caJTies the war against the adversary. This Christian combatant who has been described is what every Christian is bound to be. The Church militant is.to have, in every one of its members, a combatarrt. And the apostle lays stress upon every one taking the whole armour (and not merely some of its parts). No onC', for instance, is a worthy combatant who feels no responsibility in the carrying of the gospel message. If we would have the strength our Captain wouhl see in us, wo must use all the pieces of the Christian armour. v. 'l'HAT WHICH ACCOMPANIES THE USE OF THE CHRISTIAN ARMOUR. 1. .Prayc1·. "With nil prayer and supplication, praying at nil seasons in the Spirit." \Ve are not to think of "all prayer" as a separate weapon. We are rather to think of it ns that which conditions the right uso of the whole :umour. Without prayer we cannot gird ourselves for the conflict, but are cumbered as with loose robes. Without prnyer we cannot have that pnrification of motives, thnt rectification of life, which the conflict demands. Without prayer we cannot have swift-footedness in carrying the gospel. Without prayer wo shall not have faith to ward off the enemy's darts. Without prayer we shall not be able to lift our head in the assurance of our salvation. Without prayc-r we shall be unskilful in the use of the Word. Con- Rtant use and prayer, then-that will keep the helmet from being dulled, the swonl from being rusty. But: (1) Prayer must not be mere repetition. "And in praying," says our Lord, "uso not vain repetitions, as the Gentiles do." If we aro bent on having our request from God, it will come up again and again, and under now aspects. Prayer is using arguments with Goel, and, ns our mind works on our need, we shall ever be discovering new grounds on which to press our request. So, while wo arc to havo prayer for ourselves and prayer for others (supplication), it is to bo all prnycr and supplication, i.e. to say, it is to hnvc that vnriety which come~ from nn abumht11c1) of lifo, from aclivo thou«ht and fcelin~, and not that sameness which comes fron: lifelessness. (2) .Prayer ~ust not be irregular. 'l'he apostle teaches that it is to bo connected with all seasons (to vitalize them, to redeem them from nnpnfitablcnc,~). It is true that we aro not always in a moo,\ for praying; but let us keep the appoint eel season, Prayer is one of the means by which we aro to get into the right moou, And 284: THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. toH. VI. 1-24,

ifwe keep k' our plan from a sense of duty (though our feelings are cold), and when tb.e time c0mes round fall on our knees before God, then may we e::tpect liberation from our un;:piritua.l moods. (3) Prager tnust ,wt be from sel,f. "Praying in the Spirit," it i~ "-'lid here, and t.here is the same association in Jude 20. Prayer is dependence, and we h;;.<"e the infiue.nces of the Spirit on which to depend in prayer. We can only pray »right., nnder the impulse of the Spirit, when the Spirit indeed makes intercession for t:& .And, therefore, we should look to the Spirit tv pui; the right desires within us and t.:> gi,e us right words. 2. With petitions for ourselves toe a,-e to blend petitions _fur oth= "And watching thereunto in all perseverance and supplication." The apostle is here carrying forward his thought into a special channel While we are to ~ake h~ to be persevering in praying for ourselves, we are to be especially persevering Ill praying for others. And the ground of that may be that our prayers are apt to be characterized by selfishness. We may go on praying for ourselves; but we too soon give over praying for others. We unwarrantably (and to our own detriment) contract the circle of prayer. (1) Ofrcle of supplication. "For all the saints." That is not the outmost circle; for it is said in 1 Tim. ii. 1, "for all men." But the apostle is here presenting the matter under a special aspect. It is this, that the combatant is to remember his fellow-combatants. Every combatant has bis peculiar difficulties, his weak points. But, if he feels the struggle to be hard for himself, that should put him in sympathy with all others, to whom (in their own way) it is hard too. And he should manifest that sympathy by beseeching God to make their armour bright, to hold them np, to give them to win the day, wherever they are appointed to fight, (2) Special member of that cirde. "And on my behalf." (a) Special prayer he wishes them to offer for him. "That utterance may be given unto me in opening my mouth, r-0 make knoTil with boldness the mystery of the gospel." That is to say, boldness of utterance, whenever he was called upon to open his mouth in preaching the gospel. This was the great accomplishment of the apostle, that he could preach the gospel And he here disco,ers the secret of it. He put it clearly before his own mind, and got others interested in his object, so that they helped him by their prayers. (b) Special reason fur the prayer. " For which I am an ambassador in chains; that in it I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak." Reason of his offi~. He girded himself to save souls. He kept strict watch over his heart. He was swift-footed in proclaiming the message of peace. And as he sped from place to place, the fiery darts were thrown at him. Satan stirred up the Jews against him; men said that he was mad. But he interposed the shield of faith; he held up his head in the assurance of pardon. And he used the sword of the Spirit against many a heresy which threatened the peace o.nd prosperity of the Church. It was of great consequence that there should be preservctl to such a.n ambassador the courage of Lis office. Reason of hia position. He was o.t the time in chains. He was ia a condition, therefore, when his courage would be specially assailed. John the Baptist, in the gloom of his dungeon, gave way to doubts of Christ's mission. The apostle's liberty was not so much restricted. 'l'hat the liberty he had might be well used by him, that he might speak boldly as he ought to EJr.:ak, he would have them make that the subject of their prayers for him.-R. F.

, er&. 21-24.-.Affairs of tl<P- apostl-e:- L Wny he does f!Ot enter on them. "But fr.at ye also =y kDow my affairs, how I do, TychicllB . . . shall make known to you aJ things." He knew that they would be an.x.ioUB to Lave some account of his affairs. He would hal'"e gfren them a written account but for the fact that Tychicus, the bearer of hls letter to them, would be able to give them (and others too, it is implied) a more detailed account by word of mouth. We have already remarked on the absence of the personal in this rotl.ol,ic Epistle. The one exception is the introduction of the name of Tychlcna, and it is introduced to account for the absence of details about himself. In the Epistle 1.o the Colossians, along with the same reference to 'l'ychicus, there are numerolll! salutations. It favours the hypothesis of this being a circular letter (intended for a circle of which EphesUB was the centre), that none are conjoined with the apostle in sending salutations (the apostle alone may have been known to all the Churches~, and none are singled out as special objects for salutation (as in the one Church of ~olosBa!). 2. Qualifications of Tychicu,. "The beloved brother and faithful minister w the Lord." In Acts x.x.. 4 he is classed as an Asiatic. If be did not, then, belong to OH, VI. 1-24.] 'l'HE EPISTLE TO '£HE EPHESIANS, 285

the ea.me ~ity (Trophimus 11.'lsociated with him Wll.'l an Ephesian), he belonged to the same province, ~s tho~e ~ whom he conveyed the Jetter. Of more importance than his country Wll.'l his Christian character, for which the apostle vouches. He limits his consideration to t?e Christian sphere (where Christ appoints and animates), and, within that sphere, Tych1cus was both a beloved brother and faithful minister. He had those qualities of heart which attached men to him, an important element in a mission. He had also those qualities of conscience which, as they made him fit to be entrusted with the gospel, also made him fit for the special service required of him. 3. Definite statement of the object of his mission. "Whom I have sent unto you for this very purpose, that yo may know our state, and that he may comrort yonr hearts." A servant of the Church, he was, in the first instance ; but he was sent by Paul on this special errand. He was not only to communicate information to them regarding Paul, but also regarding Paul's companions in Rome. Through what he communicated, he would comfort their hearts. For the precise bea.rini,t of this we are left to conjecture. He might be able to tell them that the health of Paul and of such a fellow-prisoner as Aristarchus was not suffering from their confinement. He might be able to report that not only Paul, but all of them, were remaining steadfast in the faith of Christ. He might be able to announce some increased liberty in the preaching of the gospel. He might especially be able (with communicated apostolic fervour) to report the preaching of Paul, and himself to present the gospel as the means of comfort. DOUBLE BENEDICTION. 1. First benediction. " Peace be to the brethren, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." The source from which blessing is invoked is (as at the beginning of the Epistle) God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. There is given both the First Cause and the Second Cause. It belongs to God the Father (to whom can it more belong than to him?) to bless his children. Christ is the Second Cause, by whom God made the worlds, by whom also he redeemed aod blesses his people. He is, therefore, also invoked as the Source of ble~sing. (1) First blessing. "Peace be to the brethren." We are to understand "peace" here, as at the beginning of the,Epistle, in the sense of freedom from unrest, as being under the loving care of God. It may mean freedom from persecution, if that is lovingly arranged by God. It may also mean freedom from internal dissensions, if God sees fit to grant that. There is a limitation in the scope of the blessing compared with the langur1gc of the following benediction. We are• not to understand it as peace to the whole Church of Christ, but rather peace to the brethren to whom, in turn, the Epistle was to be sent round. (2) Second blessing. "And love with faith," The apostle (n.s he has done throughout) presupposes faith, but not as a fixed quantity. Rather does ho invoke it in its higher degrees, and, at the same time, invoke love as its concomitant. Let love not lag behind, but let it keep pace with faith. If we tum believingly to God ns our Fnther and Christ as our Saviour, we should also tum affectionately to the brethren. Let there he love (in all its beauty) to manifest the reality and activity of our faith. 2. Second benediction. "Grace be with all them that love our Lon.I Jcsu~ Christ in uncorruptness." The blessing. "Grace." 'l'his is to he understood as in other places. Let there be the outflowing of the Divine compassion. Let there be every litting manHestation of the Divine favour. The scope of the blessing. As to its form, it is catholic. It excludes selfishncsK and denominational jealousies, and takes in the whole circle which Christ acknowledges. As to matter, there are two things poin tc• l to, (1) The grand characteristic of the Christian is love to the Lord Jesus Cl11·i;t. The Christian is one who (appealed to by the Saviour) can say with Peter, "Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee." Such an affection as God has put into the nature of the child, of the parent, such (in its personal character, in its tenderness, in its strength) is to be our affection to Christ. Such a virtuous affection (as distinguished from natural affection) as we have toward the brethren, such, purified and heightened, is to be our affection toward the Master. The ground of virtuous affection is moral goodness, and especially one form of it, viz. holy benevolence. We love a man who, besides being conscientious, is filled with universal good will. So we love Christ because (with all dutifulness) he is the perfection of all unselfishness and benevolence toward men. In estimating his character (as an object for our love) we must take into account hie ,-ank in the universe, viz. that he was the Son of God. If a king and one of his subjects were both voluntarily to go into slavery for the purpose of redeeming 286 THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. [cH, VI, 1-24,

their c,mntry, t~c sac~ifice would be re,,oarded as greater on the part of the king than on the r-'lrt_ of his subject, There may be the _same patriotism; but there is something to}>_, r,:t_ c.own to the _rank. So all that Christ was and did is enhanced in proportion to the lmght from which he descended. It was not simply love to man in a human 1x,sit-ion, but lo.e that made infinite descent to bum in the human soul of Christ. We must also take into account the public capacity in which he acted. He was not ren- ,irring such help as we personally may render to one another. But he was the Christ the appointed Representative of all mankind. He had all our interests on his hands'. liis character comes out in the whole of his life. He evinced a universal benevolence: " Him thnt cometh unto me I will in no wise cast out." He was called the Friend of sinners. He loved men apart from their outward surroundings and natural capacities, he loved them as sinners in need of salvation. Especially does his character come out at the last. He went (in suffering the desert of sin) under that which is called the hiding of the Father's countenance. And it was not only dauntless trust in God, but unquenchable love to men, that maintained him there. He went down to the lowest depths for us (in experience the most terrible), that be might ca1Ty us with him to the heights. (2) .An indispensable element is pointed to in our love to Christ. "In uncorrupt- ness.." There is a spnrious love to Christ, which is founded on his sufferings withont reference to tbeir spiritnal me.ar;ing. "I wept when the waters went over his soul." Snch love, as it is not well founded, so also is it transient. The closing climactic thought hi this geat catholic Epistle is that our love to Christ is to have an immor- tafay, 8!! i~C-'c.!:iptibiliiy. M there was a deathless principle in his love to ns, so there i5 ro he a ceatb.less principle in onr lore tc him. It will have of this, according as it is fo=dai on the real excellence of Christ. The purer and clearer onr conception of ti.5 tran.scencient benevolence and beneficence, the more will our love have of undying ::na. erer-unfclding beanty.-R F.

entries.title: EPH 6:1–4
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-CAildnm and their parents. "Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right. Honour thy father and mother; which is the first command- ment with prvmise; that it may be well with thee, and thou mayest live long on the earth. And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath : but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord." In the preceding paragraph the apostle had treated of the relative duties of husbands and wives; here he directs attention to the relative duties of parents and chi"ldren. L 'l'HE DUTY OF CHILDREN. The words lead us to consider the nature and reason of the obligation which children owe to their parents. 1. The nature. The duty is: (1) "Obedience." "Children., obey your parents." This duty has its limitation. When, for example, the command is impracticable, it is not binding. When the parent makes demands surpassing the child's capacity, he is a tyrant, and the child is free from the obligation. Or when the command is morally wrong, when it clashes with the rights of conscience and the claiws of God, obedience to it is no duty, bnt would be a sin. The duty is obedience rendered in a Christian spirit. "In the Lord." Any conduct towards parents, man.kind in general, or to the great God, that is not inspired with lo.e to Christ, has T<O ffirtue in it. All acts to be acceptable to God must be dono io the name and spirit of his blessed Son. (2) "Honour." "Honour thy father and mother." That is, reverence them. This implies, of course, that they are hooour- " orthg. It is, alas! often the duty of children to abhor aud despise the character of their parents, because of its falsehood, intemperance, profligacy, and crime. Paul supposes parents to be what their relation to their children and God demands-pure, generous, and noble. Such pa.rents are to be honoured. Not to honour them is to dishonour God. 2. The reason. What is the reason for this obedience and reverence? (1) Because it is right. "For this is right." Nature teaches the rectitude of it. There is implanted in (;Very child's mind the feeling that he is bound to obey and reverence his parents. 'l'his feeling of obligation in some form or other is universal. 'l'hc Bible teaches the rectitude of it. It was ongraven by the finger of God on tho tables of stone; it was inculcated in the teaching and exemplified in the life of Jesus Chri.bt. (2) llecauro it is expedient. "That it may be well with thee, nnd thou may,ast live long on the earth." A hafJPY and a long lifo'depends·upon it. Children who are regardless of their filial duties wil be regardless of all others, and rendered liablo CII, VI, 1-24,] THE EPISTLE TO Tm~ EPHESIANS. 287

to fall into those habits of depravity which will render their life e. misery, and cut short their days on the earth, II. 'l'HE DUTY OF PARENTS, The duty of parents is here set forth in two forms, negatively and positively. 1. Negatively. "Ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath." The temper of a child is of transcendent moment; it is that which determines his character and destiny, To act upon that temper in its opening years so as to fret and sour it is to do an incalculable mischief. Against this evil it is the duty of parents strenuously to guard. Petty interferences, trivial prohibitions, incessant chidings, and an irritable spirit, are the things in parental conduct which "provoke children to wrath." 2. Positively. "But bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord." 'rrain their faculties, bring out their latent powers, teach them to think with accuracy, to love with purity, to act with adroitness ~nd pro~ptitude. D? this by aclmonishing them "in the Lord." Let the lessons of rnstruchon and warmng be drawn from the existence, the life, the character, and the teachings of the Lord, 'rhe child's faculties cannot be developed apart from God. Secular education is a contradiction in terms; it is as great a solecism as a sunless vegetation. Let parents look well to the minds of their children. 'l'he farmer who neglects the culture of bis fields will soon have his acres overrun with thorns and briars and noxious weeds; and the parent who neglects the culture of his child will soon discover evils far more hideous and disastrous. The following from the quaint pen of smart old Fuller will be read with interest aucl profit on the subject:-" The good parent. He sboweth them, in his own practice, what to follow and imitate; and, in others, what to shnn and avoid. For though 'the words of the wise be as nails fastened by the masters of the assemblies' (Eccles. xii. 11), yet, sure their examples are the hammer to drive them in, to take the deeper hold. A father that whipped his son for swearing, and swore himself whilst he whipped him, did more harm by his example than good by his correction. He doth not welcome and embrace the first essays of sin in his children. Weeds are counted herbs in th·e beginning of spring : nettles are put in pottage, and salads are made of eldern buds. 'l'hus fond fathers like the 01,ths and wanton talk of their little children, and please themselves to hear them displease God. But our wise parent both instructs his children in piety and with correction blasts the first buds of profaneness in them, He that will not use the rod on his child, his child shall be used as o. rod on him. He allows his children mainteuance according to their quality. Otherwise it will make them base, :i.cquaint them with bad company and shocking tricks; and it makes them surfeit the sooner when they come to their estates, It is observed of camels, that having travelled long without water through sandy deserts, implentur, cum ln"bendi est occasio, et in prreteritum et in futurum (' when they find an opportunity they fill thernsel ves both for the past and the future'); and so these thirsty heirs soak it when they come to their means, who, whilst their fathers were living might not touch the top of their money, and think they shall never feel the bottom of it when they are dead. In choosing a profession, he is directed by his child's disposition, whose inclination is tho strongest indenture to bind him to a trade. But when they set Abel to till the ground, aud send Cain to keep sheep; Jacob to hunt, and Esau to live in tents; drive some to school, and others from it; they commit a violence on nature, and it will thrive accordingly. Yet be humours not bis child when he m:i.kes an unworthy choice bene:i.lh himself, or rather for ease than use, pleasure than profit. If his son proves wild, he doth not cast him off so far but he marks the place where he lights. With the molhcr of Mose11. he doth not suffer his son so to sink or swim but he leaves one to stnnd :i.rar off to watch what will become of him (Exod. ii. 4). He is careful, while quenched his luxury, not withal to put out his life; the rather, because their souls who have broken and run out in their youth have proved the more healthful for it afterwards. He moves him to marriage rather by argument drawn from bis good tb:i.n his own authority. It is a style too princely for a paront herein to 'will nnd commnnd;' but, suro, ho m:i.y will and desire. Affections, like the conscience, are rather to be led than drawn; nnd it is to be feared, they that marry where they do not love, will love where they do not marry. Ho doth not give away his loaf to his children nnd then come to them for a piece of bread. Ho holds tho reins (though loosely) in his own hands; nnd keeps, to rnward duty and punish undutifulness, Yet, on good occasion, for his children's <iuvaucoment, he will depart from :rart of his mrnns. Daso is their nature who will noL 288 THE EPISTLE 'l'O THE EPHESIANS. fOH. VI. 1-24,

have their branches lopped till their body be felled; and will let go none of their goods, a~ if it pre..saged their speedy death; whe1:eas it doth not follow that _he tha~ puts oft h!s cl0:1k must present)Y: go to bed. On his death-bed he bequeaths his blessmg to nll his children. Nor reJ01ceth he so much to leave them great portions as honestly obtained. ~nlr: money well and ~w~ully gotte:1- is good and lawful money. .And if he leaves _his ~h1ldren young, ~e prmc1_pally nommates God to be their guardian; and, next to him, 1s ~reful to appomt provident overseers. The good child. He reverenceth the person of his parent, the old, poor, and froward. As his parent bore with him when a child, he bears with his parent if twice a child ; nor doth his diguity above him cance_~ his duty_ unto him. Wben _Sir Thomas ~ore was Lord Chancellor of England, a::id t;ir John his father one of the Judges of the King's Bench, he wouJd in Westminster Hall beg his blessing of him on his knees. He observes his lawful commands and practiseth his precepts with all obedience. I cannot, therefore, excuse St. Barbara' from 'tntiutiiulness, and occasioning her own death. The matter this: her futher, beina a f'3::,<"&D., commanded his workmen, building his house, to mnke two windows in a room": Barbara., knowing her father's pleasure, in his absence enjoined them to make three, that., seeing them, she might the better contemplate the mystery of the Holy Trinity. Methinks two windows might as well have raised her meditations, and the light arising from both would as properly have minded her of the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son. Her father, enniged at his return, thus came to the knowledge of her religion, and accused her to the magistrate, which cost her her life. Having }Jractised, then. himself, he euiails his parents' precepts on his posterity. Therefore such instructions are by Solomon (Prov. i. 9) compared to frontlets and chains (not to a suit of clothes, which serves but one, and quickly,wears out, or out of fashion), which have in them a real lasting worth, and are bequeathed as legacies to another age. The same counsels observed, are chains to grace, which, neglected, prove halters to strangle undutiful children. He is a stork to his parent, and feeds him in his old age. Not only if his futher bath been a pelican, but though he bath been an ostrich unto him, and neglected him in his youth. He confines him not a long way off to a short pension, forfeited if he comes in his presence, but shows piety at home, and learns as St. Paul saitb (1 Tim. v. 4) to requite his parent. .And yet the debt (I mean only the principal, not connting the interest) cannot fully be paid. And therefore he compounds with his father, to accept in good worth his ntmOIJt endeavour. Such a child God commonly re"'ards lrith long life in this world. If he chance to die young, yet he lives long that li,es well; and time misspent is not lived, bnt lost. Besides, God is better than his promise, if he takes him a long lease, and gives him a freehold of better value. As for disobedient children: if preserved from the gallows, they are reserved for the rack, to be tortured by their own posterity. One complained that never father had so undutiful a son as he had. 'Yes,' said his son, with less grace than truth, 'my grandfather had.' I conclude this subject with the example of a pagan's, which will shame most Christians. Pomponius Atticus, making the funeral oration at the death of his moth;r, did protest that, living with her three score and seven years, he was never reconciled to her, se n'Ul1UXf_'IJ,am matre in gratiam rediisse, because there never happened betwixt them the least jar which needed reconciliation."-D. T.

entries.title: EPH 6:5–9
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Servants and their masters. "Servants," etc. There are two thoughts underlying these verses. 1. The ezistence of social distinctions amongst men. There are masters and servants, ruJers and subjects. 'l'hese distinctions are no accidental phases of society, they grow out of the constitution of ~hing~. Diversity in the temperaments, tastes capacities, and circUIDBtances of men give rise to masters and servants. 2. 'I'he one ,pirit which is to guvern men of all distinctions. 'l'he rich and the poor, the sovereign and his subject, the ~ter and the servant, are under an obliga~ion ~ be animat~ hy the same moral spmt, and controlled by the same moral conmderation. "All in all things should do the will of God from the heart." L TEE DUTY ov SERVANTS. The duty of servants, of course, is obedience. "Be obedie::it to them that are your masters." But the obedience is here cb~terizcd. 1. It is obedience in bodily maUers. "According to the flesh." Their service is limited to secular concerns thincrs that have reference to the material and temporal interests of their masters. They "':re to give their muscles, ~nd their limbs, 1md their contriving cu. '\'I, 1-24.] 'l'HE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. 289

faculties, but not their souls. "Consciences and souls were made to be the Lord's alone." 2. It is obedience honestly rendered. "With fear and trembling in singleness of your heart"-" not with eye-service." These expressions mean that there should be no duplicity, no double-dealing, but downright honesty in everything. .A servant is bound to be honest towards his employer. He has no right to be lazy or wasteful. He has contracted to give, on certain stipulated conditions, his energies and time to promote the secular interests of his master. 3. It is obedience inspired with the religious spirit. 'l'hey are to regard themselves in everything as the servants of Christ, and are bound to do the "will of God from the heart." In everything the authority of Christ must be held 11s supreme. Whatsoever is done in word or deed should be done all to the glory of God. 4. It is obedience which, if truly rendered, will be rewarded of God. "Knowino- that whatsoever good thing any man doeth, the same shall he receive of the Lord, whether he be bond or free." 'l'he faithful servant may feel that the wages he receives from his earthly master a.re unjustly inadequate. Yet the great Master will award to him at last an ample compensation. Whatsoever good thing he bas done, however trivial, shall meet its reward at last. The good thing must be rewarded. Goodness carries evermore its own reward. II. THE DUTY OF MASTERS. The way in which masters should exercise their authority is here indicated. 1. They are to exercise it religiously. "Ye masterR, <lo the same things unto them." "The same things," as we have said, do not mean tho snme work, but the same spiritual attributes. Servants are to be honest and respect the will of God in all; the masters are here bound to do " the same things." Both arc to be under the domination of the same moral spirit. 2. 'l'bey aro to exercise it magnanimously. "Forbearing threatening." Though the servant may by accident, or, what is worse, by intent, by omission, or by commission, try severely the temper of his master, his master should forbear threatening. He should show his right to be a master by governing his own soul. The man who takes fire at every offence, whoso eyes flash with rage, and lips mutter threats, is too little a creature to be a master. He has no licence from Heaven to rule either children, servants, or citizens, who is not magnanimous in soul. 3. They are to exercise it responsibly. "Knowing that you1 Master also is in heaven." They are amenable to God for the way in which they use their authority. 'l'he master hns the same Lord as the servant, and they mUllt stand at last together at the great tribunal. To that Master all social distinctions vanish in the presence of moral charnctor. " Neither is there respect of persons with him."-D.T.

entries.title: EPH 6:10–20
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Soul-mi'litancy. "Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord," etc. The subject of these words is soul-militancy, and they bring under our notice the soul's foes, the soul's strength, the soul's weapons, and the soul's religiousness. I. THE eom'e FOES. "We wrestle not against flesh and blood." Tho passage teaches the following things in relation to the antagonists of souls :-1. 'l'hey arc spiritual personalities. They are spiritual, not" flesh and blood." 'l'hey exist apart from matter-apart from all animal incarnations. 'l'hey are personalities. We cannot accept the interpretation of tbose~wbo regard Paul as speaking here only of evil principles. If language means anything, personal agents are here indicated. A priori reasoning renders the existence of such beings probable; human experience and the Bible place their existence beyond all reasonable doubt. 2. They are wicked personalities. "Spiritual wickedness," or, as the margin has it," wicked spirits." They are out of sympathy with God; they are in bitter and practical hostility to all that is Divine, benevolent, and happy. 3. They are diverse personalities. 'l'hey differ in their make and their rank; they are not all of the same nature and measure of faculty, nor of the same rank in the uuiverse. There are "principalities," "rulers," and "powers" amongst them. Some, as compared to others, may be as wasps to vultures, as mosquitoes to dragons. 4. They are organized principalities. They are under one head, here called the "devil." "That ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil." There is one gigantic intellect that manages and marshals the whole: be who seduced our first parents, be with whom Christ battled in the wilderness-the Satan of God, the .Apollyon of man. These boats of evil spirits are not left to themselves; they are welded together by one master inlellect. "Devil with devil damned firm concord EPHESIANS. C 290 THE EPISTLE TO 'l'HE EPHESIANS. [oH, VL 1-21.

hold." They are managed by force and frnud, all of them. Tho passage sui(gests that under his control they act: (l) Craftily. Hence the expression, the "wiles of tho dc,-il." All his movements are cunningly methodized, for such is the meanin" of the "w:l ". wiles." These eYil spirits attack us in ambush; they steal upon us slyly a.nu s:e.'.1,tluly. (2) In da.rl.,'fless, "The rulers of the darkness of this world." Where do t h<'y reign? Where ignorance spreads her gloom : in the cold region of atheism where the mental energies are benumbed, and in the tropic realm of superstition where the soul is stirred into an agony of fear and scared 'l\ith the horrid forms of its own crrotk1ns. Amidst the gloomy recesses of ignorance they rear their throne· throu"'h the di~tricts of intellectual darkness they prowl about in search of their l)rey. Th~y reign where dcpraYity beclouds the heart, nhere passion is stronger than principle, the s~nses than the soul, the Joye of the world than the love of God; whether that be amidst the districts of heathenism or civilized life, in the marts of business, the temples of devotion, or the flowery scenes of gaiety aud pleasure. They enshrine themselves amidst the benighted chambers of an impure imagination, they haunt the atmospher& of pollution, impregnate it with their spirit, causing it to stimulate the unrighteous zeal of the selfish, to fire the passions of the carnal, and to swell the vanity of the ambitious and the proud. They reign where sorrow and suffering darken all. They delight in misery. The wretchedness of the indigent, the sighs of the distressed, the groans of the oppressed, and the agonies of the dying gratify their maligna.nt natUies. IL THE souL's STRENGTH. "Finally, my brethren, be stroag in the Lord, and in the power of his might." The soul requires tremendous strength to grapple successfully with these mighty spirits of evil. What is the strength required? It is nothing less than Dimne. It is to be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might. But what kind of Divine strength is required, for strength of all kind is from the Lord? Is it muscular 1 No. Samson, with his hercnle.an physical force, fell beneath these spirits; an en! genins touched him, and the giant fell as a child. Is it mental 1 No. Men of the greatest intellect and of the loftiest genius have not been able to stand for a moment before these spirits. It is not by this "might or this power" that souls can stand before these infernal hosts. It is moral strength. l. The strength of faith in tf.e .Absoluu. Faith in that which changes not, which is true to man as man, which is independent of times and circumstances-faith in the Everlasting. With this faith men participate in the omnipotence of God, work wonders, and dare the universe. Men, through this faith, have "subdued kingdoms," etc. 2. The strength of love for the Sup'T"emely good. Love, when it is fastened even upon the frail and the imperfect, gives strength to the soul-strength to nerve a mother for the most trying services, strength tn brace a patriot for the thunders of the battle. But when centred upon the eternally Good, its strength is increased a thousandfold ; it gives the soul a power that " never faileth," a power that" endureth all things." 3. .An invincible attachment to the rig/it, To "be strong in the Lord" is to be strong in sympathy with the right. It is to prefer the right with hell to the wrong with heaven. It is this moral strength alone that will enable ns to "stand against the wiles of the devil," and to battle successfully with the host of wickedness. 'l'his strength makes a man more than a conqueror, enables him to glory in tribulation and shout tiiumphantly in tho agonies of death. ill THE soUL's WEAPOBS. 'l'he panoply is here described'. It consists of two parte-tbe defen.sive and the offensive implements. 1. '!'he defensive implements. What is the defensive? "Truth." This is the girdle which belts the loins with strength, and binds all the other parts of the panoply together so as to protect all the Yitai parts. "Righteousness." This is the" breastplate." The man who lacks integrity can offer no successful defence to the foe; the dishonest man is vulnerable at every point. "The gospel of peace." This, like the boot of the old Roman conqueror, makes the soldier firm in his step and terrible in the echo of bis tread. "Faith." This is the "shield," protecting the whole body. Faith, not in creeds, but in Christ, is the true shield of moral soldiership. "Salvation "-that is, the hope of salvation. This is the " helmet." As the helmet guarded the head of the Roman soldier, the hope of salvation protects the 59ul. Let despair come, and the hea.d of the soul is wounded and the whole syMtem enda.agered. 2. The offensive. What is the o1Tensivc? "The eword of the Spirit." 'l'he true soul has not only to stand its ground, to maintain its position, to keep its territory, but to advance, to extend its boundaries, to prosecute an

invasion; it ie to conquer all other 60uls to Christ, and the weapon is the "Word of God." '!'hie ie the sword by which the Christian soldier has to cut his way from soul to soul through the wholo world: "For the Word of Goo, is quick and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword," etc. (Heb. iv. 12). God's Word is the truth that slays error, the love that slays- selfishness, the right that slays the wrong, the happiness that slays the misery of the world. IV. 'l'HE som.'s RELIGIOUSNESS. Religiousness, viz. a conscious dependence on God, lies at the foundation of all true soul-milit.'\ncy, A man can do nothino- ril7htly or successfully in spiritual soldiership who is not religious in the very spirit if his being. Ticligiousness is the only soil in which man's spiritual faculties can grow into heroic vigour. In materialism they wither; in mere intellectualism they are only skeletonic at best; in religiousness they are like the tree planted by the rivers of water,-their roots are in the Everlasting, they drink into them the very life of God. Religiousness, in one word, is the source that supplies the muscle and the instinct that giveM the skill in true moral warfare. It teaches our "hands to war and our fingers to fight." This religiousness is here <lescribed by the apostle in these words," Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication for all saints," etc. These words are so true to the original and so obvious in their significance that they call for no minute examination. 'l'bcy show us how this religiousness in the soul of the true spiritual soldier is to express itself; and it is to do so: 1. In prayer. "Praying always with all prayer," or, as Ellicott bas rendered it, "with all prayer and supplication praying always in the Spirit." The words tea.eh us: (1) That the prayer is to be comprehensive. "With all prayer and supplication.n All kinds of prayer, expressed and ejaculatory, private and social. Prayer is not so much a service as a spirit, not so much an a.et as a sentiment. Hence we are commanded to "pray without ceasing." Consciousness of dependence on God, which is tho very essence of prayer, shonld run as a living current through the whole of our life. Our whole life should be an unbroken litany, (2) 'l'hat the prayer is to be Divine. "fo tho Spirit." That is, under the influence of the Divine Spirit, who is to make intercessions for us with groanings that cannot be uttered. 'l'here is no true prayer that is not dictated by this Spirit. Man's great care should be to lay bis sonl open to tbo Divine. If a man would have his body crave healthily for food, be must drink in as much as possible the fresh air of God; and if he wonld have his soul cravo for spiritual food, he must breathe into bis spiritual nature the breath of the Divino. (3) '!'hat tho prayer is to be watchful. " And watching thereunto." '!'be soul bas its moral moods. It bas seasons fovourable for culture, weathers for launching out on the deop. Its duty is to watch for these moods-watch the motions of the Divine Spirit upon tho heart. Watch, as Elijah did on Carmel, for promising signs in the heavens, (4) '!'bat tho pmyer should be persevering. "With all perseverance." ,ve aro to bo instant in J)myer. Our Saviour taught tho duty of importunnto prayer in tho parable of tho "unjust judge." Importunity is needed, not to influence the Eternal to mercy, but to proparo our hearts rightly to receive his gifts. 2. In prayer for the good in general. "For all saints." 'l'ho npostlo would not have them merely to pray for thcmselve8. He who prays exclusively for himself never prays nt nil. His prayers nro but the breath of selfishness. Paul required them to pray for "all saints "-saints of every intellectual grade, of every social position, of every ecclesiastical sect, of every theo- logical school, of every kingdom and every tribe. Why for all saints? Bccauso all saints are members of the grand army battling against tho common foo-against tho "principalities of evil," etc. The more force, courage, skill, each member of an army possesses, the better for the cause, the more likely the victory in whoso ndvantagcs all participate. 'l'he battle of Christianity is a common battle-a battlo against error, wrong, and depravity everywhere. All snints are engaged in it, and they should be pro.yed for. 3. In prayer for gospel ministers in particular. "And for me, that utterance may be given unto me." Why does Paul wish them to pray for him? Is it that be might be liberated from prison? No. Ho was now, ho tolls us, an" ambassador in bonds." '!'he clanking chains of the prison hung heavily on him, and one would not have wondered ir bis first request had been to tho Ephesians to pray for his bodily deliverance. But this ho dues not. Ho is too absorbed in tho causo of Christ and universal happincs8 for thi~. What he prayed for was that ho might be cnal,Ierl 292 THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. [OH, TI, 1-24,

properly and successfully to pre11ch the g°!!pel. "That I may opan my mouth boldly, to make kn?wn the mystery of the ~os~l, that ~ the gospel that was once a mystery. :he preachm~ of the gospel ~ Gods grand instrument for restoring the world t-0 mtelhgence, d1gmty, and happiness, and because of that, he desired to do it in the most effective way. There are several remarkable things in these words. (1) Paul was an ambassador from heaven-God's messenger sent to proclaim restoration to fost humanity. The grandest commission this. (2) God's ambassado1· from heaven in bonds. Wonderful that the great King, whose word could have shivered Rome into atoms should have allowed his ambassador to have been in chains. But so it is; and we ;hall have an explanation ere long. (3) God's ambassador from heaven in bonds, losing all idea of his own pers()'ff(i/, sufferings, in the desire to help his race. Though a prisoner at Rome he was permitted to preach (Act.<! xxviii. 30, 31). And as a prisoner he wanted t~ discharge that high mission in the most effective way. For that he prays. A true gospel minist.er has a right to ask the prayers of Christians for him particularly. Like a general in the army, he has the most responsible position, the most arduous task. Failure in him may tum the tide of battle in favour of the foe. Prayer, then, is a necessary qnali.6.cation of spiritual soldiership. The victory cannot be won without it. "Restraining prayer, we cease t.o fight: Prayer makes the Christian's armour bright : And Satan trembles when he sees The weakest saint npon his knees." Even the great Commander of all the legions of the good recognized the mighty power of prayer during his struggles on this e.arth. "Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels?" As if he had i-aid, "With one breath of prayer I could bring the mighty battalions of eternity to my aid."-D. 'l'.

entries.title: EPH 6:21–24
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Types of tra,nscendent 11irluea. "But that ye also may know," etc. In these verses we Lave three types of transcendent virtues-a type of elevated friend- ship, a type of spiritual benevolence, and a type of Christian catholicity. L .A TYPE OF ELEVATED FRIENDSHIP. Pan! here does two things which show the purity and the worth of his friendship. 1. Introduces a noble man to his friends, Some are very anxions to keep their friends to themselves, and, if possible, to monopolize thcir thoughts and their hearts; and some, if they introduce a friend at all, only those of an inferior type. Paul introduces Tychicus, "a beloved brother and faithful minister." Yon cannot confer a greater benefit on your friends than to commend to their confidence a noble man; the gift of such a man to them is more valuable than lordly estates or mighty kingdoms. 2. He introd'IJeU a noble man to their friendship entirely for their own advantage. There are those who introduce men to their friends fur the sake of getting something fur them; bnt not so in this case. Paul does not ask them to do anything for Tychicus ; nor does he ask them to send back through Tychicus any favour to hiru. He sends 'l'ychicus in order to serve them in two ways. (1) To satisfy their anxieties as friends. They would naturally be anxious to know something concerniog the "affairs" of the man who lived and laboured in their city for three years, and arormd whose neck their fathers fell in tears when he bade them adieu. They would like to know how this their father in Christ fared now a prisoner ill Rome. To satisfy the natural craving of their hearts, he now sends Tychicus; he would tell them alL I should like to have seen Tychicus deliver this letter, and to have heard the thousand cager questions. (2) 'l'o promote their happiness as Christians. " And that he might comfort your hearts." Paul knew well the trials to which the Church at Ephe51ll! was exposed, both from Jews and pagans. He knew they wanted comfort. The letter he sent abounded with comforting thoughts, and he knew that a loving brother like Tychicus would skilfully and efficaciously apply the healing balm. Here is- Il. A TYPE OP SPIRITUAL BENEVOLENCE. Panl'e heart goes out in well-wishing. Ar,d what did be wish for his brethren at Ephesus? No secondary favours, but the highest t1"'1'sings fr,,m God the Father and hie blessed Son. 1. Divine peace. "Peace bt tc, tle brethren." Mark where the peace comes from-" From God the Father and OH, VI, 1-24.] THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. 293

the Lord Jesus Christ." There is a peace that does not come from that source-a. peace that comes from the devil, a moral stagnation of soul, something like the stillness of that murky atmosphere that nurses and forbodes the thunder, the lightning, and the hurricane which spread devastation over sea and land. 'l'he peace of God is: (1) Peace of an approving conscience. (2) Peace of conscious security. (3) Peace of accordant affections. (4) Peace of hannonions activities. 2. A confunction of love and faith. "Love with faith." There is a love and also a faith that are not of Heaven. Divine love and faith are always united in a good man. Divine faith "works by love," works by love as the labourer works by the sun. These are the blessings spiritual benevolence desires for men, and they are in truth the germs of all good. Give me these, and I want no more. Out of them my Paradise will bloom; they are the nebulre which will one day encircle me with the brightest of heavens. Give the race these, and soon all crimes, sufferings, discords, miseries, will cease. III. A TYPE OF CHRISTIAN CATHOLICITY. "Grace be with all them that love our Lord Jesus "-love him purely, love him iu reality, love him as he ought to be loved. Wherever they are, in whatever land, of whatever tribe or kingdom, happiness to them. The language of modern sects is-Grace be to all them that are Baptists, Methodists, Independents, Episcopalians, etc. The language of the true Christian catholicity is -" Grace be to all them that love our Lord Jesus Christ," of all creeds or no creed, Churches or no Church. CoNCLUSION, Here end our reflections on this wonderful Epistle. Our walk through this section of the great garden of truth, whose aromas have refreshed, whose beauty has charmed, and whose objects have challenged our thoughts and excited our devout admiration, is now ended. Should others follow our footsteps with keener eyes and finer senses, more apt to discover the beautiful and the good, they will be able to discover for themselves, and reveal to others, much more than we have done. ·when we began our walk we were afraid that we should meet some of those grim Calvinian dogmas which certain theologians assured us were there, but we never met their shadow. '!'here are no theological weeds and thistles here. All is free and fresh as nature, as fitted to the human soul as light to the eye and breath to the lungs.-D. T.

entries.title: EPH 6:1–4
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-0hildren a.nd parents. Christianity purifies aud elevates family lifr. It is supremely natural, orderly, and reasonable in the treatment of domestic affairs. We meet with frequent allusions to families and households in the New Testament. The order and health of the home are clearly recognized as of primary importance. This is seen in the treatment of parental relations. I. THE DUTIBS OF OHILDREN To THEIR PARENTS. 1. The duties. (1) Obedience. A condition of subjection is necessary and right for childhood. Children must be taught to reverence an authority above them and to yield their will to a higher will. Thus the first principle of what, in after life, must be the fundamental relation to God, i~ instilled. Children should obey, for the very sake of obedience, orders for which at present they see no reason, and from which they can foresee no good results. But thero is a limit to obedience. "Obey your parents in the Lord." When parents command what is plainly contrary to the will of Christ, disobedience becomes a duty, (2) Honour. It is not enough to obey in act. Love and reverence should he found in the heart of children. It is most injurious for children to lose reverence for their parents. '!'hey are themselves degraded when this is the case. 2. The grounds on which these duties to parents are enforced. (1) It is right. '!'his comes first. It is au appeal to conscience, No obedience or honour can be of worth when only low, selfish motives prompt the performance of filial duty. (2) It is profitable. In the long run the principle that underlies the ancient promise of the fifth commandment is abundantly exemplified. Family life is the root of social order. When this is corrupt that will be upset. Good domestic habits are the safeguards of the best kind of conservatism, The most frightful revolutions are those that begin at the family hearth, II. Tm: DUTIES OF PARENTS TO CHILDREN, The family relation is reciprocal, anrl so are the duties of parents and children, It is most unreasonable to expect tho children to discharge their share of domestic duty if parents, who have so much larger knowledge and experience and whose example is tho most powerful instructor of their children, fail in theirs. 'l'o stern Roman fathers the Christian view of parental duty Tirn EPISTLE TO 'l'IIE EPHESIANS. [OH, VI. 1-24.

was novel. Even now it is too little re,,"'Mlled. 1. The negative dvty. " Provoke not yonr children _to wrath." W11ile strictly enforcing n~essary commands, parents should be most caretul not to lay on the shoulders of their children unnecessary burdens. Ol>< dience is hard_ e~ou~h _tm~er the best of circumst.ances. Especially is it desirable

not to provoke chlld1sh 1mtat1on by hasty, harsh manners when a wiser kinder method might be more effiCRcious in securing obedience and respect. 2. Th~ positive duty. "~~rture the~ in the _chas~uing and admonition of the Lord." The parent is the ~pmtual guard11m of his children. He cannot delegate to another the responsibility that God will some day call him to account for. In caring for their children's health, happiness, and worldly prospects, etc., parents are often least anxious about the most essential point, the spiritual welfare of their family. Let it be remembered that the first requisite in training children for Christ is that the parents should be themselves his disciples.-W. F. A.

Vers. &--9.-Servants and masters. The early preacherR of the gospel were wise in 11ot provoking futile and fatal attempts at a social revolution by denouncing slavery. Nevertheless, they laid the foundation of that revolution and secured its peaceable and bloodless accomplishment. Slavery could not permanently survive the establishment of the principle of Christian brotherhood. :Meanwhile under the then existing circum- stances Christianity taught certain necessary duties of slaves and masters, the essential ideas of which apply to so much of the present state of society as is at all analogous to that of the first cenrory. - L TllE DtJ'IlES OF SEBVA.?s""TS. 1. TM duties. (1) Obedience. The position of se..·,i.::e, w!letber Ltroed as in sla,a-y or freely accepted. as among us, implies obedience. Inaet'd, whEre t.be condition of service is volantarily entered upon for the sake of adequate payment t.he duty is so much the stronger. The disobedient servant commits a double sin; he is unfa.ithful to his engagement, and he is robbing his master of unearned. wages. (2) Singleness of heart. Half-hearted service is semi-disobedience. (3) Ko eye-service. How common is this degrading and dishonest ha.bit in all walks of life, from that of the ma.id who is idle when her mistress is a.way, to that of the states- man who works for what will win the applause of the multitude to the neglect of the real welfare of the nation, or the preacher who preaches popular sermons to catch the i.:ar of the congregation and hides unpopular truths that men much need to hear I (4) Serving the Lord. We are all to serve Christ in our daily work. 'fhis consecrates tbe most menial task. 2. The reward. Gross injustice characterized the old-world treatment of slaves, and tempted to disloyal service. This injustice will not be seen at the great reckoning. The slave will be as fairly judged as his master. The lowliest work will win as high a reward as the most pretentious if the motive is equally good. Here iB an inducement to faithfulness in little things. IL THE D17TIES OF ll.ASTERS. It was hard to teach a slave-holder his duty. Yet it is fair to observe that in ma.ny households the rigour of servitude was much softened, and kinder and more humane relations maintained than those that sometimes characterize our modern commercial connection of workman and employer, relations out of which all humanity seems to have vanished. It is interesting to see that in the :Kew Testament a hired servant is considered to be worse off than a household slave (e.g. Luke xv. 17). 1. The duties. (1) Fairness. "Do the same things unto them." 'l'he duties are reciprocal. Masters have no right to expect more devotion to their interests from their servants than they show to their servants' interests. (~) Kindness. "Forbear threatening." It is cowardly to use the power of the purse, as old masters used the whip, to gain an unfair advantage over a servant. In the end sympathy and genial friendliness will secure the best service. 2. The motives, (1) Servants and masters have one common Master. Both are alike servants of Christ; both must give account to him of their stewardship. (2) Christ will judge without respect of persons. The advantages of social superiority are but temporary. They will be of no use at Christ's judgment.-W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 6:10
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Divine strength. Al> the Epistle draws to a close, St. Paul gives emphasis to the reg_uibition of Divine strength by singling it out for a final word of exhortation. The dr.K;\rinAI principles of the earlier chapters lead up to the practical duties of on. v1. 1-2·!.] 'l'HE EPISTLE 'l'O 'l'HE EPHESIANS. 295

the later, and these several duties to the need of Divine strcn"th wherewHh to dischar"e them in face of the assaults of evil. I. CIIRIBTIANS ARE EXHORTED TO BE BTBONG, Spiritual strength is decision of character and forco of will. Religion centres in our will and character. Un less there is strength, fixity, determination, and energy, then all our elaborate thinking and all our beautiful sentiments are worthless. 1. Clear belief in the gospel is not sufficient. We may believe intellectually, but if we are too weak to act according to our belief that counts for nothing. 2. Feelings of love to Christ are vain if they do not inspire us to faithful service and sacrifice. 3. Passive reliance on Christ will not avail us unless we have also the active faith that puts forth spiritual strength in obedience to his will. We are not only to flee to the refuge in Christ. We are to go forth to battle in the open field. .And then we are not only to be endued with Divine armour, but first to be made strong ourselves. First comes the exhortation to be strong, and only second that to arm in the Divine panoply. It is only the strong man who can wear this armour. 4. It is our duty to be strong. Weakness is not merely a calamity to be bewailed. It is a sin to be repented of. It leads to our falling into temptation and our failing in duty. II. SPIBITUAL STRENGTH IS A DIVINE INSPIRATION. We cannot be strong by merely willing to be so. A wish will not convert the feeble body of the invalid into the robust frame of a healthy man, nor will a wish give to the weak soul fixity of character and energy of will The body must gain strength through nourishing diet, bracing air, exercise, etc. So spiritual strength arises from feeding upon Christ in faith and prayer. 1. There is might in Christ. He is the Lion of the house of Judah. 2. Christ puts forth that might. The strength is the might in exercise. The oak is strong, but passive, and therefore it can do nothing for us. The horse, though less strong, puts forth his power in action, and so works for us. Christ's great might is not a mere latent force. It flows out in energy. 3, This strength is ours by our union with Christ. "Be strong in the Lord." We must, therefore, be in Christ in order that we may have this strength, and the more close our union to Christ becomes the more vigorously shall we be supplied with his strength.-W. l!'. A.

entries.title: EPH 6:12
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-The/oe. The Christian life is a warfare. In order to wage this successfully we must understand the nature of the foes we have to contend with, because the weapons and armour will have to be selected according to the character of tho attack thnt is made upon us. I. 'l'HE NATURE OF TIIE FOE. 1. Negatively considered. (1) Not material. Imagination has given the tempter a material form, e.g. in the legends of St. Anthony, because it is so much easier to grapple with the most fearful enemy that can bo seon and touched than with an invisible, intangible foe. But our foe is not of flesh and blood. 'l'he subjugation of the physical world is easy compared with the task of conquering this invisible enemy. (2) Not human. It is hard enough to think of the obstructive nnd tempting influence of bad men. But we have something worse to re8ist. ,vo aro attacked by an unearthly army. The black tide of hellish sin surges against the shores of our human world and bespatters us with its withering spray. 2. Positively con- sidered. (1) Spiritual. The fact that the word "immaterial" has come to menu "unimportant," is a striking proof of our earthly-mindedness. 'l'he spiritual workl is the most real world. These spiritual foes are the most truly existing enemies we can ever meet. Our experience of them is in spiritual attacks, i.e. in temptations. (2) Dominant. They ure "world-rulers," they are in "heavenly" (or high) places. When St. Paul wrote this Epistle evil was uppermost in the world. Is it not also supremo in many regions now? We have to oust the forces that hold the field and to storm the citadel. II. THE ORABAOTEB OF THE WARFARE. Medireval armour is useless before rifle- bullets. Old castle walls are no protection against modern artillery. Nor will modem cannon drive back noxious gases. Sennacherib's hosts were powerless before that invisible angel of God, the pestilenco. So the foe in the Christian warfare determines the character of the armour and weapons and the tactics to be pursued. 1. Negatively. (1) Physical force will not servo us. Samson's strength is of no avail against teruplb- tion. Money, material resources, scientific skill, arc useless. This is the age of steam, 296 'l'HE EPISTLE '.l.'O 'l'Hbi EPHESIANS. (ol:I. VL 1-24,

steel, and electricity. But such things give us no help in subduing greed, lust, and se\fwill. (2) Httman i11fluen°" is vain. Arguments, threats, and promises; influences of authority and of sympathy; appeals to the reason, the feelings, and the conscience;- these methods that affect our fellow-men do not touch the awful foes we have to contend ~O'llinst. 2. Posi,tivdy. (1) Spiritual armour and weapons are needed, i.e. truth, righteousness, the preparation of the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the Word of God, prayer (ve.rs. H-18). (2) These must be obtained from God. They constitute "the wh_ole armour of~•• There is nothing !n the armoury of human resources, physical or mtellecto.al, that 1s adequate for meeting the dread spiritual foes of our warfare. The Christian warn.or must be a man of Divine strength girded about by Divine graces.-W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 6:13–17
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content: -TM wAole annour oj God. L CmusTIANS NEED TO BE ARMED • ..\.ldershot csnnot dispense with Woolwich. The army must be equipped before it can r:J.e the field. 'l'he knight must don his coat of mail and draw his sword if he is to make any use of his martial skill and prowess. So the Church must be prepared for the great oonflict with unbelief, worldliness, and immorality. The individual Christian must be armed to meet temptation and to win a triumph. Many a sanguine young Christian soldier has fallen shamefully through rushing rashly into the fray without <lue preparation. II. THE REQUISITE ARMOUB MUST BE DIVINE. "Annour of God.n l. Provided by God. We cannot forge our own armour. Our own resolutious, like home-made weapons, will be sure to betray some weakness and clumsiness. 'l'he Christian armour consists of God-given graces. The pilgrim had his armour given him at the house "Beautiful." 2. God-like. A steel breastplate is no protection against a poison-cup. The character of our defences must be spiritual and holy, like the character of God, in order that we may be able to withstand great spiritual foes. IIL IT IS l>""ECESSARY TO SECURE A COMPLETE SUIT OF ABMOUB. "The whole armour." We are assailable in every part of our nature. It is w;eless to be only half-armed, for the subtle tempter is sure to aim his dart at the most vulnerable spot. We are all inclined to make much of favourite graces and to fortify ourselves against certain selected sins. "'here we think onn;elves most secure we are likely to be most open to attack. It wili not be sufficient t.o be sound on all points but one. Achilles was said to be n.ilnerable only on the heeL But that was enough. His one weak place was fatal to him. God knows both the variety of foes we harn to face and the ditforent susceptibilities of our own constitution, and has provided complete armour accordingly. IV. THE ClmisnAN ABllOUB IS VA.B.Ious IN x:nm. l. Defensive. (1) We have first to be braced and girded by a firm grasp of the eternal verities of the faith. Looseness uf conviction is a fatal source of weakness. Truth being the girdle we are not to embrace it, but it is to encircle us, i.e. we not to be satisfied with holding the truth, we mw;t let the truth hold w;_ (2) Our heart must be protected by righteousness. An evil conscience, with sin unrepented, unforgiven, and unamended, is fatal to future firmness. (3) We mu6t be active in spreadiug the gospel of peace. (4) Where we have not sufficient resisting power in our own persons let us trust the defending grace of God. Then if the breastplate of righteousness is thin, the shield of faiih held before it may still protect us. (5) Salvation in part secured, in whole promised, will help us to hold our head erect in calm confidence. 2. Offensive. We have not only to stand the shock of the enemy's blows; we have to return them. 'l'ho necessary weapons are supplied from the Divine armoury. (1) The Word of God. This is the sword of the Spirit, because G?<1's Spiri~ in.qJ?ired it an~ now gives _it ed~e and pene_trating JJ"Jwer. Christ used this sword m hlS temptation. Wo resist evil by dwellmg on Divine truth.a. (2) Prayer. In the garden Christ prayecl and l'eter slept; iD the house of Caiaphas Christ was faithful and Peter fell.-W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 6:18–20
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-Trru prayer. The arming and fighting referred to in the previous Yel'Se6are to be accompanied with praying. Prayer is as necessary as action. The part of Moses on the mount was at least as important as that of Joshua on the plaiu, Gun.sider the character and object of true prayer. L THE CHARACTER OF TBUE PRA n:11. 1. Earneatneu. What a ring of vel1e1ncnt OH, VJ. 1-24,) 'l'HE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. 297

intensity sounds through the apostle's words I Here is a man who believes in prayer and is greatly anxious to secure it. It would be wonderful if somo prayers were answered. When the prayer does not affect the heart of the suppliant how can it touch the heart of God? A half-hearted pray1ir can bring no blessing from heaven because it is too feeble even to reach h~aven. 2. Spirituality. We must pray in the Spirit. Our own thoughts must be spiritual and we must seek the inspiration of God's Spirit to give light and life to our praying (Rom. viii. 26). 3, Indep~ of hindering circumstances. "At all seasons." Prayer is always in season. But we are not always inclined to pray. Yet when we least desire to pray prayer is most necessary. 4. Watching, in order that our prayers may be apposite to the occasion, that we may discern the Divine response, and that we may be roused to renewed earnestness in face of the dangers and needs of the times. 6. Earnest prayer will be persevering prayer. It need be so, for God sometimes delays his reply to test our faith, IL THE OBJECTS OF TRUE FB.A.YEB. 1, On behalf of all saints. We should pray for e.11 mankind, but especially for those who are of the household of the faith. Christian brotherhood should be seen in prayer. Mutual prayer is the greatest bond of union in the Church. 2. For any in trouble. St. Paul, the "ambassador in chains," seeks the prayers of his friends. He in Rome can find comfort from the prayers of Christiaus in Asia. It would be well if, instead of condemning our brother when he falls beforo temptation, we would pray for him while he is in it, 3. For the spread, of the gospel, St. Paul is not so anxious that prayer should be offered for the alleviation of his harsh imprisonment and for safe deliverance from the hands of his foes, as for grace to be faithful and bold in his declaration of the mystery of the gospel----a. noble, self-forgetrul request. If the Church at home believed more in the efficacy of prayer and practised it more earnestly, the missionary abroad would be more successful in his work.-W. F. A.

entries.title: EPH 6:24
entries.author: William Garden Blaikie
entries.content:
-The notes of a true (Jhristian. This benediction differs from the beneJ.ictions with which all other Epistles of St. Paul close in one respect, viz. while on every other occasion the second person is used, here the blessing is described in the thinl person. Elsewhere we read," Grace be to you,'' etc. Here and hem only wo rca,\, " Grace be with all them," etc. This variation is in keeping with the catholic charnct('1· of the whole Epistle, which is much concerned with the unity of the Church. It is a rebuke to the narrowness of Christians who care only for the prosperity of their own community, and even labour to win adherents from other Christian denomiuations ('r regard the prosperity of neighbouring congregations with the jealousy of a trauesm3n for a rival shop-keeper. How miserably low, narrow, worldly and unchrist-like is the competitive Christianity of our day I St. Paul prays for a blessing on all true Christians. In doing so he describes the essential character of ~uch men: they "love our Lord Jesl\s Christ in uncorruptness." The question has been so much abused and misunucrstoo,l that it is quite as important to point out what is not requisite RB what is requisite. l. WHAT THINGS .A.RE NOT REQUISITE IN MEN IN ORDEllTHAT THEY MAY BE llECl.A.BDED AS TRUE CHRISTI.ANS. 1. External badges of unity, We need not speak the same shibboleth, practise the same external habits, etc. The test is internal. 2. .Agreement in tl1eologicul opinion. Men may love the Lord Jesus Christ while they differ profoundly on many points of doctrine. 3. Uniformity of ritual. Love may express itself in various voices, from the shouting hallelujahs of a crowd of street revivalists to the elaborate !lnthem of a cathedral choir. If the love is there we have all that is essential. 4. Unity of Church order, Equal lovo for Christ may be found in Churches that observe the greatest variety of discipline. The proud bigotry of orthodoxy will have to be ~reutly humbled when many a des1,ised sectary proves his right to a higher place Ill the marriage feast because he has possessed a warmer love for his Lor<l. Il. WHAT IS BEQUISITE IN ALL PEOPLE WHO ARE TO BE REGARDED AS TRUE CHRISTl.A.NB. To" love our Lord Jesus Christ in uncorruptness." 1. The first essential iH personal attachment to Christ. Our assent to a creed, diligent performance of devotional exercises, and connection with a Church fellowship count just for nothing if we are not in living relation to Christ. What think ye of Jesus? How does your Honl's affection regard him? These a.re the primary questions. 2. This attachment i~ to be one of love. A cold devotion of conscientious but heartless duty will not suffice. Happily, Christ does inspire love in his disciples by his wonderful loveo.bll!ne:;,1 THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS. [CB. VI. 1-24.

his love to them, his great sacrifice of himself. 3.. This love must be uncornipttd. A c..,rrupte.i lo.e is one that is lowered by selfish thoughts. If we only love for whnt we are t.:i receive our love is, of course, worthless. If, therefore, we only turn to Ch1ist in selfish anxiety to be delivered from trouble to secul'e certain benefits, if this be tho secret of our apparent warmth of devotion, the thing is a mockery. They love in uncorruptness who love purely, unreservedly, simply. The idea also implies a 1,ermanence of devotion. It is not a mere passing emotion, stirred, perhaps by a se11tirnental hymn, but a deep, strong affection that outlasts time and persists through nil our varying moods, and shows itself in action, and, when occasion requires, in sacrifioe.-W. I<', A.
